name: Cycle Wars
pitch: You write a tiny program, upload it, and it fights for territory on a shared map forever — and the only resource in the game is how much compute your program is allowed to spend each turn.
coreLoop: Spectate loop (30s): the map ticks every 2 seconds; you watch your bot's last 15 ticks replayed with a per-tick CU trace. You see it blew 11,400 of its 18,000 CU allowance on a pathfind and had no budget left to reinforce a border hex, so it lost the hex. Tinker loop (10-20 min): you rewrite that routine, run it locally against a live map snapshot, watch the Mollusk CU report drop from 11,400 to 6,200, redeploy. Hot-swap takes effect at the next tick boundary — no round reset, no downtime. Territory is the score AND the resource: allowance = 8,000 CU base + 150 CU per controlled hex, capped at 60,000. More land literally makes your bot smarter, which is the whole strategic feedback loop.
whyOnChain: Strong but not absolute — be honest: Screeps proved this genre works on a normal server with a JS sandbox. What on-chain genuinely adds is that the game's central resource IS the SVM compute meter, not an invented number. The 200,000 CU/instruction ceiling, the 1.4M CU/tx cap, and `sol_remaining_compute_units()` are the referee. Players optimize real sBPF against real Anza tooling, and Mollusk's CU benchmarking is simultaneously a dev tool and the in-game scoreboard. Second: every opponent's bot is a deployed program — readable, callable, forkable by anyone, permanently. You can literally CPI into the reigning champion to see what it would do. Third: the ladder is a public good; if the studio dies, anyone can run the crank and the season keeps ticking. That combination does not reproduce off-chain.
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock Ephemeral Rollup for the 2s tick loop (10ms slots, 64KB txs) with the shard's map account delegated for the season
MagicBlock Cranks for the tick timer — no studio server in the loop
`sol_remaining_compute_units()` syscall measured before/after each CPI to enforce per-bot CU allowance; overspend voids that tick's orders and applies a 25% allowance penalty for 30 ticks
CPI depth 4 — engine (depth 1) CPIs each player program (depth 2), leaving bots 2 levels of headroom and no path to reenter the engine
Pinocchio 0.11.2 for the tick/resolve hot path (every CU is literally gameplay budget); Anchor 1.1.2 for the outer season/registry program
Mollusk 0.15 shipped as the player-facing bot benchmarker; LiteSVM 0.15.2 + Surfpool for local map replay against fetched mainnet snapshots
Per-writable-account fee markets: each bot writes only its own order-buffer PDA, so 256 bots never contend; the shared map is written once per tick by the resolve instruction
MagicBlock in-ER VRF (free, <50ms) for resource-node respawn positions and tie-breaks
Kora fee relayer so a player deploys and plays with zero SOL in their wallet
Metaplex Core for season trophy assets (cosmetic, non-yielding)
moneyFlow: In: flat $12/season USDC per bot slot on a public shard, $30/season for a private shard your league controls. No entry-fee-to-prize-pot at launch — prizes are sponsor-funded (infra vendors, RPC providers, and hiring companies will genuinely pay for a Rust-optimization ladder), which keeps consideration+chance+prize from ever assembling and avoids the entire gambling analysis. Rent-exemption deposits (~0.0855 SOL for a 12KB bot program, ~$6.85) are refundable on close and are NOT revenue — say that in the UI. Out: 100% of sponsor pools to top 20 in USDC; studio takes zero rake on prizes. Named sinks: (1) season entry is consumed, not staked; (2) redeploy fee — first 20 hot-swaps per season free, then 0.25 USDC each, which prices bot-spam and is the main variable sink; (3) in-game 'cycles' earned from territory can be spent to temporarily buy allowance above cap, are non-transferable, and decay 5%/day so they can never accumulate into a currency. Operator cost is trivially small: ER txs are 0 SOL base, 0.0001 SOL/commit × 672 hourly commits ≈ 0.067 SOL (~$5.40) per shard-season. NO TOKEN. Ever. If we need a token to make this work, it doesn't work.
firstSession: 0:00-0:30 — Land on a live shard. No wallet, no signup. Full map ticking in real time, 256 bots, hexes flipping color. Click any bot: its source code and its live CU trace open in a side panel. 0:30-1:30 — Hit 'Fork this bot'. Get a `git clone` + `cargo build-sbf` command and a 40-line template (MVP is CLI-first; the browser editor comes later — in-browser Rust→sBPF in 3 weeks is a lie). Run `cycle sim` locally: LiteSVM replays 200 ticks of the real shard against your bot in ~4 seconds and prints a per-function CU table. 1:30-2:30 — `cycle deploy --sandbox`. An embedded Privy wallet is created silently; Kora sponsors the deploy fee, so the player has never seen the word SOL. Bot appears on the free sandbox map within one 2-second tick. 2:30-3:00 — First tick notification: 'Tick 14: your bot requested 22,100 CU against an 8,000 allowance. All orders voided.' That specific, brutal, mechanical failure message is the hook — it is a puzzle statement, and the player immediately knows what to do about it.
viralMechanic: Structural, and it is the same act as playing: every bot is a deployed program with public source, and the only way to beat someone is to read their code. Each bot's page shows a live lineage tree — 'forked from CRAB_v3 · 47 descendants'. When your code gets forked, you get credited permanently and your lineage score rises, so strong players want to be copied. Second driver: any shard is embeddable as a live iframe with a commentary API, so anyone can run a stream, a stats site, or a betting-free prediction overlay without asking us — we do not own the spectator layer, which means we do not have to build or fund it. Third: the ladder is chain-persistent, so a bot you wrote in season 1 is still findable and forkable in season 12, and 'the oldest still-winning bot' is a recurring content story.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks, devnet only. One shard, 64 hexes, 64 bot slots, 2-second ticks in a MagicBlock devnet ER driven by a Crank. One resource, capture-and-hold scoring, allowance = 8,000 + 150/hex capped at 30,000. Engine in Pinocchio; crank batches 16 bots per tx (16 × 30k = 480k CU, well under 1.4M). Deliverables: the engine program, a GitHub bot template, `cycle sim` (LiteSVM) and `cycle deploy` (Kora-sponsored) CLI commands, and a read-only web map with per-tick CU traces. CUTS: browser editor, seasons, prizes, payments, mainnet, L1 settlement beyond a daily commit, the cycles economy, allowance market, mobile, spectator API, private shards. The single question the MVP must answer: do 30 Rust developers voluntarily rewrite their bot a second time?
biggestRisk: The addressable audience is 'people who will write and optimize Rust to play a game', which is realistically five figures worldwide and where roughly half write one bot and never come back — Screeps took nine years to sell a couple hundred thousand copies and it is far more accessible than this. Second, real and technical: CPI-ing arbitrary player-supplied programs is a live security surface. A malicious bot in a 16-bot batch can grief the other 15 by exhausting the shared 1.4M CU tx budget before they execute, and the `sol_remaining_compute_units()` check only detects it after the damage. The clean fix is one bot per transaction, which is safe but multiplies crank cost and tightens the tick budget. Third: MagicBlock's trust model — fraud proofs, data availability, undelegation under validator failure — is not documented publicly. A stalled shard freezes a 28-day season, and there is no published recovery path. That is a blocking question to put to MagicBlock in writing before a paid season, not after.

critique.name: Cycle Wars
technicalBlockers: FATAL AS SPECIFIED: the SVM has no per-CPI compute meter. A CPI that returns Err or exhausts the budget aborts the *entire* transaction — there is no catch, no try/except, no partial rollback. `sol_remaining_compute_units()` can only measure a callee that already returned successfully. So the batched design (16 bots/tx) isn't merely griefable, it's griefable in three lines: one bot does `loop {}` or `return Err` and voids all 16. Your own risk section reaches the only correct construction (one bot per transaction, with the ComputeBudget CU limit set to base+allowance so overspend self-voids) — that is elegant and it works, but it is not an optimization, it is mandatory, and it changes every cost number in the doc.

Cost model collapses under one-bot-per-tx. 256 bots × 1800 ticks/hr = 460,800 ER txs/hr per shard = 128 sustained TPS, ~310M transactions over a 28-day season, all serialized on a single writable map account. That is not a 'public node at 0 SOL base fee'; that is a dedicated MagicBlock node at undisclosed enterprise pricing. The quoted $5.40/shard-season operator cost is wrong by orders of magnitude, and the crank now has to sign and land 128 tx/s for 28 days without a gap.

The tinker loop depends on an unverified vendor behavior. MagicBlock clones programs JIT and their own docs warn that program upgrades do not propagate instantly. 'Hot-swap takes effect at the next tick boundary — no round reset, no downtime' is an assumption about clone-cache invalidation that is not documented anywhere. If the ER serves a stale clone for even a few minutes, your 10–20 minute core loop is broken. Separately, on L1 an upgrade only takes effect at the next slot, and pushing a 12KB program takes ~13 buffer-write transactions before finalize.

Rent is ~2x understated and inverts unit economics. `solana program deploy` defaults programdata to 2× program length: (2×12,288 + 45) × 6,960 lamports = 0.171 SOL ≈ $13.71 at SOL $80 — more than the $12 season fee. Even with `--max-len` pinned exactly it is 0.0855 SOL = $6.85 = 57% of revenue. And Kora relays *fees*, not rent-exemption deposits. Someone funds that, and it only returns if the program is closed, which contradicts 'forkable forever'.

Unmentioned security boundary: never `invoke_signed` into a player program. PDA signer authority extends to the callee for the duration of the CPI, so a malicious bot could sign as your engine PDA. The engine must pass zero signer seeds and zero writable accounts it owns. Reentrancy into the engine is blocked by the runtime (only direct self-recursion is permitted), so that part of your claim holds — but the signer-extension vector does not.

MVP is internally inconsistent. 64 hexes / 64 bots / cap 30,000: the maximum attainable allowance on a 64-hex map is 8,000 + 64×150 = 17,600, so the cap is dead code. Worse, with 64 bots on 64 hexes the median bot holds zero hexes and is pinned at 8,000 CU permanently — of which ~1,000+ is consumed by CPI invoke overhead and account serialization before the bot executes a single instruction of its own logic. The floor allowance needs to exclude engine overhead or it is unusable.

CU is not a stable ruler. CU costs shift with sBPF version, platform-tools, and Agave releases — you have lived through Anchor 1.0→2.0-rc and solana-sdk 3.x→4.1 inside twelve months. Every toolchain bump is an unannounced balance patch that silently invalidates every deployed bot's tuning, and unlike a normal game you cannot hotfix players' code.
economicHoles: The addressable market is measurable and it is tiny. Screeps — same genre, JavaScript instead of Rust, Steam distribution, ten years of runway — sits at 45 concurrent players as of Aug 2026, peaked at 125 CCU in Nov 2023, and moved 200k–500k lifetime copies at $19.99. Cycle Wars demands Rust plus `cargo build-sbf` plus a ~1GB platform-tools install. That funnel is strictly narrower than Screeps'. At full 256-slot occupancy you gross $3,072/shard-season and spend $1,750–$3,500 of it on refundable program rent — negative gross margin before a single dollar of infra.

Runaway leader with no negative feedback. allowance = 8,000 + 150/hex is pure positive feedback: more land → more compute → more land. The 7.5x spread between floor (8,000) and cap (60,000) means a bot that falls behind in week one of a 28-day season cannot mathematically recover. Expect one bot to own the map by day three and 250 paying players to stop opening the tab on day four. Territory games need a catch-up term (diminishing returns per hex, or allowance decay proportional to lead) and there isn't one.

Sponsor-funded prizes are the load-bearing revenue assumption and the comparables all failed. Two Sigma discontinued Halite in 2019. TopCoder's sponsored-tournament model collapsed into enterprise crowdsourcing. MatchboxDAO, who tried to commercialize 0xMonaco as a product, no longer exists. Building the entire prize pool — and therefore the entire competitive reason to play — on a revenue line no comparable property ever sustained is the most fragile assumption in the document.

Sybil collusion is trivially cheap and the game is a territory game. Nothing binds identity to a slot. One strong author buys 40 of 256 slots for $480, runs 39 sacrificial bots that walk their hexes into a single champion, and that champion hits the 60,000 CU cap by tick 200. Per-slot pricing with no attestation in a land-control game is an open invitation; you have Solana Attestation Service listed in your own stack and are not using it.

The 'player never sees the word SOL' story dies on rent. Kora sponsors transaction fees. It does not sponsor a 0.0855–0.171 SOL rent-exemption deposit for a program data account. Either the studio fronts it (and eats the working capital plus SOL price exposure) or the player must acquire SOL, which breaks the onboarding claim that the first-session script is built around.
legalFlags: VRF-decided tie-breaks and VRF resource-node respawn positions inject chance into prize determination. Sponsor funding correctly dissolves the pooled-stakes problem, but consideration ($12 entry) + prize (USDC) + chance (a coin-flip that decides who takes a prize position) still assembles. In material-element states this is precisely the fact pattern to avoid. Fix is free: deterministic tie-breaks (lowest slot index, or hash of bot pubkey) and a deterministic respawn schedule. Do this before the first paid season, not after.

Prize administration: a paid-entry contest with USDC prizes to a global player base is a skill contest/sweepstakes with per-state registration and bonding obligations above certain prize thresholds (NY and FL bonding kicks in above $5,000), plus OFAC screening and 1099/W-8BEN reporting on payouts. Small, but it is real paperwork that the $12/slot revenue cannot fund.

You become a distributor of unaudited executable mainnet code. Every bot is a real deployed Solana program surfaced in a studio-run registry with a 'Fork this bot' button. If a forked 'bot' is a drainer wearing a lineage badge, your UI recommended it and your registry hosted it. You need a scanning/quarantine story and an explicit disclaimer before the fork button ships.
critique.priorArt: Extensive, and it converges on the same answer. Core War (1984) is the direct ancestor — programs competing in a shared arena under an explicit cycle budget, which is literally your central mechanic; 42 years, never escaped hobbyist scale. Screeps (2016) is the modern commercial attempt: 45 concurrent players as of Aug 2026, peak 125 CCU (Nov 2023), 200k–500k lifetime Steam owners at $19.99, and its Screeps: Arena spinoff is effectively dead. MIT Battlecode, Robocode, CodinGame and Two Sigma's Halite (discontinued 2019) round out the off-chain graveyard. On-chain, 0xMonaco (Paradigm CTF 2022) is the near-exact analogue: immutable player-submitted contracts, Elo ladder, and the same 'read your opponent's code' loop — it was beloved, it lasted a weekend, and MatchboxDAO, who tried to productize it, is gone. Solana's own Feb 2026 $100k Agent Hackathon covers adjacent ground. Conclusion: the mechanic is proven fun and proven un-monetizable at consumer pricing.
critique.suggestedFix: Stop selling $12 season slots to individuals and sell the ladder as a B2B benchmark and recruiting product. The genuinely rare, genuinely hard-to-copy asset here is a public, adversarial, independently-verifiable sBPF optimization ranking with permanent provenance — Anza, Helius, Jito, Jump and every Solana infra vendor has a real need to demonstrate CU efficiency, and hiring pipelines pay for verified skill signal that a take-home test cannot provide. Charge $2–5k/quarter for a branded shard plus a verified leaderboard export, make player entry free, and have the studio eat the 0.171 SOL program rent as customer acquisition. That is 10x the revenue per participant, it restores the zero-SOL onboarding story, and it deletes the entry-fee-plus-prize gambling analysis entirely. Then spend the freed engineering time on the two things that actually decide whether it survives: one-bot-per-transaction with CU-limit-as-allowance (mandatory, not optional), and flattening the allowance curve so a snowballing leader does not end the season on day three.

name: Vaultbreak
pitch: A heist is one transaction: you plan it as a hand of cards, hit run, and if any single step fails the whole thing rewinds and everyone can see exactly how you screwed it up.
coreLoop: 30 seconds, end to end. Pick a vault off the board (500 live at any time, each holding 5-500 USDC). You get 3 probes: each is a real instruction that returns one bit — 'balance ≥ 1,000?', 'is guard slot 4 occupied?'. Then you drag instruction cards into a plan strip that shows three live counters you cannot fake: 1,232 bytes / 64 account locks / 1,400,000 CU. Cards are real CPIs — pick_lock(n), cut_power, flash_borrow + flash_repay, swap (a real Jupiter route), stack_alt (an address lookup table card that RAISES your account-lock ceiling — the protocol constraint is the power-up), accomplice (a Jito bundle slot for a second human). Hit RUN. The transaction lands on-chain and each instruction lights green or red in sequence; one red and everything reverts. You paid 0.50 USDC either way, and your failed transaction is now permanently public, which means the next robber can read your plan and the defender can patch against it.
whyOnChain: The strongest of the three, and it is not decoration. The mechanic IS Solana's execution semantics: atomicity (all-or-nothing reversion is the core dramatic beat), the 1,232-byte / 64-lock / 1.4M CU budget as the real puzzle constraint, address lookup tables as a genuine capability upgrade, Jito 5-tx atomic bundles as the co-op mechanic, and permissionless composition — your heist can call a real DEX or a real lending pool that we did not build and cannot revoke. Failed transactions being permanently recorded and readable is a Solana property that becomes a social mechanic: your failures are public intelligence. A Web2 clone would be a puzzle game with invented limits and a make-believe economy; here the limits are the machine's and the money is real. This is composability-as-gameplay in the literal sense.
solanaPrimitives: Atomic transaction semantics as the win/lose condition — partial execution is impossible, and that is the game

1,232-byte tx limit / 64 account locks / 1.4M CU as the explicit, displayed puzzle budget (SIMD-0296's 4,096-byte v1 format is NOT live; do not design around it, but note it would be a future 'bigger briefcase' tier)
Address Lookup Tables surfaced as the `stack_alt` card that expands the account-lock budget
Jito bundles (up to 5 txs, atomic, same slot) as the `accomplice` two-player co-op card with the loot split enforced inside the bundle

MagicBlock Private ERs (TEE-backed) to seal each vault's interior — probes execute inside the PER and return only partial information; 'hot vault' tier runs delegated in an ER with 64KB txs for elaborate multi-step heists, 'cold vault' tier runs on L1 at 1,232 bytes for tight-budget puzzles
Switchboard On-Demand (crate 0.13.0) commit-reveal for the pre-PER MVP vault combination — collateral taken at COMMIT time, never at reveal, per Switchboard's own rule, or losers simply never reveal
Metaplex Core (mpl-core 1.10.0, ~0.0029 SOL/asset) for rare tradeable cards; Bubblegum V2 soulbound compressed assets for the free starter deck so it can never be farmed and dumped
Kora fee relayer + Privy embedded wallet so a first-time player never touches SOL
Helius/Triton DAS API for card inventory reads (hard dependency — budget for it)
USDC only as the unit of account; no game token, and no oracle in the gameplay path
moneyFlow: In: 0.50 USDC per heist attempt, 1.00 USDC to list a vault, and Metaplex Core cosmetic card skins sold in USDC. Out: 0.25 of every attempt goes to the defender as a repel bounty, loot goes to successful robbers from the defender's own deposit. Studio takes 0.10 per attempt and 20% of listing fees; the remaining 0.15 funds an insurance pool that caps maximum single-heist loot so one whale defender cannot be farmed by a searcher. Named sinks: attempt fees are consumed outright (the primary sink and the primary revenue — they scale with engagement, not with new-user inflow, which is the whole failure mode of P2E); single-use consumable cards are burned on play; vault listing fees are consumed. Value enters as USDC from players and exits as USDC to players — it is a zero-sum PvP transfer with a rake, which is exactly why it needs the legal work below and exactly why it does not need a token. NO NATIVE TOKEN. Prizes and loot are USDC, following BattleFrens' no-native-token precedent.
firstSession: 0:00-0:45 — Board loads with no wallet. A live ticker shows other people's heists resolving in real time; each row links to the actual transaction on Solscan. Watching three strangers fail and one succeed in 45 seconds is the entire pitch, delivered without a word of copy. 0:45-1:30 — 'Try the practice vault' (holds 0 USDC). A Privy embedded wallet is created silently; Kora sponsors the fee. You drag three cards; the byte counter turns red at 1,247/1,232; you drop one card; RUN; green, green, green. You have now internalized the core constraint by hitting it, not by reading it. 1:30-2:30 — Real 5 USDC vault. Two free probes reveal a guard that checks 'holder balance ≥ 1,000 USDC'. The card tray highlights flash_borrow — the game teaches the flash-loan concept by making it the obvious answer to a lock. You RUN and it fails: 67 account locks, over the 64 cap. 2:30-3:00 — You add the stack_alt card, RUN, and it succeeds. 5 USDC lands in your wallet and the UI shows your winning transaction signature. That explorer link is the receipt, and the receipt is the hook — it is the one thing a Web2 game structurally cannot hand you.
viralMechanic: Two structural drivers, neither of them marketing. (1) Grudges are built into the ledger: every attempt, successful or failed, is a public transaction, and the defender is notified with a replay link showing exactly which card broke their vault. Defenders re-list specifically to beat the person who got them. Robbers share replays because a clean 4-card heist inside 1,232 bytes is a flex that reads instantly. (2) The `accomplice` card is a Jito bundle, which requires a second signer and encodes the loot split in the bundle itself — the highest-value vaults are gated behind two-player heists that you cannot run alone and cannot run trustlessly with a stranger, so players recruit friends and build crews. Co-op is not a mode we bolted on; it is the atomicity primitive doing social work.
mvpScope: 3-4 weeks, devnet, SCORE-ONLY (no USDC) to defer the legal work while proving the fun. 12 card types, 100 vaults, L1-tier only (1,232 bytes / 64 locks / 1.4M CU), Switchboard commit-reveal for vault combinations with collateral at commit. The plan-strip UI with live real counters and real transaction submission is the entire product — it must be gorgeous and it must show the green/red instruction-by-instruction resolution with drama. Build the failed-tx replay viewer; it is half the retention. CUTS: Private ERs (v2), hot-vault 64KB tier, Jito accomplice bundles, real DeFi CPIs, cosmetics, marketplace, mobile, and all real money. The question the MVP answers: do people run a second heist after their first failure, or does reversion feel like a bug?
biggestRisk: Bots eat the game. A deterministic vault with public state is a solvable optimization problem, and Solana already has a professional class of searchers with staked connections and Jito access who will clear every profitable vault within a slot of it being listed. The human player's experience becomes 'every vault worth robbing is already gone.' Probe budgets, per-wallet rate limits, and sealing interiors in a Private ER all help, but none of them are a proof — and the ER trust model is itself undocumented. If the mitigations fail, the game is an MEV venue with card art. The second risk, close behind: this is real-money PvP with a prize, and while it is deterministic and therefore skill-predominant, information asymmetry gets treated as chance in material-element states, and the 2026 enforcement climate is openly hostile (Louisiana: $100k + 5 years; Oklahoma: felony; Stake.us founders named personally in the LA City Attorney action, with suppliers and geolocation vendors named alongside them). Real money means Skillz-style state geofencing, age verification, responsible-gaming tooling, and $50k-$250k of multi-jurisdiction counsel before the first paid heist. Ship score-only first and let the legal spend be a decision made against real retention data.

critique.name: Vaultbreak
technicalBlockers: The signature tutorial beat is physically impossible. '67 account locks, over the 64 cap' cannot occur: 64 account keys × 32 bytes = 2,048 bytes, already 66% over the 1,232-byte transaction limit before the 64-byte signature, 3-byte header, 32-byte blockhash, or any instruction data. Without an ALT the real ceiling is ~(1,232 − 99 − compact-array overhead)/32 ≈ 33 accounts with *zero* instruction data. You always hit bytes long before locks. Your two on-screen budget meters are not independent and do not trade against each other — and `stack_alt` is not a power-up that raises the lock ceiling, it is the only mechanism by which more than ~33 accounts is possible at all, and it *relieves* the byte meter (1 byte per index) rather than costing against it. The central UI conceit needs re-derivation from first principles before anything else is built.

'Probes return one bit' is theater on public L1 state. Anyone can `getAccountInfo` the vault PDA and read the entire guard configuration for free, instantly, forever. The information asymmetry that makes the game a game requires the Private ER (TEE) — which is explicitly cut from the MVP. So the MVP tests a version of the game that structurally does not contain the mechanic, and cannot answer its own stated question. Meanwhile the PER trust model (fraud proofs, data availability, undelegation under validator failure) is undocumented, and you are proposing to route player USDC through it in v2.

Switchboard commit-reveal for the vault combination has a liveness hole distinct from the economic one. Collateral-at-commit correctly stops losers from declining to reveal for profit — it does not stop an unrevealed vault from being a stuck vault holding robbers' accumulated attempt fees. You need a timeout-and-slash path and a defined disposition of fees paid into a vault that never resolves.

Fee arithmetic on the real-DeFi cards works against small vaults. A single Jupiter route routinely costs 100–300k CU; a 4-card heist with flash_borrow + swap + flash_repay lands at 400–800k CU. Priority fee scales with the CU limit you *request*, not what you consume (SIMD-0096), so on any contested vault the fee to attempt a 5 USDC vault exceeds the loot. Your low-tier vaults are unplayable the moment the game has competition.

Jito bundles and ephemeral rollups are mutually exclusive as specified. Bundles are an L1 leader-auction mechanism. Delegated ER accounts are not writable from L1, and the ER runs its own sequencer with no Jito auction. 'Hot vault tier runs delegated in an ER' and 'accomplice = a Jito bundle slot' cannot both be true for the same vault. The co-op mechanic and the elaborate-heist tier are on different layers and you have to pick.
economicHoles: Professional searchers clear the board within one slot of every listing, permanently. Documented 2026 behavior: searcher bots execute at minimum profit thresholds around 3,000 lamports (~$0.0004) and pay Jito tips of 50–60% of expected profit. A 500 USDC vault therefore justifies a ~250–300 USDC tip. A human paying a 5,000-lamport base fee loses that auction 100% of the time, on every profitable vault, forever. You are publishing a deterministic, public-state, positive-EV extraction opportunity with a queue, to an industry that already runs colocated bare metal on sub-5ms Geyser streams. Per-wallet probe budgets and rate limits do not help: wallets are free and Kora sponsors their fees for you.

The rational defender equilibrium is a risk-free fee farm, and it kills the game from the supply side. Guard configs are public. A defender publishes a vault whose guards are provably unsatisfiable inside 1,232 bytes / 64 locks, deposits the 5 USDC minimum, and collects 0.25 USDC per failed attempt indefinitely at zero risk. Your insurance pool capping maximum single-heist loot makes this strictly *better* for the defender (bounded downside, unbounded fee income). Robber EV goes negative, robbers leave, and there is nothing to rob.

The rake is 2–5x what PvP grinders tolerate. 0.25 of every 0.50 attempt fee (50%) leaves the player pool — 0.10 studio plus 0.15 insurance, and insurance only returns in the tail. Poker rake is ~5%; sportsbook hold is 5–10%. A player running 100 attempts burns 25 USDC in pure vig before any loot moves. Anyone who plays for a week computes this and posts it.

Wash-heisting costs 0.25 USDC per cycle and needs two wallets. List a vault, rob it yourself: 0.50 out, 0.25 back to yourself as defender, loot round-trips. Net 0.25 to manufacture 'this vault is crackable' bait, a leaderboard position, and fake replay content that funnels real robbers into a rigged vault. No identity layer is proposed.

Revenue requires engagement no crypto game has ever demonstrated. At $0.10/attempt, $1M/yr needs 10M attempts = 27,400/day = roughly 1,000 DAU each completing 27 real-money heists per day, sustained. For calibration: Photo Finish LIVE, the best-documented Solana game economy in existence, did $23M in cumulative horse sales over multiple years and still did not clear $100M revenue in 2025. You are underwriting a 30-second real-money loop against retention curves that do not exist in this category.
legalFlags: All three gambling elements are present, by your own design. Consideration = 0.50 USDC per attempt. Prize = USDC loot. Chance = a Switchboard commit-reveal randomized vault combination. The doc's defense ('deterministic and therefore skill-predominant') is contradicted by the randomness primitive listed two bullets above it. Either the vault combination is deterministic and public — in which case searchers solve everything and the game is dead for a different reason — or it is random and this is gambling in dominant-factor states, not just material-element ones.

The rake structure is independently disqualifying in several states regardless of skill. 2026 practitioner guidance is explicit: where both contestants fund the prize and the operator deducts a percentage of pooled entries, states read the operator as raking wagers, selling pools, or acting as a paid custodian of stakes — offenses that do not care whether the underlying game is pure skill. Vaultbreak is a textbook instance: the defender funds the pot, the robber pays consideration, and the studio takes 20% of every entry plus 20% of listing fees.

Custody and money transmission, which the $50k–$250k counsel budget does not cover. Holding player USDC in escrow, netting robber-versus-defender flows, and paying out is money transmission unless the architecture is genuinely non-custodial. A PDA escrow where the studio retains program upgrade authority will be read as control. FinCEN registration plus meaningful state MTL coverage is $1M+ and 18–36 months — an order of magnitude past the budgeted figure, and it is the line item that decides whether the company exists.

The DeFi cards add a second regulatory surface. Routing player funds through a live Jupiter route and a real lending pool as a game mechanic is arranging financial transactions for retail users, layering broker/adviser and consumer-protection exposure on top of the gaming analysis, in a product whose target user does not know what a flash loan is.

Distribution is closed. Apple and Google real-money gaming policies require per-jurisdiction licensure, so mobile app stores are unavailable. The Solana dApp Store becomes your only channel — which specifically forfeits the single strongest 2026 distribution tailwind (Seeker, SMS opening to all Android OEMs, 1,561 apps at 0% fee).

The 2026 enforcement climate is actively hostile and it names suppliers, not just operators: MA AG action against Kalshi, Nevada action against Kalshi, NY S5935 banning dual-currency sweepstakes outright (Dec 5), and the LA City Attorney action naming Stake.us founders personally alongside their suppliers and geolocation vendors. Your oracle provider, your RPC provider and your fee relayer are all in that blast radius with you.
critique.priorArt: Fomo3D (2018) is the canonical and near-exact precedent: a public, deterministic, real-money on-chain game whose grand prize was taken by a bot that spammed high-gas transactions to congest the chain and lock every human out. That is your searcher problem, already run to completion, eight years ago, and it is the single most-cited cautionary tale in the genre. HEISTED launched on Solana on 2026-07-16 as a co-op heist sim gated behind holding 5,000 $HEISTED — different mechanic, same theme, and it is a memecoin funnel rather than a game economy. 0xMonaco (Paradigm CTF 2022) proved the 'your opponent's transaction is public intelligence' loop is genuinely fun as a weekend event. Hats Finance's gamified vaults and DEFCON 27's Chain Heist are the security-CTF instantiations and both work — because neither has a rake or an adversarial fee market. The broader pattern is unambiguous: 'put money in a public contract and dare people to take it' has a 100% historical record of being solved by professionals within hours of listing.
critique.suggestedFix: Delete the money permanently — not 'defer it to v2', delete it — and sell the constraint instead. The one thing a Web2 game structurally cannot hand a player is a real transaction signature, and that receipt is worth exactly as much with 0 USDC at stake as with 500. Convert every vault into a fixed, authored, deterministic puzzle with a global first-solver leaderboard and permanent on-chain proof-of-solve (the Curta / Advent-of-Code model, which has a live audience of exactly your target user), charge a flat $15 season pass for the puzzle set plus Metaplex Core cosmetics, and let the ALT/byte/CU budget be the entire game. In one move this deletes the searcher problem (nothing to extract), the defender fee-farm equilibrium (no defenders), the chance element, the 50% rake, the custody question, the MTL question, the app-store block and the $250k of counsel — while preserving 100% of the first-session script that is the strongest writing in this document. If the puzzle version cannot hold players, the money version was never going to either; it would just have taken $250k and eighteen months to find out.

name: Wild Type
pitch: Write 128 bytes of DNA, drop it into a shared pond, and never touch it again — then watch a thousand generations decide whether your idea was any good.
coreLoop: 30-second spectate loop: open the pond viewer, your lineage's biomass line has moved since yesterday. Zoom into one cell, diff its genome against the one you released — six mutations have accumulated. Hit 'trace ancestry' and find the exact generation where a single flipped bit turned your grazer into something that waits at light gradients. 10-minute authoring loop: open the editor, write 64 instructions from a 12-opcode VM (SENSE, MOVE, EAT, SPLIT, STORE, JMP, and friends), run it against a local snapshot, release it for a 0.02 SOL refundable spawn permit. Then you have zero further agency — that is the design. You are not playing a creature, you are proposing a hypothesis and the pond adjudicates it over 17,280 ticks a day. Fixed physics: each 1 MiB pond holds 4,096 organisms at 256 bytes each, emits exactly 500,000 joules per tick on a light gradient, and burns 1% of standing energy per tick as metabolism. Carrying capacity is therefore a constant, independent of how many players show up — the economy literally cannot inflate.
whyOnChain: Weakest of the three, and I am going to say so plainly rather than dress it up. You could build this on one server for a fraction of the cost, and it would run better. What being on-chain actually buys, honestly: (1) the world outlives the studio — the tick is a MagicBlock Crank and the rules are a program, so if we stop paying, anyone can run the crank and the ponds keep evolving; that is a real property for something whose entire pitch is permanence. (2) Determinism plus public state plus hourly L1 commits means any claim about what evolved is independently replayable in LiteSVM by a skeptic, which is the whole point of a scientific toy — 'trust our server logs' would be fatal. (3) Authorship and priority are settled by slot number, so who first evolved a self-replicator is a fact, not a forum argument. That is a real but modest list. This should be built as a Web2-quality toy that happens to be on-chain, and if the on-chain part ever makes it worse, cut it.
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock Cranks driving a 5-second tick with no studio server in the loop — the mechanism by which the world survives us

MagicBlock ER for the tick itself: ~20 txs per pond-tick, each processing ~2,000 organisms at ~500 CU each (~1M CU, under the 1.4M cap); all writes hit one pond account, which is fine in the ER's single sequencer and would be fatal on L1 against the 12M CU per-writable-account cap
Hourly L1 commits (0.0001 SOL each) as public, replayable checkpoints anyone can fork with LiteSVM 0.15.2
MagicBlock in-ER VRF (free, <50ms) for mutation — one bit flip per 1,000 bytes copied, verifiably random rather than 'trust us'

1 MiB pond accounts (~7.3 SOL rent-exemption deposit, fully refundable) — anyone can fund a pond and set its physics constants from a bounded parameter space, making pond creation the player-extensibility layer
Pinocchio 0.11.2 for the VM interpreter — the CU cost of one opcode directly sets how many organisms a pond can hold, so CU optimization is world-building
Solana Attestation Service for lineage authorship attestation (who released a genome first, provably)
Kora + Privy so a spawn permit costs a card payment and never requires the player to acquire SOL
NO token, NO NFTs, NO tradeable assets — deliberately
moneyFlow: In: a $6 one-time lab license (entitlement, not an asset, not resellable), 0.02 SOL refundable spawn permits that exist to rate-limit genome-flooding rather than to make money, and $40/month pond sponsorship for a club or lab that wants to name a pond and tune its physics. Out: nothing. Zero. No player ever extracts value, which means no gambling analysis, no money-transmission exposure, no securities analysis, and no ponzi arithmetic — this sits at Tier 0 of the legal risk stack by construction. Sinks are trivial because there is no economy to sink: the lab license is consumed, sponsorships are consumed, spawn deposits are recoverable and are explicitly labelled as deposits in the UI. Be honest about the size: 3,000 paying users at $6 plus 40 sponsored ponds is roughly $200k/year. That is a sustainable one-or-two-person project and a bad venture case, and pretending otherwise is how the 93% got built.
firstSession: 0:00-0:40 — Land directly in a live pond viewer, no wallet, no account. 4,096 organisms moving on a light gradient, a biomass chart with six colored lineage bands, and a 'most successful mutation in the last hour' callout. Click a cell: its 128-byte genome renders as 64 readable instructions with the mutated bytes highlighted red. 0:40-1:40 — 'Remix this genome'. The editor opens with that organism's DNA and a local simulator; you change one SENSE target and hit Simulate. 400 generations run in about three seconds in-browser and the chart says your variant dies out at generation 90. You change it back, alter something else, and it survives. 1:40-2:30 — 'Release'. A Privy wallet appears silently, the $6 license is a card payment, Kora covers the fee, and the 0.02 SOL permit is shown as a refundable deposit with the refund button visible immediately. Your organism enters the pond within one 5-second tick, tagged with your name, and you can watch it. 2:30-3:00 — You get an opt-in for one notification type only: 'your lineage crossed 1% biomass' or 'your lineage went extinct'. Both are compelling. Then you close the tab, and the pond keeps running without you, which is the actual product.
viralMechanic: Genealogy, and it is the game mechanic rather than a growth hack. Every organism carries an immutable ancestor chain, so when someone remixes your genome — which is the primary authoring flow, because remixing something that already works is far easier than writing from scratch — you are credited on every descendant's page forever, at every generation, permanently. Strong authors want to be copied because their lineage count is the real leaderboard. Layered on top: the two notification events, extinction and biomass milestones, are both intrinsically screenshot-shaped, and 'my thing that I made survived a week of evolution without me' is a boast that needs no explanation to a non-crypto audience. Pond sponsorship makes the second-order community: a Discord, a university class, or a streamer funds a pond with custom physics and recruits people to seed it, and we do not run any of it.
mvpScope: 2-3 weeks, devnet. One 1 MiB pond, 4,096 organisms, 12 opcodes, 5-second ticks via a MagicBlock Crank in an ER. Herbivores only — NO ATTACK opcode in v1, so competition is purely for light, which halves the tuning problem and removes every PvP-value question. Web viewer with zoom, a live biomass chart, a genome inspector with mutation highlighting, an ancestry tracer, and an in-browser editor with a local simulator (LiteSVM compiled to WASM). Daily L1 commits, not hourly. CUTS: multiple ponds, player-created ponds, physics mods, ATTACK and all predation, payments, spawn permits, mobile, attestations, notifications. The MVP question is narrow and answerable: after 72 hours of unattended ticking, has anything interesting and unplanned happened, and can a stranger see that it happened without us narrating it?
biggestRisk: The physics collapse into monoculture. Evolution sims fail in a well-known way: within days one degenerate hyper-replicator dominates every pond, diversity goes to zero, and the biomass chart becomes a single flat band forever. Tuning light gradients, metabolism curves, mutation rates, and opcode costs so that the system stays interesting for months is genuine research, not sprint work, and Tierra and Avida both took academic careers rather than sprints to get there. If it collapses, there is no content patch that saves it — the whole product is 'unattended emergence', and a monoculture is the visible proof there is none. The second risk compounds it: the audience for a genome-authoring toy is genuinely tiny, plausibly low tens of thousands of people worldwide, and unlike the other two concepts there is no real-money hook to subsidize a slow burn. Third and most honest: the crypto here is load-bearing for permanence and verifiability but not for fun, so if the fun does not land, no amount of on-chain purity rescues it — and the correct response to that outcome is to ship it as a $6 web toy and stop paying for the ER.

critique.name: Wild Type
technicalBlockers: The in-browser simulator is the largest hidden cost in the doc and it is unbudgeted. The first-session script depends on '400 generations in about three seconds in-browser' via 'LiteSVM compiled to WASM'. LiteSVM's npm package is a Node build over native bindings, not a WASM target, and the SVM's sBPF execution path is not something you drop into a browser. You are actually committing to write a second, independent implementation of your VM in TypeScript or Rust-to-WASM — which then has to stay bit-identical to the on-chain Pinocchio interpreter forever, or the local sim lies to the player and the authoring loop is worthless. Budget this as its own workstream, not a line item in a 2–3 week MVP.

The CU budget for the VM is 3–5x optimistic. 500 CU for 64 interpreted opcodes = 7.8 CU/opcode. A realistic interpreter dispatch — PC bounds check, opcode fetch, jump table, operand fetch, memory bounds check, execute, advance — is 15–40 sBPF instructions and therefore 15–40 CU per interpreted opcode, before SENSE (a neighborhood scan) or SPLIT (a 256-byte memcpy plus mutation). Budget 2,000–4,000 CU/organism. 4,096 organisms = 8–16M CU per tick = 6–12 transactions of 1.4M each every 5 seconds. Survivable in an ER, but it means pond capacity is inversely proportional to VM expressiveness: adding ATTACK in v2 roughly halves organism count, and organism count is the thing that determines whether evolution is interesting.

Two arithmetic errors in the spec as written. (1) '20 txs per pond-tick, each processing ~2,000 organisms' = 40,000 organism-slots for a 4,096-organism pond — a 10x overcount; the correct figure at your own CU assumption is 2–3 txs, and at realistic CU it is 6–12. (2) 4,096 × 256 bytes = 1,048,576 bytes = exactly 1 MiB, leaving zero bytes for the account discriminator, the light-gradient state, energy totals, the tick counter, the RNG state, or the physics constants. Neither is hard to fix; both indicate the numbers weren't checked, which matters more in a design whose entire pitch is fixed, verifiable physics.

Hourly L1 commits of a fully-dirty 1 MiB account are unaffordable. Every organism moves every tick, so the entire 1 MiB is dirty at every commit. Pushing 1 MiB back to L1 through 1,232-byte transactions is ~900–1,000 transactions; at 5,000 lamports/signature that is ~0.0045–0.005 SOL ≈ $0.36–0.40 per commit in base fees alone, before priority fees or MagicBlock's own 0.0001 SOL/commit. 24 commits/day = ~$9/day = ~$3,200/yr per pond, against $480/yr of sponsorship revenue. Every sponsored pond loses ~$2,700/yr. Daily commits (~$130/yr) are the only affordable cadence — which is what the MVP already specifies, so strike 'hourly' from the pitch and the primitives list.

The permanence claim — the concept's *only* stated justification for being on-chain — rests on the one thing your own research marks UNVERIFIED. 'If we stop paying, anyone can run the crank and the ponds keep evolving' is true only if the state lives on L1 and the tick is an L1 program. It doesn't and it isn't: the pond is delegated into a MagicBlock ER, and MagicBlock's fraud-proof, data-availability, and undelegation-under-validator-failure story is explicitly undocumented. If MagicBlock stops running the ER, your pond may be frozen in a delegated state with no published recovery path. Every other on-chain justification in the doc (replayability, authorship priority) is downstream of the state actually being reachable.
economicHoles: The revenue projection is off by roughly 5x and the model is one-time rather than recurring. 3,000 licenses × $6 = $18,000, *once*. 40 ponds × $40/mo = $19,200/yr. Steady state is ~$19–25k/yr, not $200k. Reaching $200k/yr on a one-time $6 license requires ~30,000 new paying users every single year — more than the entire TAM the doc itself estimates ('low tens of thousands worldwide'). Year two revenue is the sponsorship line and nothing else. This is a $20k/yr side project, which is a fine thing to be, but the doc's own honesty section undersells how honest it needs to be.

Pond rent is a balance-sheet item, not a rounding error. (1,048,576 + 128) × 6,960 = 7.298 SOL ≈ $584/pond at SOL $80. Forty sponsored ponds locks 292 SOL ≈ $23,360 of working capital to earn $19,200/yr, with unhedged SOL price exposure on the principal. If SOL halves while ponds are open, the refundable deposit is worth half when you close them.

Spawn permits denominated in SOL are a support burden and an own goal. A '0.02 SOL refundable deposit' is ~$1.60 today and plausibly $0.80 or $3.20 by the time anyone clicks refund. A product whose entire brand is 'no token, no NFTs, no financialization' should not hand every user a small unhedged SOL position as their first interaction. Denominate the permit in USDC or make it a non-refundable $2 fee and drop the deposit framing entirely.

LTV is $6 and there is no second purchase. By design the player has zero agency after release, and the two notification hooks (extinction, 1% biomass) fire once or twice per lineage. There is no subscription, no consumable, no reason to buy anything again. Every dollar of growth requires a new human, from a TAM you estimate at low tens of thousands.

Worth stating plainly because it is genuinely rare: there is no bot exploit. Nothing here is extractable, so 'who bots this on day one' has a boring answer — nobody, because there is no payout. The only adversarial vector is genome flooding, and a rate-limited permit handles it. Of the three concepts this is the only one where the adversarial analysis comes back clean, and that is a real asset.
legalFlags: Essentially none, and that is this concept's strongest property — it sits at Tier 0 by construction, exactly as the doc claims. Two things to keep clean rather than fix: (1) the 0.02 SOL spawn deposit is custody of customer crypto if it ever routes through a studio-controlled wallet; keep it in a program PDA the depositor can unilaterally close, with a permissionless refund path, and the money-transmission question never opens. (2) Keep the $6 lab license as a non-resellable, non-yielding entitlement with the 'not an asset, not resellable' language in the ToS, and never ship a marketplace, a transfer path, or a 'rare genome' tier — the moment a genome becomes tradeable, the entire clean legal posture inverts and you are in securities and consumer-protection territory that the $20k/yr revenue cannot defend.
critique.priorArt: Direct, deep, and mostly discouraging. Tierra (Ray, 1991) and Avida (Ofria/Wilke) are the ancestors: free, open-source, 25–35 years mature, and they run orders of magnitude faster on a laptop than any on-chain pond will. Tierra's documented failure mode is precisely the risk you name — after an initial burst of parasites and hyperparasites it stagnates, and the literature on 'Tierra's missing neutrality' and open-ended evolution exists specifically because it did not achieve open-endedness. Avida needed a multi-decade academic program with NSF funding to produce interesting results; it is not a sprint problem, and your biggestRisk section is correct to say so. On-chain: Cellula tokenized a Conway-derived 'on-chain life evolution' game with a vPOW mechanism, and CELA went from a $0.1039 ATH (Nov 2024) to roughly $0.0000091 by Jan 2026 — a ~99.99% drawdown. Spore.fun ran TEE-secured autonomously-breeding on-chain agents and produced an ALIFE 2025 conference paper rather than a business. Consumer-side, The Bibites and Lenia command far larger free audiences than any paid a-life product has ever converted. The pattern: this genre reliably produces a paper, a YouTube audience, or a token collapse. It has not yet produced a business — which is a reason to build it cheaply, not a reason not to build it.
critique.suggestedFix: Cut the ephemeral rollup and the 1 MiB pond-as-account entirely, and ship the identical product as a free desktop/web toy with an optional $6 'publish to the shared pond' upgrade — where the shared pond is a single L1 program, ticked by a permissionless crank at 60s, holding only lineage roots, genome hashes, and authorship timestamps rather than the full organism array. This makes the permanence claim actually true (no vendor, no delegation, no frozen-state risk, anyone really can run the crank), removes $584/pond of locked rent and the SOL exposure on it, removes the 1 MiB commit problem completely, and removes the WASM-LiteSVM dependency — because the local simulator is now just your own VM in TypeScript, which you have to write anyway. The on-chain layer is then doing only the two jobs it is uniquely good at: timestamped authorship priority and a tick nobody can switch off. Spend the entire saved budget and schedule on the physics-tuning problem, because that is the only variable that decides whether this is interesting, and treat it as a six-month research task with an explicit kill criterion (e.g. 'Shannon diversity across lineages stays above X after 30 days unattended') rather than a three-week sprint.

name: Ghostline
pitch: A 45-second time-trial racer where you can challenge anyone's lap for money, and the track itself decides who won — no referee, no server, no argument.
coreLoop: Pick a track. Drive a 40-50 second lap in a top-down drift racer with one car and three inputs (steer, throttle, handbrake). Your rival's ghost car drives the line beside you in real time and a split bar at the top reads +0.14 / -0.09 against them, updating every corner. You cross the line, see the delta, and hit retry — which is instant and costs nothing. The entire dopamine loop is shaving 0.08 seconds off a corner you have now driven 40 times. Sessions are 20-60 laps long. Input runs at 60Hz with client-side prediction and rollback against the ephemeral rollup, so it feels like a 50ms-ping racing server, which is to say: it feels normal.
whyOnChain: Three things break in Web2. (1) Peer-to-peer stakes: I want to post "beat my 41.203 on Track 7, 0.1 SOL on it" as a link that anyone on earth can accept, with adjudication that neither of us controls. In Web2 that requires me to be a licensed money handler with a payments stack, and the loser has to trust my server's replay validator. Here the physics sim IS the settlement program — the escrow PDA re-simulates the challenger's input log on L1 and pays out. (2) Leaderboard integrity you don't have to take on faith: anyone can re-run the 2,700-tick input log through the same deterministic program and confirm the time. Trackmania validates replays server-side too, so this is a trust delta, not a capability delta — but it is exactly the trust delta that makes the stakes work. (3) The prize pool cannot be rugged by us because we never custody it. If you strip the stakes out, this is a good free racing game with no business model — and I would say that out loud rather than pretend otherwise.
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock ephemeral rollup for the 60Hz authoritative sim (~10ms slots, 0 SOL base fee per ER tx, 0.0003 SOL per session at undelegation)
MagicBlock Session Keys — one signature buys 60 minutes of driving, zero wallet popups mid-lap
Magic Router — practice laps route to the ER, challenge settlement routes to L1 automatically based on delegation state

Pinocchio 0.11.2 for the fixed-point physics crate (i16.16, no floats, no sqrt outside a lookup table) — target under 500 CU per tick so a full 45s lap re-sims in ~1.08M CU, inside the 1.4M CU per-transaction ceiling in a single L1 verification tx
Mollusk 0.15.0 in CI to fail the build if a physics change pushes per-tick CU over budget — CU regression is literally cost regression here
Kora fee relayer (shipped Apr 2026) so players never hold SOL and can pay in USDC
Openfort or Privy embedded wallet — silent creation from a social login
Metaplex Core (mpl-core 1.10.0, ~0.0029 SOL/asset) for cosmetic liveries and horns
Solana Attestation Service for one-human-per-ranked-account on the paid ladder
@solana/kit 7.1.1 + Codama-generated TS client
Deliberately NO VRF anywhere — zero randomness in the game is a legal design decision, not an oversight (see biggestRisk)
moneyFlow: Value enters three ways: (a) challenge stakes escrowed in SOL or USDC, (b) cosmetic purchases in USDC, (c) daily open-track entry fees. Value exits only to winners of challenges and tournaments. The team earns a 5% rake on challenge escrow (0.1 SOL vs 0.1 SOL pays the winner 0.19) and an 8% rake on the daily 0.05-SOL open track that pays the top 10% of the field. Sinks: the rake itself, cosmetic mints (pure burn — no resale value promised, though Core assets are transferable), and a 1% cut of rake routed to the community creator of the track you raced on, which is a real sink because it moves value out of the prize economy and into content supply. No native token, ever — the game is priced in USDC, stakes are in SOL or USDC, and there is nothing to emit. Per-player infrastructure cost is genuinely trivial: a 40-lap practice session is one ER session (0.0003 SOL) plus a handful of commits at 0.0001 SOL each, i.e. under four cents.
firstSession: 0:00 Player taps a friend's challenge link on ghostline.gg. No wallet prompt, no signup, no install. Track 3 loads with a ~900KB wasm build of the same Rust physics crate the on-chain program uses. 0:15 First lap, running purely locally, nothing touches a chain. They finish in 51.4s against a rival ghost that ran 41.2 and beat them to the line by half a screen. 1:00 Laps 2 through 4, free instant retries, down to 46.8. The split bar is doing all the work; there is no menu, no shop, no currency visible anywhere. 2:00 Prompt: "Put it on the board?" One Google login creates an Openfort embedded wallet in about six seconds; Kora sponsors the fee so the balance is zero SOL and nobody cares; one signature issues a 60-minute session key. 2:20 Lap 5 now runs ER-authoritative at 60Hz — the player cannot tell the difference, which is the point — and posts 45.9, landing at rank 4,102 on Track 3. 3:00 Two buttons: accept the 0.1 SOL challenge (requires funding, most people don't yet) or post your own free challenge to a friend (most people do). Funding is deliberately pushed past the three-minute mark.
viralMechanic: The challenge IS the invite, and it is asymmetric in the right direction: posting one costs the sender nothing and the recipient can drive the track before they ever create a wallet. "Beat my 41.203" is a taunt with a scoreboard attached, and taunts propagate. More importantly, asynchronous ghost racing has no matchmaking liquidity problem — the single most common death of small PvP games. A player at 4am with eleven other people online still has 4,000 ghosts to race, so the game is never empty, so early word-of-mouth doesn't hit a dead lobby and die. Secondary loop: community track creators earn 1% of rake on their tracks, so they promote their own tracks unprompted.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks: one Rust crate implementing fixed-point 2D car physics, compiled twice (Solana program via Pinocchio, wasm for the browser client). Three hand-built tracks. One car, no tuning. ER integration with session keys and the Magic Router. Ghost record/playback and the split bar — this is the whole game feel and gets the most polish time. Challenge escrow program with L1 re-simulation as the dispute path. Embedded wallet plus Kora. LiteSVM tests, Surfpool for local. Devnet/USDC-testnet money only; a real-money switch, geofence and legal review are explicitly out of the MVP. Cut: mobile build, track editor, cosmetics, tournaments, DAS indexing, any leaderboard beyond a single Postgres mirror of committed times.
biggestRisk: Skill-wagering law, and it is not close. Challenge stakes are consideration plus prize; we have removed chance entirely (deterministic sim, no VRF, no loot) which is the strongest possible position, but material-element states still exist, Florida bars wagering on skill games by statute, and Louisiana/Oklahoma-style 2026 statutes reach suppliers and geolocation vendors, not just operators. The Skillz-model compliance stack — per-state geofence, age/ID verification, responsible-gaming tooling, a real multi-state opinion at $50k-$250k — is a precondition for revenue, not a later chore. Second risk, smaller but real: cross-compiling one deterministic fixed-point sim to both wasm and sBPF and keeping them bit-identical forever is unglamorous, unending work, and a single divergence invalidates every escrow settlement. Third: with the wager turned off, there is no business.

critique.name: Ghostline
technicalBlockers: The headline CU claim is internally inconsistent and the architecture derived from it is wrong. 45s @ 60Hz = 2,700 ticks. "Under 500 CU/tick" = 1.35M CU, not the stated 1.08M (1.08M implies 400 CU/tick). 1.35M leaves 50,000 CU — 3.6% — for program load, account deserialization, reading the input log into heap, escrow bookkeeping and payout. That is not a budget, it is a rounding error.

Worse, the 200,000 CU **per-instruction** cap was ignored. Even at a fantasy 500 CU/tick you can run at most 400 ticks per instruction, so a lap needs ≥7 instructions, and 1.4M/200k = 7 is the hard ceiling of instructions-worth-of-CU in one tx. There is zero headroom left for the settlement logic. At a realistic 1,500–2,500 CU/tick for a fixed-point tick containing heading integration (sin/cos LUT + lerp), a lateral-slip tire model, handbrake state machine, track-boundary collision against even a coarse polyline, and checkpoint tests, a lap is 4.0M–6.75M CU = **3–5 transactions of 7 instructions each**. Settlement becomes a non-atomic multi-tx state machine with a persistent intermediate sim-state account, not "a single L1 verification tx". 400 CU is roughly 400 sBPF instructions total; that buys you Euler integration and nothing else.

The input log does not fit in a transaction. Even bit-packed to 1 byte/tick, 2,700 bytes > the 1,232-byte L1 tx limit. At 3 bytes/tick it is 8,100 bytes = ~9 upload txs. Rent-exemption on an 8,228-byte account = 8,228 × 6,960 = 57.3M lamports = **0.0573 SOL ≈ $4.58 at $80/SOL — 57% of the 0.1 SOL wager it is escrowing.** Delta/RLE encoding gets a real lap to maybe 200–400 bytes (0.0023–0.0037 SOL) and rescues this, but that compression scheme is now load-bearing on settlement correctness and is not in the design.

The verifiability story is circular. If the ER is authoritative at 60Hz, the L1 re-sim is theatre. If you do not trust the ER (and MagicBlock's fraud-proof / DA / validator-failure model is explicitly undocumented — the landscape flags this as a blocking question), then every settled lap needs the full multi-tx L1 re-sim, and you have re-invented an optimistic rollup with a 5–7 tx challenge path and no dispute window design.

Program-version skew is a silent fund-loss bug specific to this architecture. Programs are **cloned, not delegated** into the ER; upgrades do not propagate atomically. During any upgrade window the ER runs physics vN while the L1 escrow verifier runs vN+1. Every in-flight challenge then settles to a different winner than the one the players watched. There is no mention of pinning a physics version hash into the escrow PDA at challenge creation, which is the mandatory fix.
economicHoles: **Adverse selection makes the challenge model a one-directional money pump against the poster.** The poster's time is public and fixed; the acceptor's ability is private. A shark with a 39.8 PB only ever accepts "beat my 41.203" challenges they will win. Rational acceptors accept ~100% of +EV challenges and ~0% of −EV ones, so the expected return to posting a challenge is strictly negative for everyone except the current world-record holder. This is not a tuning problem; it is the structure. 1v1Me ran exactly this model, did millions in payouts, and **shut wagering down on 2024-11-01, stating that only the top few percent of players could consistently win** — then pivoted to staking pro players instead.

**A deterministic physics sim with a public wasm build is an offline optimal-control problem, and this is the fatal one.** Three inputs, 2,700 ticks, a bit-exact simulator shipped to every player. Anyone can run CMA-ES / MCTS / gradient-free search against the exact physics crate overnight and produce a tick-perfect input log that beats every human on every track by 1–3 seconds. The chain verifies that the log produces the time — it cannot verify a human produced the log. The property that makes Ghostline trustless ("the physics IS the settlement program") is the same property that makes it perfectly TAS-able, and there is no on-chain fix. Trackmania is the exact precedent and Nadeo's answer was a **client-side Competition Patch that records anti-injection metadata** — i.e. exactly the trusted server-side anti-cheat this design claims to have eliminated. Day one, one person with a laptop drains every open challenge.

Input-entropy heuristics (jitter, sub-tick human noise, reaction-time distributions) are the only defense, they are statistical, they are run off-chain by you, and the moment you run them you are the referee — which deletes the entire "no referee, no argument" pitch and every reason the game is on Solana.

Rake math is thin against the compliance bill. 5% of a 0.1 vs 0.1 SOL challenge = 0.01 SOL ≈ $0.80. $1M/yr gross requires ~1.25M settled challenges = **~3,400 settled money challenges every single day, forever**, from a player base that must be simultaneously large enough to sustain that and naive enough to keep posting into adverse selection.

Track-creator 1% of rake is described as a sink but is a subsidy for creating tracks. It will be farmed: create a track, self-challenge across two wallets, wash the rake back to yourself minus the 4% house cut — profitable the moment your creator share exceeds the spread, and trivially sybil-able through gasless embedded wallets.
legalFlags: Player-vs-player staking with a house rake is the operator posture, not the platform posture. Removing chance is the strongest available position but it does not clear the material-element states, and the 2026 record is worse, not better, than the design assumes: **the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled on 2026-06-15 that skill games are illegal gambling devices under state law**; Tennessee refuses skill claims outright; Maryland, Louisiana and New York have issued cease-and-desists against unlicensed skill/sweepstakes operators; roughly 12 states restrict cash skill gaming. Per-state geofencing, age/ID verification, responsible-gaming tooling and a multi-state opinion are a precondition to revenue, correctly identified — but so is the fact that a 5% rake on P2P stakes is closer to bookmaking than to Skillz's tournament structure in several of those states.

The daily 0.05-SOL open track paying the top 10% is a **paid-entry prize contest** — a separate and in several states more heavily regulated animal than 1v1 staking, requiring AMOE consideration in sweepstakes states and hitting contest-registration/bonding thresholds (NY, FL, RI) once prize pools cross statutory limits.

**Your chosen wallet vendor will refuse you.** Privy was acquired by Stripe in June 2025; Stripe's prohibited-business list covers gambling and skill-based wagering absent explicit written approval. Openfort, Kora relayers and any fiat on-ramp partner will run the same diligence. Plan for crypto-only funding and no card on-ramp, which deletes the frictionless "Google login, six seconds" funnel exactly at the moment money enters.

Escrow re-simulation makes the smart contract the adjudicator of a wager, which in several jurisdictions makes the program itself the gambling device and the deployer the operator. 2026 enforcement is naming founders personally.
Zero-chance design does not exempt you from UIGEA-adjacent payment exposure, because UIGEA's predicate is state law, and the material-element states supply it.
critique.priorArt: Directly and repeatedly tried. **1v1Me** (P2P cash wagering on 1v1 video game matches, thousands of users, millions in payouts) killed its wagering product on 2024-11-01 with the explicit post-mortem that only the top few percent could consistently win — the exact adverse-selection failure predicted here — and pivoted to staking pro players. **Skillz** is the compliance blueprint and is a public-market cautionary tale about the cost of that stack. On Solana specifically: **MixMob 'Racer 1'** (race-to-earn plus wagering on other players' matches) and **RaceFi** (Solana racing with PvE practice, PvP tournaments and 'dedicated betting') both shipped this thesis and are both effectively gone. **Trackmania** is the strongest precedent and the most damaging one: 100Hz fully deterministic physics with built-in replay validation, and Nadeo still had to ship a client-side Competition Patch recording anti-injection metadata before Campaign leaderboards were trustworthy; TMInterface and TMTAS Exchange exist precisely because deterministic input logs are trivially machine-optimized, and donadigo's TMX Replay Investigation documents the leaderboard fraud that followed. Nobody has shipped deterministic-replay P2P wagering, and the reason is not that nobody thought of it.
critique.suggestedFix: Kill the 1v1 challenge as the money product and accept that you need anti-cheat. Replace it with a **fixed-entry daily pool on a track whose geometry is revealed at pool open and closed 24h later**, split into two segregated divisions: an open/TAS division (bots welcome, prize is glory or a tiny purse — this makes optimizer players your content, not your predator) and an attested Human division gated by Solana Attestation Service one-human-per-account plus a client-side input-provenance attestation, where you publicly own the fact that you run a statistical input-entropy check server-side. Pool entry removes adverse selection (everyone pays the same price against the same field with no ability to select opponents), a same-day track reveal caps offline optimization time, and rake on a pool is a contest fee rather than a P2P bookmaking spread — which is also the easier legal posture. Then spend the first six months shipping the free game and the split bar, because that part is genuinely good and is the only part you can validate before the $50k–$250k legal spend.

name: Blindside
pitch: A five-minute arena brawl where you fight over supply drops by secretly bidding your own stamina — and stamina is the only thing keeping you alive.
coreLoop: Twenty players, one top-down arena, five minutes, twin-stick movement with a dash on a 0.9s cooldown. Energy is a single 0-100 bar that regenerates at 8/sec; dashing costs 25, taking a hit costs 15. Every 6 seconds a supply crate lands somewhere contested. Any player standing inside its 8-metre radius when a 3-second clock expires submits a sealed bid: 0-100% of their current energy, on a slider, while still moving and still being shot at. Highest bid takes the crate and pays the second-highest bid (Vickrey) out of their energy. Losing bidders pay nothing. On resolution the arena reveals only the winner and the clearing price — so the whole lobby learns "someone was willing to spend 62" without learning who. That is the game: you just won a shotgun and you have 18 energy for the next six seconds, everyone watching knows it, and the crate landed 8 metres from a guy who bid nothing. It is a real-time auction where money is the ability to run away.
whyOnChain: The honest version first: a trusted Web2 server does sealed bids and fog of war perfectly well, and if this game never touches real money, crypto adds a distribution channel and an aesthetic, not a capability. What the chain adds is specifically this — a MagicBlock Private ER (TEE-backed) means the bids are hidden from the opponent AND from us. That stops mattering never, because the instant a third party wants to run a stake tournament on top of our matches, "trust the studio not to sell the bid stream" is the whole ballgame. The second, harder argument is about the primitive: naive on-chain sealed bidding uses commit-reveal, which is fatal here twice over — a 3-second window cannot fit a reveal round trip, and losers simply never reveal (Switchboard's own docs say take collateral at commit time for exactly this reason). The Private ER deletes the reveal step. That is the mechanic being enabled by the infrastructure rather than decorated by it, and it is genuinely new in 2026.
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock Private ERs (TEE-backed region, mainnet + devnet) — holds sealed bids and per-player fog-of-war state; the enclave is the auctioneer
MagicBlock ephemeral rollup at ~10ms slots for the 30Hz movement/combat tick; 64KB ER transactions mean a full 20-player match state commit fits in one tx without ALT gymnastics
MagicBlock Cranks for the 6-second crate timer, the 3-second bid clock, and end-of-match rollover — time-based on-chain automation instead of a bot we have to babysit
MagicBlock Session Keys — sign once at queue time, play the whole match

Per-match state sharding: one ~8KB MatchAccount plus 20 PlayerAccounts per match, all delegated together, so we never build a global hot account and never touch the 12M CU per-writable-account per-block L1 ceiling
Match accounts are closed on settle to reclaim the rent-exemption deposit — rent is a refundable deposit, and 10,000 matches a day of leaked deposits is a real number
MagicBlock VRF in-ER (free, <50ms) used ONLY for cosmetic spawn variety; crate loot tables are deterministic from a seed published before the lobby opens, so the match itself contains zero chance
Bubblegum V2 (mpl-bubblegum 5.1.0) soulbound compressed NFTs for achievements — ~$500 per million assets vs $15-30k for regular accounts
Metaplex Core for tradeable equipped skins
Anchor 1.1.2 (@anchor-lang/core — note the rename; @coral-xyz/anchor is frozen legacy) with LiteSVM as the default test template
moneyFlow: Value enters exclusively as USDC for cosmetics: a $6 seasonal pass and one-off skin purchases. Value exits nowhere — cosmetics are non-cashable by default and ranked play is free. The team earns the full margin on cosmetic sales; there is no rake because there is no wagering in the base product. Sinks: the pass and skin purchases are terminal burns, and the seasonal soulbound achievement drops are deliberately non-transferable so they cannot become a secondary market that turns cosmetics into an asset class with holders to appease. No native token — the research record on that is unambiguous (95% average drawdown, 97% of 2025 gaming token launches underperformed) and there is nothing this design needs a token for. If entry-fee tournaments are ever added, they run on the chance-free property built in from day one: deterministic loot seed, no VRF in outcomes, skill-predominant, geofenced.
firstSession: 0:00 Web client, one button, "Play". No wallet, no account, no download. 0:20 Tutorial match against 7 bots. Movement and dash teach themselves in ten seconds; the first crate lands and the game stops for exactly one beat to show the bid slider and the 3-second clock. 1:00 The player bids 80 of their 94 energy, wins a shotgun, and is immediately dashed into by a bot they cannot outrun on 14 energy. They die holding the best weapon in the match. This is the entire design lesson delivered in one four-second beat, and it is the moment they either get it or leave. 2:00 Second bot match. This time they bid 22, lose the crate, and win the fight against the guy who spent 70 to get it. 2:30 "Queue for a real lobby?" A Privy embedded wallet is created silently from an email or social login, Kora covers fees so no SOL is ever required, one signature issues a session key, and they enter an 8-player queue. 3:00 Live match starts with real humans, who are much worse at bidding than the bots and much better at ambushing.
viralMechanic: Pacts and betrayal. Two players standing together when a crate lands can form a pact by holding a button for 1 second — the pact splits the crate's effect at half strength each, and either player can renege at the moment of resolution and take the whole thing while the other's bid still clears. The betrayal is the shareable artifact, and it always has a victim who will tell people about it. Structurally, the sharper hook is the dead-player spectator view: eliminated players see the full arena with every bid amount and every identity revealed, so they are the only ones who know a betrayal happened, and they are sitting there with a clip button. Beyond that, lobbies are 20 players and private lobbies reserve 4 free slots to anyone the host invites — a game that needs bodies gives players an explicit reason to bring bodies.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks: 8 players not 20, one arena, three crate types (shotgun, shield, speed), 3-minute matches. Movement, dash, bid slider, Vickrey resolution in the Private ER, cranked timers. Bots good enough for the tutorial and to backfill an empty queue — non-negotiable, because a 20-player synchronous game with 6 players online is a dead game and bots are the only bridge. Cut: ranked, seasons, cosmetics, pacts, the achievement NFTs, the spectator view, mobile. Ship the loop and find out in week five whether losing a fight because you overbid is exhilarating or just annoying, because the entire concept rests on that single feeling.
biggestRisk: The Private ER trust model is explicitly undocumented — no public answer on fraud proofs, data availability, or what happens to hidden state and in-flight matches when the ER validator goes down. Our core mechanic lives entirely inside that box. This is a blocking question for MagicBlock before a single line of the auction code is written, and if the answer is "trust the sequencer," the honest positioning of this game changes from "provably fair" to "fast, with a nice enclave story." Second risk, equally lethal and more likely: 20-player synchronous matchmaking. Small PvP games die of empty lobbies, not of bad design, and no amount of ER latency wizardry fixes a 40-second queue. Third: the mechanic may simply not be fun. Economic decisions under a 3-second clock could read as stressful rather than tense, and I would not know until people play it.

critique.name: Blindside
technicalBlockers: **The control scheme cannot execute the core mechanic.** Twin-stick movement plus dash commits both thumbs (or both hands on KBM). There is no free input for a continuous 0–100% slider under a 3-second clock "while still moving and still being shot at." The only implementable version is a small set of discrete bid buttons (d-pad / number keys), which converts a continuous auction into a 3–5 point lattice — and a lattice auction has mass ties at the top bid and makes shilling trivially precise. This is not a polish problem; the pitch's central sentence is not physically inputtable.

**The Private ER's performance envelope is unpublished, and the entire tick loop lives inside it.** "~10ms slots" is documented for ordinary ERs. PERs run inside Intel TDX enclaves; memory-encryption and enclave I/O overheads are real and MagicBlock publishes no PER slot time, throughput, or concurrency numbers. You are betting a 30Hz twin-stick shooter on an undocumented number. Every latency claim in the design is inherited from a different product.

The trust model is undocumented in exactly the place it matters. Fraud proofs, DA, and what happens to hidden state and in-flight matches when the PER validator dies are not in public docs. The design correctly flags this — but then builds the game's only defensible feature on top of it.
