If the answer is "trust the sequencer," the honest claim collapses from "provably fair" to "we promise we didn't look," which is precisely what a Web2 server already offers for free.

The primitive list contains a factual error that would burn a sprint: "64KB ER transactions mean a full 20-player match state commit fits in one tx." The 64KB limit applies only to transactions where **all writable accounts are delegated**, i.e. transactions executing inside the ER. A commit to L1 is an L1 transaction and inherits the 1,232-byte limit; large-account commits are chunked. Budget the commit path as multiple L1 txs at 0.0001 SOL each, not one.

Delegation latency is not in the session flow. Delegating 21 accounts (MatchAccount + 20 PlayerAccounts) requires L1 confirmation before the match can start — 21 × 32-byte pubkeys is 672 bytes of a 1,232-byte tx before instruction data, so you need an ALT, and you eat a 350ms–1s+ L1 round trip at queue-pop and again at settle. On top of a 20-player queue wait.

Compute is genuinely fine and should be stated as such: 20 players at ~1,500 CU each plus spatial-hash broadphase and projectiles is ~50k CU/tick, comfortably inside the 200k per-instruction cap, ~1.5M CU/s per match. Concurrency per node is the unknown, not per-tick cost.
economicHoles: **The TEE protects information the HUD publishes one tick later.** You reveal winner + clearing price. The winner's energy bar then visibly drops by exactly the clearing price. Everyone standing inside an 8-metre radius is on screen. With the typical 2–3 contested bidders, revealing the clearing price plus the winner de-anonymizes the second-highest bidder by subtraction. The hidden-information surface the Private ER exists to protect is therefore: the losing bids of the fourth-and-beyond bidder in a crowded scramble. That is not worth an undocumented TEE dependency. Fixing it (hide the clearing price, or hide energy bars) either removes the mechanic's legibility or removes the reason for the TEE.

**Vickrey plus free losing plus free accounts equals shill bidding, which is why Vickrey is rare outside ad auctions where the auctioneer controls entry.** Losing bidders pay nothing, so entering a bid is a costless option. A second account — created by social login, gasless via Kora, zero SOL required, zero marginal cost — stands in the crate radius and bids just under the expected winner, converting your enemy's second price into a first price. Collusion also runs the other way: partner bids 1 so the clearing price collapses. The literature is explicit that shill vulnerability and bidder collusion are the reasons the format failed to spread; a free-entry 20-player lobby is the most shill-friendly environment imaginable.

**The design does not say what happens when you die, and the auction breaks under either answer.** If death is elimination, this is a 5-minute battle royale where most players are spectating dead — the precise problem Crashout in this same portfolio was invented to solve. If death respawns you at full energy, then dying is the cheapest way to refill your bidding currency, so the correct strategy is to bid 100 whenever you are about to die anyway, and a player with zero shadow price on energy wins every contested crate. Energy-as-both-life-and-money only works if losing life is expensive, and that is unspecified.

Energy arithmetic is tight in a way that makes big bids nearly unplayable. Regen 8/s with crates every 6s = 48 energy of sustainable spend per crate cycle. A dash costs 25 on a 0.9s cooldown = up to ~27.5/s of spend against 8/s of regen — combat outruns regen 3.4x before any bidding. So the interesting bids (62, 80) are only available to players who have not fought for ~8 seconds, meaning the auction systematically rewards passivity in a twin-stick brawler. That is an anti-fun gradient baked into the numbers.

**Cosmetic-only revenue requires an audience no crypto game has ever had.** A $6 seasonal pass at a generous 3–5% conversion needs ~3.3M–5.5M players to clear $1M/yr. The best-performing Solana game economics on record (Photo Finish LIVE) still did not reach the $100M-revenue tier; Star Atlas SAGE runs ~750 DAU. There is no wagering, no token, and no rake — so the business model is 'be a top-100 F2P game', while the only crypto-specific feature is invisible to players.

**20-player synchronous matchmaking is the most likely cause of death and the design knows it.** Sustaining sub-20s queues needs ~20 in-pool at all times and realistically ~60 CCU per pool; split across 3 regions × 2 skill brackets = 6 pools = ~360 CCU, which at a typical 3–5% CCU/DAU is **7,000–12,000 DAU minimum just to have a working queue.** Bot backfill is proposed, but a 20-player lobby that is 14 bots is a well-trodden road to churn.
legalFlags: Genuinely light, and this is the design's real strength. Cosmetics-for-USDC with no cashout, no token, no emissions, soulbound achievements, and deterministic loot from a pre-published seed is a clean posture. Consumer-protection and disclosure rules apply, nothing more.

One live exposure: Metaplex Core skins are transferable and will have a secondary market. Keep every path from gameplay performance to a tradeable asset severed, or the cosmetics become a prize and you re-import the entire sweepstakes analysis you correctly avoided.

If entry-fee tournaments are ever added, the chance-free property is necessary but not sufficient — see the Pennsylvania Supreme Court's 2026-06-15 skill-games ruling and the 2026 state cease-and-desist wave. Treat it as a separate licensed product, never a toggle.

The design's own honest framing — 'a trusted Web2 server does sealed bids and fog of war perfectly well' — is also the regulator's framing, and it is the correct one. Not a risk, just a reminder that the chain is buying you nothing legally here.
critique.priorArt: No direct prior art for real-time sealed-bid auctions in an action game, and that absence is informative rather than encouraging: bidding is a beloved board-game mechanic (Ra, Modern Art, Cosmic Encounter) and is universally turn-based, because a sealed bid is a considered decision and real-time controls are a reflex channel — the two compete for the same hands and the same attention. **Dark Forest** is the canonical on-chain hidden-information game (zkSNARK fog of war), was critically celebrated, and never sustained a meaningful player base; it is the closest analogue for 'the cryptography is the point and players do not care.' MagicBlock's TEE-secured ERs were announced as a Solana industry-first with the Private Payments API shipping March 2026, and as of 2026-08-20 there is **no shipped hidden-information game on PERs** — you would be the first production user of an undocumented trust model. For the F2P-crypto-arena-with-cosmetics-only outcome, Blast Royale (shut June 2025) and Mojo Melee (shut July 2025) are the comparables, and Mojo Melee's studio said crypto itself made the game too big and complex to build.
critique.suggestedFix: Delete the TEE and the Vickrey auction, and keep the tension. Replace the continuous sealed slider with a **simultaneous discrete commit — three buttons: 20 / 45 / 80 energy — resolved first-price, highest bid wins and pays their own bid, ties split the crate**. Discrete buttons are inputtable with a thumb already on a stick. First-price removes the shill exploit entirely (a shill who overbids now wins and pays, which is punishment, not leverage) and removes the reveal problem, because the winner paying their own bid is exactly what the energy bar already shows — so a plain ER, or frankly a plain Web2 server, is sufficient and you stop being MagicBlock's first PER guinea pig. Then answer the death question explicitly and make respawn cost energy, so bidding currency and survival stay genuinely coupled. Ship the 8-player version with bots and find out in week five whether overbidding-then-dying is exhilarating or annoying — because that single feeling is the whole product, it costs nothing to test, and none of the crypto is needed to test it.

name: Crashout
pitch: A sixty-player physics knockout where getting eliminated is the second half of the game — you become the crowd, and the crowd has money on the survivors.
coreLoop: Sixty players spawn on a floating platform. Twin-stick movement plus one dash-charge on a 0.9s cooldown; momentum is real, mass is real, and shoving someone at the right angle sends them off the edge. Every 25 seconds the platform shrinks. Matches end in about three minutes. The moment you are eliminated — median survival is roughly 45 seconds, meaning most players spend most of the match dead — you drop instantly into a spectator camera with a live parimutuel board on the surviving field. You hold 1,000 match-scoped Chips and can back survivors continuously; odds are time-decayed, so backing someone while 40 players remain pays far more than backing the last two. Odds re-price every ER tick, which is only a meaningful sentence at 10ms slots. Chips settle at match end into ladder points and cosmetic currency. The design claim: the standard battle royale wastes 90% of player-minutes on a death screen, and this converts them into the highest-arousal minutes in the match.
whyOnChain: Honestly: with non-cashable Chips, close to nothing — this is a Web2 physics game with a wallet, and I will not dress it up. The crypto content is the option value. A live, continuously-priced market on an in-progress match, settled without an operator holding anyone's money, is a thing Web2 cannot ship without a sportsbook licence, a payments stack, and per-jurisdiction banking. On Solana it is a program. The research record is blunt about this: the only categories in crypto with genuine retention are markets and gambling ($51B on-chain gambling volume in 2025, prediction markets at $44.8B notional in a single month, zero games in Solana's $100M+ revenue club). This design takes that finding seriously and builds the market first, with a good physics game attached to it, rather than building a game and bolting a token on. The secondary real add: the market's settlement and the match's physics are the same verifiable record, so "the house rigged it" is checkable rather than deniable — which the research identifies as an actual product feature for money games (Zeebit's whole pitch).
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock ephemeral rollup for the 30Hz physics tick — likely a dedicated node, because 60 rigid bodies with a spatial hash broadphase runs roughly 60-120k CU per tick and 30Hz of that is a real, sustained load we should not put on a public node
Quadrant-sharded physics accounts (4 delegated PhysicsAccounts + 60 PlayerAccounts per match) so writes parallelize instead of serializing behind one global world account
MagicBlock Ephemeral SPL Tokens for the in-match Chip market — SPL transfers at ER speed are what makes tick-level odds re-pricing possible at all
MagicBlock Cranks for the 25-second platform-shrink timer and match settlement
Magic Actions to trigger base-layer payouts while match accounts are still delegated, so settlement does not have to wait on undelegation
MagicBlock Session Keys + Kora fee relayer — a spectator who has never held SOL can place a bet with one tap

ZK Compression (Light Protocol) for per-player ladder records and match history — compressed accounts at ~1000x less than standard accounts is the difference between a viable and a non-viable ladder at millions of matches

Helius DAS API and a Yellowstone-compatible stream for the spectator/odds feed; budget this as a five-figure annual line item, and validate LaserStream's Yellowstone compatibility yourself rather than assuming it
Metaplex Core skins, Bubblegum V2 for mass seasonal drops
Solana Mobile dApp Store as the launch channel — 1,561 apps, 0% platform fee, and the only mobile storefront where the crypto does not have to be hidden
moneyFlow: Default (non-money) configuration: value enters as USDC for an $8 seasonal pass and cosmetic skins; Chips are match-scoped, non-cashable, and reset every match, so nothing exits. The team earns cosmetic margin. Sinks: pass and skin burns, plus a Chip burn to enter high-table lobbies, which is the important one — it gives Chips a use that destroys them and keeps the ladder from inflating into meaninglessness. Real-money configuration (a separate, licensed, geofenced product, not a toggle): parimutuel pools in USDC with a 6% rake taken from the pool at settlement, plus the existing cosmetic revenue. Value enters as bettor deposits, exits as winning payouts, and the rake is the business. There is no native token in either configuration and no emissions of any kind — every unit of value paid out came from a unit of value paid in during the same three-minute match, which is the only structure in this space that has never collapsed.
firstSession: 0:00 A friend sends "I'm in, back me" — a link that opens a live match in the browser with no wallet, no install, no account. You are watching 23 ragdolls shove each other off a shrinking hexagon and it is immediately legible; nobody needs the rules explained. You are handed 1,000 spectator Chips on arrival. 0:20 You put 400 on your friend at 11:1. He survives a shrink and your board goes green, which produces an entirely disproportionate amount of shouting. 1:20 He gets dashed off the edge by someone with better timing. Your Chips die with him. 1:40 "Next match starts in 12 seconds — play or watch?" You tap play; a Privy embedded wallet is created from an Apple login in seconds, Kora sponsors the fee, one signature issues a session key. 2:00 You are in a 20-player match. 2:40 You get shoved off at the 40-second mark, having accomplished nothing. 2:41 You are back on the market with a fresh 1,000 Chips and 19 people to bet on, and you do not close the tab. That 2:40-to-2:41 transition is the entire product.
viralMechanic: Backing someone pings them mid-match: a small marker over your head reading "3 backing you." Survivors feel watched, which makes them play to the crowd, which produces the moments the crowd came for. But the structural mechanic is the entry point — a spectator can join a live match through a link with zero install, zero wallet, and zero skill, and be emotionally invested inside twenty seconds. Every other game in this genre requires a competent player before it requires an audience; this one lets you arrive as an audience and get converted into a player by the third match. And because the median player is dead for most of the match, the game manufactures a permanent supply of bored, invested people whose only available action is to pull their friends into the lobby to bet alongside them.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks with an experienced netcode engineer; 8 weeks without one, and I would say so up front. Twenty players not sixty. One arena, one shrink schedule, 2.5-minute matches. Deterministic fixed-point rigid-body physics with client-side prediction and rollback — this is the hard, unavoidable core, and the concept has no fallback if it feels mushy. The parimutuel board with fake Chips, non-cashable, settled to a local ladder. Web client only. Cut: sixty players, real money, cosmetics, seasons, mobile, ZK-compressed ladder (Postgres is fine at MVP scale), the DAS/streaming layer, and every legal workstream. The single question the MVP answers is whether betting on strangers you just lost to is compelling with worthless chips. If it is not compelling for free, real money will not fix it, it will only add liability.
biggestRisk: Two, and they point in opposite directions. If Chips stay non-cashable, this may simply be a Web2 game with a wallet and no reason to be on Solana at all — I would rather state that than defend it. If Chips become cashable, it is a real-money gambling product with real-money gambling law: the outcome depends on collision physics with meaningful chaotic variance, so the skill-predominance argument that saves a deterministic time trial is much weaker here, US sweepstakes-style structures are being criminalized state by state through 2026 (Oklahoma felony, Louisiana $100k plus five years, New York Class E felony), an offshore Curaçao CGA licence at $50-200k confers no right to serve US or UK players, and 2026 enforcement is naming founders personally. The third risk is technical and immediate: 60-body deterministic physics at 30Hz across an ER, with rollback netcode that stays convincing, is unproven at that body count and is the kind of problem that eats a quarter.

critique.name: Crashout
technicalBlockers: **60-body deterministic rigid-body physics with rollback netcode is not a 2–4 week task with a good engineer; it is a multi-quarter research problem, and no shipped game does it.** GGPO-class rollback is proven at 2–8 players because rollback cost scales with bodies × rollback depth: at the design's own 120k CU/tick, an 8-frame rollback is ~1M CU of re-simulation per correction, up to 30 times a second, per client. Fall Guys — the direct 60-player physics-knockout reference — is server-authoritative with client interpolation and no rollback, and is famously loose on contact resolution for exactly this reason. The MVP scope is misbudgeted by roughly an order of magnitude, and the concept has no fallback if contact feels mushy.

**Concurrency per ER node is the real ceiling and it is small.** All 4 quadrant accounts plus 60 player accounts are written every tick, so every tick transaction for a match conflicts with every other — a match executes strictly serially. At 120k CU/tick × 30Hz that is **3.6M CU/s of serialized execution per match**. A single SVM node sustaining a generous 50M CU/s supports **~14 concurrent matches ≈ 840 concurrent players**, and the design already concedes it needs a dedicated node (custom enterprise pricing). So the '0 SOL base fee, gameplay is effectively free' economics that make MagicBlock attractive do not apply to this game; you have converted a variable cost into an unpriced fixed cost, and horizontal scaling is a per-node enterprise contract, not an autoscaler.

**Commit fees are the hidden operating cost and they collide head-on with the non-money configuration.** Bets held only in the ER are lost if the ER dies, and the ER's failure model is undocumented — so a money product must commit bets to L1. At 0.0001 SOL/commit and a 3-minute match, committing every 5s = 36 commits = 0.0036 SOL ≈ $0.29/match; every 1s = 180 commits ≈ **$1.44/match**. At 10,000 matches/day that is **$1.1M–$5.3M/yr in commit fees alone**, against which the default configuration earns exactly zero variable revenue (an $8 seasonal pass and skins). You either pay this against nothing, or you skip it and hold player money in a box whose failure semantics nobody has published.

Rent working capital is real but survivable: a 128-byte player account is (128+128) × 6,960 = 1.78M lamports = 0.00178 SOL; ×60 = 0.107 SOL, plus four 4KB physics accounts at 0.0294 SOL each = 0.118 SOL, so **~0.225 SOL ≈ $18 of refundable deposit locked per live match**. At 500 concurrent matches that is ~112 SOL ≈ $9,000 of studio-fronted float, and any settlement path that fails to close accounts leaks it permanently. Design the close path as the first thing you write, not the last.

The odds engine is a second hot account inside the same serialized match. 'Odds re-price every ER tick' means ~100 writes/s to the market account by a crank, plus every Ephemeral SPL Token transfer, all serializing behind the physics ticks they share a match with. The betting layer roughly doubles your per-match CU load, which halves the concurrency number above.
economicHoles: **Bettors are participants, and time-decayed odds pay maximum on early death. This is a collusion machine, not a game with a collusion risk.** Two accounts: A suicides at t=0 into the exact moment the payout curve is steepest, backs B at 11:1, and B plays to survive. In the money configuration it is worse — A backs C, then still-alive B suicides into C's threats. Every regulated market bans in-play betting by participants for precisely this reason, and this design makes participation the *entry requirement* for betting. The payout curve is literally steepest at the instant a colluder chooses to die.

**Free chips are an infinite faucet plumbed directly into transferable assets.** Every eliminated player receives 1,000 fresh chips every match, chips settle into cosmetic currency, and cosmetics are Metaplex Core — transferable, secondary-market-tradeable. So chips are cashable, and the 'non-cashable Chips' claim in the money-flow section is false as designed. A bot joins via social login (Kora sponsors fees, zero SOL required, zero marginal cost per account), suicides at t=0, and runs a script that reads ER state and backs whoever has the best position/health. It farms chips → cosmetic currency → tradeable NFTs → USDC, at whatever rate you can spin up wallets. **The primitives list has no Solana Attestation Service and no sybil defense of any kind** — it was listed for Ghostline and omitted here, which is exactly backwards, since Ghostline gates on skill and this gates on nothing.

The design's own honest admission is the correct verdict on the default configuration: with non-cashable chips this is a Web2 physics game with a wallet, carrying a dedicated-ER bill and a $1M+/yr commit-fee exposure against cosmetic-only revenue. The crypto is pure cost until the chips become real, and the moment they become real the legal section below activates.

Parimutuel pools on 60 anonymous strangers in a 3-minute chaotic physics match have no information edge to reward and near-zero liquidity per market — 40 bettors × a few hundred dollars is a thin pool where a single whale moves the odds enough to make everyone else's price bad. Prediction markets work at $44.8B notional because participants have views; nobody has a view on ragdoll #37.

The '1,000 free Chips per match' faucet also destroys the ladder it feeds. High-table chip burn is the only sink, and it is a burn against an unbounded, per-match, per-account faucet. Ladder points inflate to meaninglessness within weeks unless the faucet is per-human rather than per-account, which requires the attestation layer that isn't there.
legalFlags: **The 'safe' default configuration is a dual-currency sweepstakes casino under 2026 law — which is the single most aggressively criminalized structure in US gambling this year.** Free chips → cosmetic currency → transferable Core assets is a virtual currency redeemable for things of value. **Oklahoma SB 1589 (enacted May 2026 over a veto override, effective 2026-11-01) attaches felony penalties to dual-currency casino play. Louisiana's regime carries felony charges and large fines reaching operators, promoters and payment processors, with enforcement from 2026-08-01 — today.** The New York AG has moved against 26 sweepstakes platforms using virtual coins exchangeable for cash or prizes. Approximately 8 states have outright bans in force in 2026 and the list is growing. The design believes it has a compliant default and a risky upgrade path; it actually has two illegal configurations.

The money configuration is unlicensed in-play sports/esports betting on events the operator itself produces and whose outcome its own software determines — self-dealing plus in-play plus participant-bettors is roughly the three things every regulated book is built to prevent. A Curaçao CGA licence at $50–200k confers no right to serve US or UK players, and 2026 enforcement is naming founders personally.

The skill-predominance defense that partly protects a deterministic time trial is unavailable here and the design says so: chaotic collision physics with meaningful variance is chance in the eyes of a material-element state, and under the 2026-06-15 Pennsylvania Supreme Court skill-games ruling, even a strong skill argument is not reliably a defense.

Betting on the outcome of matches you also play in raises match-fixing exposure independent of gambling licensure — in several jurisdictions facilitating manipulated betting outcomes is its own offense, and the collusion vector above is not theoretical, it is the dominant strategy.

IP surface worth ten minutes of counsel time: US7740539B2, 'Multi-person games for parimutuel betting on live events,' covers real-time parimutuel wagering on in-progress live events by large numbers of internet participants. Likely expired given its early-2000s priority, but confirm before building the odds engine.
critique.priorArt: The exact mechanic already exists, works, and is deliberately kept non-cashable by the only operator with the scale to know: **Twitch Predictions** is a free parimutuel market on live in-progress gameplay with time-limited windows, run at enormous scale, and Twitch keeps channel points strictly non-redeemable precisely to stay outside gambling law. That is the strongest evidence both that the mechanic is fun and that the cashable version is the part nobody has been able to ship legally. On the game side the graveyard is direct: **Blast Royale** (mobile crypto battle royale, NFT collection, shut to players 2025-06-30 after 'exploring every path and possibility', code open-sourced) and **OpenSeason** (Fortnite-style crypto BR on Epic Games Store, now offline, studio out of funding, token cratered) — both crypto battle royales, both dead in 2025, neither killed by physics. In-play battle-royale betting with fluid late-circle odds is already a live product at Rollbit, Stake and every crypto esports book, licensed and geofenced. **Zed Run** is the closest working model and is instructive by contrast: spectators bet on chance-based races they cannot enter, which is exactly the participant/bettor separation Crashout removes.
critique.suggestedFix: Sever the bettor from the participant and make chips terminal. Concretely: chips are minted per match, spendable only on that match, and expire worthless — no cosmetic currency, no ladder points, no conversion path to any transferable asset, ever; and a player eliminated from match N may bet only on matches they are not in, which in practice means the market runs on a *separate* live match feed rather than the one you just died in. That kills the collusion vector, kills the sybil faucet, and kills the dual-currency sweepstakes analysis in one change — at the price of admitting that the money layer is a licensed product for a later company, not a toggle. Then build the actual asset you have discovered, which is real and which nobody in this space owns: **the zero-install, zero-wallet spectator link that turns a bystander into an invested viewer in twenty seconds and a player by the third match.** That funnel is worth more than the betting is, it is legal everywhere, and it is testable next month with 20 players, fake chips and a Postgres ladder. If backing strangers you just lost to is not compelling for free, real money will not fix it — it will only add a felony statute in Oklahoma.

name: Split or Bust
pitch: Six friends, one shared pot, and each of you secretly writes down how much of it you want — if everyone's greed adds up to more than the pot, nobody gets paid and the pot rolls over bigger.
coreLoop: A card lands in the group chat: "Round 4. Pot is 24 USDC. What's your claim?" You open the mini-app and see every player's full public claim history from every previous round — Dave has claimed 40%+ three times running. You drag a slider to an integer 0-100 (percent of pot) and tap Claim. Your 1 USDC ante is taken at commit, not at reveal. Then the chat detonates for 24 hours: lobbying, pacts, obvious lies, "I'm going 10, I swear." At 21:00 UTC a crank resolves. If claims sum to <=100, everyone gets exactly what they claimed. If they sum to 101+, it's a BUST: nobody gets paid, the entire pot rolls into next round, and next round's antes stack on top. The reveal card shows all six claims, the sum in huge red type, and circles whoever pushed it over. You screenshot it. You come back tomorrow because the pot is 30 now and because Dave has to be punished. 30-second decision, 24 hours of argument.
whyOnChain: Three real things, and one honest deduction. (1) The whole game is simultaneous sealed commitment among people actively trying to manipulate each other. A Discord bot that knows all six claims before resolution is a bot that can be bribed, and in a game literally about greed among friends that suspicion is fatal to the fiction. Commit-reveal with collateral taken at commit, resolved by an on-chain crank, removes the host from the trust graph. (2) Six people in six countries settling a 24 USDC pot in seconds with no bank, no minimum withdrawal, no Venmo. (3) Claim history is permanent and unfakeable, which is the only reason a cross-table reputation ladder means anything. Honest deduction: a well-run Web2 server publishing hash commitments gets you ~80% of (1). What the chain actually buys is credible neutrality plus the payment rail — which for strangers staking money against each other is the difference between shipping and not.
solanaPrimitives: Commit-reveal on L1 with collateral (the ante) taken at commit time, per Switchboard's own rule — non-reveal scores as claim 0 and forfeits the ante, killing the 'never reveal a losing hand' attack
MagicBlock Private ERs (TEE-backed) for v2: sealed claims with no reveal step at all, so the UX is one tap instead of two
MagicBlock Cranks for deterministic fixed-time round resolution and forfeit handling
MagicBlock Session Keys so submitting a claim is one tap with zero wallet popups
Kora fee relayer (Solana Foundation, shipped April 2026) — players hold only USDC and never need SOL
Ephemeral SPL Tokens for in-ER USDC movement; settle to L1 at season end (0.0003 SOL/session, 0.0001 SOL/commit)
One delegated PDA per 6-player table — tables are independent shards, so the 12M CU per-writable-account-per-block ceiling is never a factor and local fee markets stay at zero
Metaplex Core (~0.0029 SOL/asset) for season trophies; Bubblegum V2 soulbound cNFTs for per-round badges
Anchor 1.1.2 (@anchor-lang/core, not the legacy @coral-xyz/anchor), Pinocchio for the resolve instruction hot path, Mollusk for CU-regression tests in CI, Surfpool + LiteSVM locally
moneyFlow: Value enters as antes: 1 USDC per player per round at the base tier (tiers at 1 / 5 / 25 USDC, plus a permanently free chips ladder). Value exits as payouts — the pot is fully redistributed, and a bust redistributes nothing, it just compounds. The studio earns a 5-8% rake taken ONLY from successful payouts, zero on a bust, aligning us with players wanting rounds to resolve rather than grind. Sinks: the rake, and nothing else — this economy is closed and conserved by construction, no emissions, no token, no faucet, so it cannot inflate. Secondary revenue: reveal-card cosmetic skins ($2-4) and branded tables. Honest about scale: at the 1 USDC tier a 15-round table season pays out ~70 USDC and rakes ~4 USDC, so this needs ten thousand concurrent tables to be a business, and the higher tiers are where the real revenue is.
firstSession: 0:00 a friend drops the table link into the group chat. 0:10 the Telegram Mini App opens to "Join Dave's table — 4/6 seats." 0:20 a passkey-backed embedded wallet is created silently: no seed phrase, no SOL, no chain vocabulary anywhere in the UI. 0:30 a forced 30-second tutorial round against five bots — you claim 40%, the sum comes back 118%, you bust, and you instantly understand the entire game. 1:10 you take the sixth seat in the real table, which starts in free-chips mode. 2:00 you submit your first real claim: Kora sponsors the fee, the session key means no popup, confirm latency under a second. 2:20 the app kicks you back into the chat with a prefilled "I claimed reasonably, unlike SOME people." 2:30 you are arguing. USDC deposit is never mentioned until season 2, after fifteen free rounds.
viralMechanic: The game does its own recruiting because a table is dead below six players and the join card in the chat shows a live "4/6 seats" counter — every empty seat is a standing reason to @ someone, and the existing four players do that work for you because they want the season to start. Then the bust card is a weaponized share artifact: it publicly names the greediest person in a friend group, and the culprit's only social move is to post it themselves with a defence. Third loop: your claim history is a permanent public profile that follows you across tables, so joining a stranger table means arriving with a reputation — which is what pulls players out of one closed chat into the open ladder.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks. Telegram Mini App plus a plain web client — explicitly NOT Blinks/Actions, which are a zombie channel (packages unpublished since 2024, X never natively unfurled them). Contains: one table type (6 players, 24h rounds, 15-round season), free chips only, table PDA with blake3 commit-reveal, Crank-driven resolution, forfeit-on-no-reveal, passkey embedded wallet, Kora fee sponsorship, session keys, server-rendered PNG share card. Cuts: all USDC and all rake (v2, gated on legal), Private ER/TEE (v2 UX upgrade), seasons, trophies, any NFT, the cross-table ladder, 90-second blitz mode, cosmetics, Discord. The MVP's only job: do six real friends voluntarily play fifteen rounds for zero money?
biggestRisk: The moment real USDC sits in the pot and the house takes a rake, this has online poker's exact regulatory footprint — a peer-to-peer stakes contest with a cut — and the 2026 US posture is hostile: the LA City Attorney named Stake's founders personally, and the new state statutes (LA, OK, NY, IN, IA, ME, TN) extend liability down the stack to platform providers, RNG suppliers, and geolocation vendors. That's a $50k-250k counsel and geofencing line item before the first paid table, and it is not optional. The pure-skill structure (literally zero randomness in the game) helps in predominance-test states and is worthless in Florida. Secondary and nearly as lethal: the acquisition unit is a six-person friend group, not a player, so the funnel is six times harder than it looks and one flake kills a table mid-season — the MVP must prove groups form and survive before a dollar of legal spend.

critique.name: Split or Bust
technicalBlockers: Distribution surface is prohibited by the platform it targets. The MVP is a Telegram Mini App settling USDC on Solana. Telegram's Blockchain Guidelines (core.telegram.org/bots/blockchain-guidelines, effective 2025-02-01, migration deadline 2025-02-21) require a Mini App to 'exclusively use the TON Blockchain for the creation and distribution of cryptocurrency tokens or blockchain assets' and to 'only interface with cryptocurrency wallets connected by the TON Connect SDK,' and explicitly prohibit 'promoting other blockchains, cryptoassets, wallets or multichain wallets based on blockchains other than TON' and 'directing or linking users to external platforms or websites where cryptoassets not based on TON are promoted or utilized.' A Solana/USDC Mini App with a passkey Solana wallet is a direct violation, and the entire viral loop is the in-chat share card. This is not flagged anywhere in the concept.

The claim space and the player count are arithmetically incompatible. Six players, integer claims 0-100, payout iff sum<=100. 100/6 = 16.67, which is not an integer, so there is NO symmetric profile that sums to exactly 100. The obvious focal point is inexpressible: 16 each sums to 96 (4% of the pot stranded every round), 17 each sums to 102 (guaranteed bust). Every table must choose between wasting or self-destructing on the single most natural coordination point. Fix is trivial (5 players at 20, 4 at 25, 10 at 10, or basis-point claims) but it is a design defect sitting at the exact center of the game.

The MagicBlock stack is over-specified by ~5 orders of magnitude and costs more than L1. The game is one action per player per 24 hours. At 10,000 concurrent tables that is 60,000 txs/day = 0.7 TPS. The listed ER + Private ER + Ephemeral SPL Tokens + Cranks architecture costs 0.0003 SOL/session + 0.0001 SOL/commit; at 15 rounds x 10,000 tables that is ~60 SOL/season ≈ $4,800 against a stated season rake of ~$40k — 12% of gross revenue for latency nobody needs. Plain L1 is 6 sigs x 5,000 lamports = 0.00003 SOL/round, roughly 10x cheaper than the ER session fee alone. Also note the concept's own landscape doc flags the ER trust model (fraud proofs, DA, undelegation-under-validator-failure) as UNVERIFIED — you would be routing player funds through it for zero benefit.

Holding a delegated PDA open for a 15-day season is undefined territory. MagicBlock's own docs warn that composability breaks during delegation (other L1 programs can read but not write a delegated account) and that 10ms slots are not guaranteed. A 15-day-long ER session with USDC inside it, on a system whose failure/recovery semantics are not publicly documented, is the highest-risk possible use of the primitive for the lowest possible payoff.
economicHoles: Every player is a long-run loser with mathematical certainty, and there is no fish to feed on. At the symmetric equilibrium (16 each on a 6 USDC pot) each player claims 0.96 USDC for a 1.00 USDC ante, and the studio takes 5-8% of that. Unlike poker — where the rake is beaten by skill dispersion, so good players are net-positive — Split or Bust has no dispersion at equilibrium: claim less and you self-harm, claim more and you bust the table and everyone loses 100% of the round. The concept's own numbers confirm it: 15 rounds x 6 players x 1 USDC = 90 USDC in, '~70 USDC paid out' = a 22% hold. That is 4x online poker rake and worse than a slot machine, imposed uniformly on all six players. Retention half-life for a game where nobody can win is measured in weeks.

The rollover is a divergent feedback loop that terminates in permanent lockup. Pot after n consecutive busts = 6n USDC while the ante stays at 1. The marginal value of claiming one extra percent grows linearly in n (+0.06n USDC), so the incentive to escalate strictly increases every time the table busts, and busts are what cause the pot to grow. Escalation -> bust -> bigger pot -> more escalation. The steady state is a large pot that never pays out. The design has no cap, no decay, no forced resolution, and no stated destination for a season-end unresolved pot.

Six-seat stranger tables are trivially sybil-farmable and the design explicitly wants stranger tables plus a cross-table ladder. Passkey embedded wallets cost nothing to create, there is no KYC, and Kora sponsors the fees, so one operator takes 5 of 6 seats and claims 19/19/19/19/19 = 95, leaving the mark <=5%. Sybil stakes 5 antes and recovers ~0.95 of a 6-USDC pot; net ~+0.4 USDC/round after rake, fully automatable, scaling linearly in tables. The 'friend group' framing is the defence, but the growth story is precisely the part where that defence is absent.

Kora fee sponsorship is an uncapped, free griefing faucet. Every sponsored transaction costs the studio 5,000 lamports and costs the attacker zero. A bot farm submitting junk claims/joins on free-chip tables drains the fee budget at infinite ROI to the attacker. Nothing in the design rate-limits sponsored txs per identity, and the identity is a free passkey.

The stated scale requirement is not survivable at the stated ARPU. Own math: ~4 USDC rake per 15-round table season at the 1 USDC tier, i.e. ~$0.27/table/day. Ten thousand concurrent tables (60,000 committed humans returning daily for 15 consecutive days) yields ~$2,700/day gross, before the ~$4,800/season infra, before legal, before geofencing vendors. The higher tiers are said to carry the revenue, and the higher tiers are exactly what the regulator looks at.
legalFlags: Rake taken from a player-funded pool is the specific structure that converts a skill game into an illegal gambling operation in a large set of states, independent of the skill question. Practitioner guidance is explicit: 'when both contestants fund the prize and the operator deducts a percentage of the pooled entries, several states read the operator's role as raking wagers, selling pools, or acting as a paid custodian of stakes, and those offenses do not care that the underlying game is pure skill.' The concept's 5-8% rake is taken from the pot. This is the exact fact pattern.

The skill defence is much weaker than claimed. 'Literally zero randomness' is not the same as 'predominantly skill.' The outcome of a simultaneous sealed Nash demand game is determined entirely by other players' unobservable choices; no court has blessed 'reading your friends' as skill the way it has chess or even DFS. Poker's skill argument is far stronger, backed by decades of expert testimony and statistical evidence, and poker is still prohibited in most US states. Assume you lose the predominance test more often than the concept assumes, and lose outright in FL/AZ/AR/IA/LA/MT/SC/SD/TN and the rest of the Skillz-restricted 12 (≈15% of US population, where Skillz itself disables cash entry).

Money transmission is unpriced. Holding player USDC balances across a 15-day season, across jurisdictions, is a custodial money-transmitter analysis: FinCEN MSB registration plus state MTLs at roughly $50k-150k per state in surety bonds, capital, and counsel. The stated $50k-250k budget covers gambling counsel and geofencing, not a 40+ state MTL footprint, which realistically runs $1-3M and 12-24 months. The alternative is geofencing the US entirely, at which point the SAM is non-US friend groups.

Unresolved rollover pots create an unclaimed-property/escheatment liability. USDC held indefinitely on behalf of identifiable users is abandoned property under state law after 3-5 years dormancy and must be escheated with records. A smart contract holding balances for pseudonymous PDAs cannot do this. Given that the rollover mechanic mathematically tends toward never paying out, this is not a corner case.
Telegram Blockchain Guidelines violation (see technical blockers) — a platform-policy takedown risk on the primary distribution surface, separate from state gambling law.
critique.priorArt: The mechanic is the n-player Nash demand game / 'divide-the-dollar' (Nash 1953), one of the most-studied games in economics; the academic literature is deep and the empirical finding is that repeated play with communication converges on an equal split, i.e. the boring outcome, while the entertaining outcome (bust) is the value-destroying one. I found no shipped on-chain implementation of exactly this, but the closest crypto analogue is instructive: FOMO3D (July 2018, exitscam.me), self-described as 'a psychological social experiment in greed,' built on a growing pot plus a rollover timer. It grew past $3M, was widely believed 'too big to fail,' and was ended by a player executing a block-stuffing attack to rig the outcome — i.e. the pot-escalation dynamic attracted a technical adversary rather than more players, and the round terminated in an exploit rather than a resolution. Its ancestor, Reddit's The Button, was free and produced identical social energy with no financial liability, which is the relevant lesson. Golden Balls' 'Split or Steal' is the TV precedent and it was a segment inside a show, never a standalone repeat-play product. Related and closer to the business risk: Skillz built a peer-to-peer entry-fee-plus-rake skill platform, and as of 2026 disables cash entry in ~12 states.
critique.suggestedFix: Remove the real-money pot and the rake, and make the bust always produce a winner. Specifically: run it entirely on non-cashable chips, and on a bust pay the whole pot to the LEAST greedy player instead of rolling it over. That single change does four things at once — it kills the escalation-to-permanent-lockup loop (the pot always clears), it kills the gambling/MTL/escheatment stack in one move, it makes the share card better (the bust card now names both the villain AND the beneficiary, doubling the social payload), and it restores skill dispersion so some players can actually win. Monetize on cosmetics, table branding, and a season pass — which is where the concept already says the secondary revenue is. Separately and independently: change the table to 5 or 10 players, or make claims basis-point-denominated, so the equal-split focal point is expressible; and ship on plain L1 with a web client, not an ER and not a Telegram Mini App.

name: Callout
pitch: Bet on your friends: turn anything anyone in the chat claims they'll do into a live market and let the group price it, with no real money anywhere in the system.
coreLoop: You're in the chat. Someone says "I'm definitely finishing the deck tonight." You reply /callout @sam finishes the deck by 9am. A market card appears inline at 50 cents, YES/NO. Six people tap in ten seconds and the card updates live in the feed as the price moves. Sam watches his own probability of being a functional adult drop to 22 cents in front of his friends — that reaction IS the product. At deadline, resolution goes to a five-juror panel drawn by VRF from OTHER groups; jurors stake 100 Nerve each, the majority splits the minority's stake plus a 50-Nerve fee from the market creator. Your calibration card updates with a running Brier score. The 30-second loop: read a claim, price it, tease the subject, watch the line move, get pinged when it settles.
whyOnChain: Honestly, close to nothing for the gameplay. A Postgres table runs this game perfectly, faster and cheaper, and if the team isn't willing to make the following three things real they should build it as a Web2 app with a login and stop pretending. What the chain genuinely buys: (1) the juror stake-and-slash is credible precisely because we cannot quietly reverse it, and cross-group juries — strangers ruling on your group's disputes — only work if the stake is enforced by something neither group controls; (2) the calibration record is a soulbound credential the player keeps if we shut down, a real portable reputation rather than the usual 'you own your items' fiction; (3) it composes — a Callout calibration score is a legible anti-sybil input other Solana apps can read via the Solana Attestation Service with no BD deal. That's a modest, defensible list. I'd grade on-chain necessity here at about 3/10: Callout is cheap top-of-funnel and a reputation layer, not a standalone crypto product.
solanaPrimitives: Solana Attestation Service for the portable calibration credential (live, with Civic / Solid / Trusta building on it) — also the anti-sybil gate for juror eligibility
Bubblegum V2 soulbound compressed NFTs for weekly badges — soulbound is native in V2, and 1M assets in one Merkle tree runs ~$500 versus $15-30k in account rent
ZK Compression (Light Protocol) for per-position records — millions of tiny 'user X holds 40 YES at 0.62' rows at ~1000x less than standard accounts
DAS-API RPC (Helius / Triton / QuickNode) — a hard third-party dependency for reading any cNFT; budget the $49-499/mo tier from day one
MagicBlock Ephemeral Rollup for the juror vote: delegate the market PDA, take five sealed votes, resolve and undelegate inside one ER session
MagicBlock VRF in-ER (free, <50ms) for drawing the five-juror panel — a low-value draw where free is the correct trade
MagicBlock Cranks for weekly Nerve resets and market expiry
Kora fee relayer plus a passkey embedded wallet — no SOL, no seed phrase, no chain vocabulary in the UI
Per-market PDA sharding — a single global orderbook account would hit the 12M CU per-writable-account-per-block cap and inherit its own fee market
@solana/kit 7.x with the new React hooks and a Codama-generated TS client (not the legacy @solana/web3.js v1 or the stale wallet-adapter packages)
moneyFlow: No player money enters the game. Ever. No token, no on-ramp, no cash-out, no sweepstakes AMOE — and that is the entire strategic point, because it removes gambling, securities, and money-transmission analysis simultaneously, in a year when eight-plus states have criminalized the dual-currency model and Louisiana attaches five-year prison terms. The in-game currency is Nerve: non-transferable, non-cashable, hard-reset to 1,000 every Monday, so it cannot accumulate, inflate, or acquire a secondary-market price. Value enters the business as (a) $5/month per group for Pro Chat — private groups over twelve people, custom market templates, unlimited concurrent markets, analytics; (b) sponsored markets priced as an ad unit against a verifiably-attended audience, not as a prize; (c) $2-4 cosmetic calibration-card skins. Nerve sinks: the weekly reset, the 50-Nerve creator fee (burned), juror slashing recycled to the majority. Costs ~$600/mo of DAS + RPC at small scale. Honest ceiling: this monetizes like a Discord bot, and low-five-figure MRR is a good year.
firstSession: 0:00 you get pinged in the chat: "@you — Marco opened a market on whether you'll actually go climbing Saturday. It's trading at 22 cents." 0:15 you tap the card; the mini-app opens, a passkey wallet is created in the background, 1,000 Nerve is granted, and the word 'blockchain' appears nowhere. 0:30 you buy 200 NO on yourself out of pure spite; the LMSR (b=200, tuned so a six-person group actually moves price) pushes it to 31 cents and the chat card updates live for everyone. 1:00 you open a revenge market on Marco. 1:30 a nudge: "price three markets to unlock juror duty." 2:15 you're pricing markets in two other groups you just got invited to, about people you've never met. 3:00 you have a calibration card with four open positions and a Brier score of --, which you now want to fill in.
viralMechanic: You structurally cannot open a market without @-tagging a person, and that person is notified their friends are pricing them. The subject is not a marketing target — they're a game piece, with exactly two moves: join and defend themselves, or be priced in absentia while the chat watches. Every market is therefore a forced invite with a built-in emotional reason to accept. The second loop is juror duty, which pushes you into strangers' groups to rule on their disputes; jurors see the funniest markets on the network, which makes juror duty the discovery surface and the cross-group graph the moat.
mvpScope: 3 weeks. A Discord bot on the Discord Activities embedded-app runtime plus a Telegram Mini App — again, explicitly not Blinks. Contains: one command (/callout @user <claim> by <time>), binary markets only, LMSR with b=200, Nerve with a hard weekly reset, creator-resolves with a 24h dispute window escalating to a five-juror VRF panel, market PDA + plain position PDAs (rent refundable on settle; migrate to ZK Compression only past ~50k live positions), Crank-driven expiry, live-updating chat cards, shareable calibration card. Cuts: SAS attestations, soulbound badges, multi-outcome and scalar markets, Pro Chat billing, sponsored markets, native mobile, any on-ramp whatsoever. The MVP tests one thing: does a group open a second market unprompted after the first one settles?
biggestRisk: It monetizes like a free Discord bot. There is no player money in the system by design, so revenue is subscriptions and ad units against a few thousand groups, and the play-money prediction-market history (Manifold) says engagement can be healthy while ARPU sits near zero. Second, the honest whyOnChain is thin enough that a competent Web2 team ships this in half the time with none of the DAS dependency or wallet friction — the only durable moat is the cross-group juror network, itself a cold-start problem stacked on the group cold-start problem. Third, quieter: even with zero cash-out, 'betting on your friends' triggers platform-policy friction (Google Play's ban on promoting earnings, Discord and Telegram ToS on gambling-adjacent content, app-store reviewer instinct) that will cost real calendar time despite a genuinely clean legal analysis.

critique.name: Callout
technicalBlockers: Same Telegram blocker, and it compounds with Discord. Telegram's Blockchain Guidelines require Mini Apps to use TON exclusively and forbid interfacing with non-TON wallets or linking to non-TON crypto surfaces; a Solana passkey wallet inside a Telegram Mini App violates this on its face. Discord Activities additionally sit under Discord's own policy review for gambling-adjacent mechanics, and the product's name and framing are 'bet on your friends.' Both of the two named MVP surfaces are policy-hostile to the exact build described.

Gasless play-money trading means the studio pays real SOL for fake-money transactions, with no offsetting revenue. Per group per day: ~3 markets x (1 create + ~15 LMSR trades + 1 resolve + 5 juror votes) ≈ 66 sponsored txs. At 10,000 groups that is ~660,000 txs/day x 5,000 lamports = ~3.3 SOL/day ≈ $264/day ≈ $8,000/month in Kora-sponsored base fees (at SOL $80), plus LaserStream/Yellowstone for the live in-chat price ticker, which the concept's own landscape prices at $500-6,000/month after the April 2026 change — not the $49 tier. Total run-rate ~$9-14k/month against a $5/month/group subscription that at a realistic 3% conversion (300 groups) grosses $1,500/month. Gross margin is roughly negative 700-900%. The stated '~$600/mo of DAS + RPC' is off by an order of magnitude and omits the sponsored-fee line entirely.

Kora sponsorship of a resource that is free and refills weekly is an unbounded griefing surface. Every player gets 1,000 Nerve every Monday at zero cost, and every trade of that Nerve costs the studio 5,000 lamports. A sybil farm with 1,000 passkey wallets can burn the fee budget indefinitely at zero marginal cost to itself. There is no rate limit, no stake, and no identity cost anywhere in the design.

LMSR subsidy is unfunded. With b=200 and binary outcomes, worst-case market-maker loss is b*ln(2) = 138.6 Nerve per market, against a 50-Nerve creator fee. Every market net-issues ~89 Nerve. The weekly hard reset masks the inflation but also means the only persistent object in the game is the calibration score.
economicHoles: The subject of a market controls its outcome, and the design encourages them to trade on it. The first-session script literally has you 'buy 200 NO on yourself out of pure spite.' With b=200, pushing 0.50 -> 0.22 requires ~253 net shares at ~91 Nerve cost, paying 253 on resolution: +162 Nerve risk-free for simply not doing the thing you said you'd do. That is 16% of a weekly budget per self-market, repeatable in every group you're in, on every claim anyone makes about you. Two colluding friends farm it without limit (open markets on each other's controllable behavior, both take the sure side). Insider trading is not an edge case here — it is the core loop as written.

The calibration credential — the entire whyOnChain justification and the SAS anti-sybil pitch — is cheaper to farm than to earn, which makes it worse than useless. A Brier score improves fastest by trading near-certainties. Nothing in the design distinguishes 'called a genuinely 50/50 event correctly' from 'priced 200 markets on things that were 97% certain.' Exporting that score into the Solana Attestation Service as an anti-sybil input actively poisons the sybil defences of any app that reads it. The one durable asset the concept claims to build is adversarially degradable at near-zero cost.

Juror incentives reward Schelling-point conformity, not truth, and the stake is free. Five jurors stake 100 Nerve of weekly-reset play money; the majority splits the minority's stake plus a 50-Nerve fee. A unanimous 5-0 correct ruling pays 10 Nerve on 100 at risk (+10%); a contentious 3-2 pays ~83 (+83%). So the payoff is maximized by being on the winning side of a split, not by being right — the classic coordination-game collapse. And because the stake is free and refills Monday, the rational juror reads nothing and votes the market-implied prior instantly. Kleros' entire answer to this problem is (a) an expensive real-value staked token whose price is the 51%-attack cost and (b) an appeal system that lets outsiders crowdfund correcting an obviously wrong ruling. Callout has neither. The 'credible neutrality' claim is therefore false: the juror layer is decorative.

Cross-group juries rule on unverifiable private facts with no evidence channel. A stranger in another group cannot know whether Sam finished his deck. The design specifies no evidence submission, no attestation, no oracle. This is not dispute resolution; it is a coin flip with a staking ceremony attached. It is also the single mechanism the concept identifies as its moat.

Group cold start stacked on network cold start, with no revenue at either stage. The moat is described as the cross-group juror network, which requires many groups; groups require the juror network to be interesting; and neither generates a dollar until Pro Chat converts. friend.tech is the cautionary quantity here: it monetized the social graph aggressively, generated $44M in cumulative fees, and still fell to ~15 DAU and $21 of protocol revenue in a 30-day window before the team burned the contract keys. Social-graph products exhaust the graph and then have nothing.
legalFlags: No consideration and no prize means it is very likely not gambling — that analysis is sound and is the concept's best decision. But adding the $5/month Pro Chat tier reintroduces a consideration argument in states that use a broad consideration test where paid access unlocks participation in a competitive-outcome game. Structure Pro Chat as strictly non-gameplay (analytics, admin, cosmetics) or the clean analysis stops being clean.

The product creates named, non-consensual financial-style instruments about identifiable private individuals. 'Will @sam get fired,' 'will @sam relapse,' 'will @sam's marriage last' are one keystroke away from the stated design and the subject is notified their friends are pricing them. The platform authors the instrument, the resolution mechanism, and the notification, which weakens a pure Section 230 intermediary posture and creates harassment, IIED, and false-light exposure that a Postgres-only competitor has identically — but that the on-chain permanence makes irreversible. There is no takedown path described for a market about a real person on an immutable ledger.

This sits at the dead centre of the 2026 regulatory heat map even without money. The CFTC's March 2026 ANPR on prediction markets specifically flags 'contracts involving sensitive events under the control of small groups or individuals' as a public-interest concern, and 100% of Callout's markets are events under the control of one named individual. Enforcement in 2026 has focused on exactly this class (DOJ/CFTC insider-trading cases; the July 2026 investigation of a Kalshi trader on speech-content 'mention markets'). Minnesota enacted the first outright state-level prediction-market ban, and such statutes are drafted broadly. Play money probably keeps you outside the CEA, but it will not keep you out of inbound state AG correspondence, and it will not stop a payments processor or app store from reading the marketing copy and declining.

Google Play's Real-Money Gambling, Games, and Contests policy plus app-store reviewer instinct on 'bet on your friends' framing will cost calendar time regardless of the underlying legality — correctly flagged in the concept, and it is the smallest of these four.
critique.priorArt: Extensive, and mostly discouraging. Manifold Markets (founded 2021, Austin) is the direct precedent: play-money prediction markets, calibration within a point or two of real-money operators on overlapping binaries, quarterly leagues for recurring status, a Manifold Plus subscription — and it retired Sweepcash in March 2025, closing the only real-money path it ever had. It is the proof that play-money prediction markets can be accurate and engaging while monetizing like a hobby project; the concept's own biggestRisk names it, correctly. friend.tech is the precedent for monetizing the friend graph directly: launched Aug 2023, FRIEND fell ~98% from its May 2024 ATH, DAU bottomed near 15, V2 generated roughly $60k of protocol fees from June 2024 onward and about $21 in one 30-day window, and the team transferred contract control to the null address in Sept 2024 — while founders retained $44M of earlier fees. Kleros is the precedent for the juror layer and is the source of the design constraints Callout omits (real-value staking, appeals, crowdfunded correction of bad rulings). On the commitment-device side, StickK (2008) and Beeminder are 15+ year-old precedents for staking on your own future behavior with verifiable resolution; both are small, durable businesses, which is a fair read of this concept's ceiling. WagerLab and similar social-bet trackers occupy the Web2 slot already, free.
critique.suggestedFix: Replace the human juror panel with machine-verifiable resolution, and only allow markets on facts a data source can settle. Wire Strava, GitHub, Duolingo, Spotify, Screen Time, Google Calendar, Steam, and Switchboard On-Demand custom feeds, and refuse to create a market that cannot name its oracle at creation time. This deletes the single most broken component (a free-stake Schelling-point jury adjudicating unverifiable private facts), gives the calibration score real information content so it is worth attesting to SAS, forces the subject to actually do the thing to win their own market instead of profiting from inaction, and shrinks the harassment surface because you cannot open a market on someone's marriage if there is no feed for it. Separately, and non-negotiably: stop putting play-money trades on chain. Batch trades in Postgres, settle only market creation, final outcome, and the calibration attestation on Solana. That drops sponsored fees by ~95%, removes the LaserStream dependency, kills the griefing faucet, and leaves exactly the three things the concept honestly claims the chain is for.

name: Cutline
pitch: A free three-minute live quiz show that drops into your group chat every night at the same time, where surviving all twelve questions pays out real dollars in fifteen seconds — and where the questions are written by the players.
coreLoop: 21:00 UTC, a card drops into every subscribed chat: "Cutline starts in 60s — 4,312 in. Pot: $1,000, escrowed." You tap, you're in. Twelve questions, ten seconds each, four choices, one tap. Two wrong answers and you're cut — unless you spend a Revive, and Revives are earned only by inviting someone who actually plays. Between questions the chat card updates in place with the survivor count and, crucially, which of your friends just died. Survive all twelve and the pool splits among survivors, paid in USDC to your wallet ~15 seconds after the last question. Then the show ends and everyone who got cut is still sitting in the chat roasting each other about Q7. Three minutes a day, same time every day, appointment viewing inside a surface people are already in.
whyOnChain: This is the strongest of the three and it has nothing to do with ownership. HQ Trivia's real operational failure was payouts: PayPal-only, a $20 minimum that stranded most winnings, US-centric, days of latency. Paying 250 people $6 each across 40 countries fifteen seconds after a game ends, for under a dollar of total network cost, is something no Web2 payment stack does — this is the 'instant global sub-cent payouts' bucket, the one place crypto is unambiguously better. Second: the prize pool is escrowed on-chain before the show starts, so 'is this rigged / will they actually pay' — the question that kills every free-prize game — is answerable by anyone with a block explorer, and the question shuffle is a verifiable draw rather than a promise. Third: the question-author revenue share is a programmatic cap table, paying twelve strangers 1.5% of a pool nightly with no contracts and no invoices (the Photo Finish LIVE track-owner pattern, which moved $9.7M). Fourth, purely technical: 5,000 sealed answers inside a hard ten-second window is a workload a 10ms ER handles and a 350ms L1 does not.
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock Ephemeral Rollup at ~10ms slots with one delegated PDA per player — the per-player shard is mandatory, since a single global show account would blow the 12M CU per-writable-account-per-block cap on question one; Supersize.gg is the existence proof at ~30ms tx cadence
MagicBlock Private ERs (TEE-backed) so submitted answers stay sealed until the window closes — no sniping the correct answer off other players' traffic
MagicBlock Cranks to close each 10-second question window deterministically, without a trusted show-runner press-the-button moment

Switchboard On-Demand randomness (commit-reveal bound to a Solana slothash, SGX enclaves, callback in the same tx) for the nightly question shuffle and survivor tiebreakers — the strongest public security story, worth its ~1s latency for a draw that decides real money; MagicBlock in-ER VRF (free, <50ms) for cosmetic rolls only

ZK Compression (Light Protocol) compressed token accounts for the payout fan-out — ATA creation at 0.0000053 SOL versus ~0.002, so paying 4,000 winners who have never held SOL costs cents rather than eight SOL
Kora fee relayer (Solana Foundation, April 2026) — players never hold SOL and never encounter the concept of gas
MagicBlock Session Keys — twelve taps in three minutes with zero wallet popups is non-negotiable, not a nicety
Bubblegum V2 soulbound cNFTs for survival streaks (~$500 per 1M assets in one tree versus $15-30k in rent)
Helius LaserStream / Yellowstone gRPC for the live survivor counter driving the in-chat card; DAS API for badges — validate LaserStream's Yellowstone compatibility yourself, the sources contradict
Anchor 1.1.2 with the answer-ingest instruction written in Pinocchio and CU-benchmarked in Mollusk in CI — that one instruction runs 60,000 times a night and IS the cost model
Payouts denominated and settled in USDC. No game token is ever issued.
moneyFlow: Value enters from sponsors only: a nightly title sponsor funds the prize pool plus a fee, sold as a media buy against a live, verifiably-attended audience — the attendance number being on-chain is a genuinely better ad-tech artifact than an impression count, and that is the actual sales pitch. Secondary: a $3/mo 'Green Room' cosmetic-and-stats subscription, and the product that is probably the real business, Cutline-as-a-service at $200-2,000 per show, where a creator, DAO, or brand funds a private Cutline for their own community. Value exits as: 100% of the escrowed pool to survivors, 1.5% per shipped question to each of twelve authors (18% of pool, funded on top by the sponsor), and under a dollar of network fees per show. No player money ever enters, which keeps this a free-entry skill contest rather than gambling — but it still needs official rules, an age gate, and exclusion of states restricting free-prize skill contests. The only internal currencies are Revives and question bonds; both expire, so nothing can inflate. Difficulty is tuned to a 3-8% survival rate: at 5,000 players that's ~250 survivors at $4-8 each; at 500 players ~25 survivors at $20-80 — deliberately more generous when the game is small, which is the correct incentive gradient at launch.
firstSession: 0:00 a friend posts the Cutline card into the group chat four minutes before showtime: "3 nights alive, come die with me." 0:10 you tap; the Telegram Mini App opens and a passkey wallet is created silently — no seed phrase, no SOL, no chain vocabulary. 0:25 you pick a handle and see the escrowed pot: "$1,000 locked · 3,180 playing," with an explorer link you will never click but whose existence is the whole trust story. 0:40 a practice question teaches you the tap. 1:00 the show starts. 1:10 Q1, you answer in four seconds, correct; the chat card behind you already shows two friends on a strike. 2:00 Q6, you get it wrong, strike one, genuine adrenaline. 3:00 you're cut on Q9 and the app immediately offers the only thing you want: "Invite a friend who plays and get a Revive for tomorrow." That is the loop closing on itself inside the first three minutes.
viralMechanic: Revives are the only scarce resource and they are purchasable exclusively in friends — one invited person who actually plays equals one Revive, expiring in seven days, capped at one use per show, so they can never be hoarded and must be continuously re-earned. On top of that, elimination is public inside the chat the players already sit in: when you get cut, everyone sees it in-feed, in real time, with a name attached, and appointment-time play guarantees the whole group is present at the same instant. The UGC layer adds a second, higher-intent loop — a question author brings their own audience to watch their question go live and see whether it survives the ambiguity flag.
mvpScope: 4 weeks, and most of it is not blockchain work. Contains: one nightly show, hard cap 500 players, 12 hand-written questions, 2 strikes, a $200 prize pool of the studio's own USDC escrowed on-chain, one batched payout after the show, Telegram Mini App and web only. On-chain: a show PDA plus per-player answer PDAs delegated to a MagicBlock ER, Crank-closed question windows, Switchboard On-Demand for the shuffle, a batched payout instruction, Kora fee sponsorship, session keys. Off-chain: the show runner, question DB, in-chat cards, survivor stream. Cuts: UGC and the author revenue share (v2 — the real differentiator, but not what the MVP must prove), Revives, sponsors, badges, Discord, Private ER (at 500 players you can withhold answers until the window closes and accept the sniping risk), and ZK-compressed payouts (500 plain ATAs is fine). The MVP proves exactly one thing: do people show up at the same time tomorrow?
biggestRisk: HQ Trivia's post-mortem, verbatim. The game works, the audience shows up, the prize pool is pure customer-acquisition cost that never converts to revenue, and HQ peaked past two million concurrent and still died. Cutline lives or dies on whether Cutline-as-a-service and sponsor sales are real, which makes this a media-sales business wearing a game studio's clothes — and most game teams are terrible at media sales. Second: a daily live show is a content treadmill needing twelve fresh, non-googleable questions every night forever, which is precisely why the UGC layer is the load-bearing wall rather than a feature, and UGC quality control (the 500-point bond, the >15% ambiguity flag, the >85% too-easy forfeit) is completely unproven at MVP. Third, the honest scale check: live Solana games run at four-to-five-figure user counts, so 5,000 concurrent is a stretch target and not a baseline — at 300 players the per-survivor payout looks great and the sponsor deck is unsellable, and that gap is where this concept most likely dies.

critique.name: Cutline
technicalBlockers: Telegram again, and it is the named primary surface. A Solana/USDC Mini App creating passkey Solana wallets violates core.telegram.org/bots/blockchain-guidelines on three counts (non-TON asset distribution, non-TON-Connect wallet interfacing, linking to non-TON crypto surfaces). Ship the web client and the Solana dApp Store listing; do not build the acquisition loop on Telegram.

The compute math actually works, and the concept deserves credit for it — but the relayer math does not. 5,000 answers x ~5,000 CU ≈ 25M CU per 10-second question window = ~2.5M CU/s, comfortable for an ER, and per-player delegated PDAs correctly avoid the 12M CU per-writable-account cap. The blocker is Kora. Every sponsored transaction requires the relayer to sign; 5,000 answers in a 10-second window is 500 signing ops/sec, twelve times per show, 60,000 per night. Kora shipped April 2026 with no published throughput benchmark, and the reference point in your own landscape is Helius Sender at a default 6 TPS on all plans. That is a ~80x gap between the architecture and the nearest published rate limit for the sponsorship path, and it is unaddressed. You will need a dedicated Kora fleet with per-show pre-warmed nonce accounts and horizontal signer sharding, or you drop sponsorship and pre-fund each player — budget this as a first-class engineering problem, not a config line.

The 'crypto fixes payouts' claim is true up to the wallet and false after it, which is where HQ actually died. HQ's failure mode was PayPal-only with a $20 minimum stranding winnings. Cutline pays $4-8 into a ZK-compressed USDC account inside a passkey wallet the player has never seen a key for. To turn that into money they can spend, the player must adopt a wallet that supports compressed token accounts (your own landscape says Phantom and Backpack, i.e. not universal), decompress, and then pass a KYC'd off-ramp whose minimum is typically $10-25 — above the prize. You have moved the $20 minimum from PayPal to Coinbase/MoonPay and added a decompression step. Fifteen-second settlement to an unspendable balance is not the win the pitch claims; the honest version of the claim is 'instant, global, verifiable prize CREDIT,' and the moment you say that, USDC stops being load-bearing versus a points balance.

Payout variance is structurally large and lands on the player-facing number. To hit 5% survival with 12 questions and 2 strikes you need per-question p≈0.66 (p^12 + 12·p^11·(1-p) ≈ 0.057). But p is strongly correlated across players — one easy question set moves everyone together — so the survivor count is fat-tailed, not binomial. With a FIXED sponsor-funded pool, that variance transfers entirely into per-survivor prize, which will swing from ~$2 to ~$200 night to night, and the $2 nights are precisely when your most engaged players learn the product is not worth showing up for. Either float the pool per survivor (and blow your sponsor budget on an easy night) or cap payouts (and break the escrow trust story that is your second whyOnChain pillar).
economicHoles: The sponsor CPM assumption is off by roughly 20-50x, and it is the whole business. A $1,000 pool plus a fee is ~$2,500 of sponsor spend against 5,000 attendees for three minutes — a ~$500 CPM. Real mobile video CPM is $10-30. The pitch asks a media buyer to pay a 20-50x premium because attendance is verifiable on-chain, and no media buyer in history has paid a premium for measurement; measurement-premium is the thesis that killed every blockchain ad-verification startup between 2018 and 2022. At a real $20 CPM, 5,000 viewers is ~$100 of sponsor revenue against a $1,000 prize liability: minus 900% unit economics. Prize pool is 100% customer-acquisition cost that never converts, which is HQ's post-mortem restated with a blockchain on it.

Cutline-as-a-service at $200-2,000/show is priced into an existing, cheap, incumbent market. Kahoot is a public company with a $30/month self-serve tier; Slido, AhaSlides, and Crowdpurr occupy the same slot. You would be asking a brand or DAO to pay 10-60x the incumbent price for a live quiz whose differentiator is a payout rail their legal team has to approve. This is described as 'probably the real business' and it is the part with the strongest competition and the weakest moat.

The UGC revenue share costs 2-4x more than simply hiring the writer. Twelve authors at 1.5% of a $1,000 pool is $180/night = ~$65,700/year for 12 questions a night. A freelance quiz writer produces 12 questions for $50-100. The 'programmatic cap table' is genuinely elegant and it is solving a problem that a contractor solves cheaper, while importing the ambiguity/quality-control problem the concept already admits is unproven at MVP.

Scale reality is brutal and correctly self-identified: HQ peaked at ~2.38M concurrent and still died in Feb 2020 when the acquisition fell through. Live on-chain Solana games run at four-figure counts. At 300-500 players the per-survivor payout looks great and the sponsor deck is unsellable, which is the stated failure mode — and it is the modal outcome, not the tail.

Revives are earned only by inviting someone who plays, which is a strong loop and also the design's biggest legal defect (below). Note also that a scarce, invite-gated, expiring resource with a real-money payoff attached is a market: expect a grey market in invited-account referrals within a week of launch, farmed with the same free passkey wallets that cost you Kora-sponsored fees on every answer they submit.
legalFlags: The Revive-for-invite mechanic is the thing most likely to convert a lawful free-entry skill contest into an illegal lottery, and it is not flagged. The 'no consideration' analysis is correct only while entry is genuinely free of value transfer. Requiring a player to recruit a new user in order to obtain a material in-game advantage in a cash-prize contest is textbook non-monetary consideration under the sweepstakes analysis used in AZ, FL, ND, and NY — you are receiving something of commercial value (a customer) in exchange for game benefit. This single mechanic is simultaneously the entire viral loop and the fastest route to a state AG letter. It needs an alternative free method of obtaining Revives, prominently offered, at equal ease.

Prize registration and bonding. A continuously-run daily cash-prize promotion is legally novel; NY and FL require registration and bonding for prizes over $5,000 and a $1,000 nightly pool is $365k/year of prizes. Whether each night is a separate promotion is exactly the kind of question that gets answered against you. Budget for official rules, an age gate, state exclusions, and a bond.

Tax and sanctions reporting collides head-on with the 'no chain vocabulary, no seed phrase' UX. A daily player winning $6/night 100 nights/year crosses $600 and triggers 1099-MISC reporting; global USDC payouts require OFAC screening. So your most engaged, most valuable users are precisely the ones you must collect a W-9 and identity documents from — the exact opposite of the frictionless passkey onboarding the first-session script depends on. There is no version of this where the top of the retention curve stays anonymous.
Telegram Blockchain Guidelines violation on the primary distribution surface (see technical blockers).
critique.priorArt: This is the most directly precedented of the three, and the precedent already ran the crypto experiment. HQ Trivia itself: peak ~2.38M concurrent, shut down Feb 2020 after laying off all 25 staff when an acquisition fell through and investors declined to fund further — the game worked, the business did not, and the payout friction (PayPal-only, $20 minimum, removed in Jan 2018 precisely because it was strangling the product) is the exact pain Cutline claims to solve. Then Internet Game raised a $7M seed in 2022 to rebuild HQ Trivia with NFTs, with participation from HQ co-founder Rus Yusupov, ParaFi, Dragonfly, Delphi Digital, Uniswap Ventures, Collab+Currency, and Magic Eden's co-founder; season one launched March 2022 with 8,000 players minting $2.2M of access NFTs, and the company subsequently pivoted and rebranded to RekTech rather than becoming a live-quiz business. That is $7M, the original founder, and top-tier crypto capital pointed at exactly this thesis, four years ago, with no surviving live-quiz product. On Solana today, Twizzin already runs staked real-time trivia with on-chain prize distribution. On the Telegram side, the tap-to-earn cohort is the retention warning: Hamster Kombat went from ~300M MAU to ~41M within four months and ~13.1M by April 2026, and The Block reported the whole Telegram games cohort struggling on both revenue and retention.
critique.suggestedFix: Invert the business: lead with Cutline-as-a-service and never fund a public prize pool out of your own or a sponsor's pocket.
