Resolution ops: 10 questions/day = 3,650/yr, each needing a pre-registered unambiguous source. Switchboard On-Demand costs are trivial (~7.3 SOL/yr at 0.002 SOL/request) but each question needs an editor, and once prizes attach, the 3-of-5 human resolver committee is a bribery surface with a 12-hour window and real money on the other side of a wording dispute.
economicHoles: The league mechanic measures luck, not skill, and this is the quantitative core of the retention risk the pitch flags but does not compute. Distinguishing a 65%-accurate forecaster from a 55%-accurate one at conventional significance requires on the order of 200+ binary resolutions. A weekly league cycle gives you 70. Promotion and relegation across 30 players on 70 noisy binary outcomes is mostly coin-flipping, which means the skilled players — the only cohort that actually enjoys Brier scoring — will correctly infer that the ladder does not reward them and leave, while the casual cohort never understood why hedging at 55% was penalised in the first place. Duolingo's leagues work because they sit on a lesson loop with immediate, deterministic feedback; Hunch's feedback is 48 hours delayed and stochastic.

The addressable market for calibration-as-entertainment is empirically small. Manifold Markets — the best-executed play-money forecasting product ever built, with a rationalist-community tailwind — hit a record low of 886 daily active traders in March 2025, sits around 50k MAU in 2026, and sunset its sweepcash real-money tier on 2025-03-28. Metaculus and Good Judgment Open are in the low tens of thousands. The pitch's own risk statement is right and the number is roughly 100-200k people globally, not a mass market.

Sponsored question packs are a weak revenue base with an adverse-selection problem: the advertisers who most want to place three cards about crypto prices are exchanges, which is the single worst sponsor category for a product whose legal defence rests on not being a betting product. Non-crypto brand sponsors will want brand-safe questions, and brand-safe questions are boring, which degrades the product to fund it.

Prize pools funded from sponsorship are a variable-revenue liability paid as a fixed contractual line item. In a soft ad quarter you either cut the prize (breaking the league promise) or pay it from margin. This is manageable but it is a real operating risk that the 'fixed weekly prize pool' framing hides.
legalFlags: The $3.99 Pro tier grants a SECOND DAILY SET, and that single line destroys the entire no-consideration defence the pitch builds. AMOE doctrine requires genuine parity between free and paid entry; a purchased path that doubles your scoring opportunities in a prize-ranked contest is a purchased advantage in the odds of winning, which is textbook consideration. The pitch asserts 'there is NO ENTRY FEE, EVER' and then, in the same section, sells extra entries. This is the exact fact pattern that drew state AG action against the sweepstakes-casino cohort. Fixable in one product decision, fatal if shipped.

Skill-vs-chance under state predominance / material-degree tests: 'Bitcoin closes above $95k Friday' resolved over 48 hours is close to pure chance, and mixing it into a prize-ranked contest imports the worst characterisation of every question in the pack. PrizePicks paid roughly $15M to the NY Gaming Commission and exited the state on this analysis, with C&Ds in FL, AR, MI and MA. The Kalshi preemption shelter (3rd Cir., Apr 2026) attaches only to CFTC DCM registration, which the pitch correctly notes a small team cannot buy.

CFTC event-contract exposure. Free play helps substantially, but an exchange paying to place three cards about asset prices, with prizes awarded on the outcomes, is an exchange paying to route retail attention onto price predictions with money attached. That is a bad optic in front of a regulator regardless of how the consideration analysis comes out.

Sponsor-funded prizes make you the operator of the sponsor's promotional sweepstakes, which triggers Florida and New York registration and bonding above the $5,000 prize-value threshold, Rhode Island retail rules, per-jurisdiction official rules, and winner-list publication. That is a recurring weekly compliance operation with a named compliance owner, not a one-time six-figure opinion.

Google Play and Apple real-money-contest policies both require licensing disclosures and geofencing for prize contests in many jurisdictions; you will need a geofence and a per-state rules matrix before the first prize is paid.
critique.priorArt: Heavily precedented, all of it small. Manifold Markets (play money, record-low 886 DAU Mar 2025, ~50k MAU 2026, real-money sweepcash sunset 2025-03-28), Metaculus, Good Judgment Open — all demonstrate that free forecasting retains a devoted but tiny audience. On Solana specifically, Hedgehog Markets raised $3.5M in 2021 for no-loss prediction markets, went quiet, and relaunched a V1 in January 2026 still at niche scale — the 'prediction market without the gambling' positioning has now been attempted on this exact chain and has not broken out. Polymarket and Kalshi took the opposite path (real money, real regulation) and are the only ones at scale. PrizePicks is the cautionary tale on the legal side. The genuinely novel elements are the swipe-confidence input and the Duolingo league wrapper; neither has been tried on forecasting, and the swipe-to-set-confidence gesture is the best single idea in this document.
critique.suggestedFix: Make Pro strictly non-scoring — analytics, history export, streak freezes, ad removal, never a second card set — and score leagues on a rolling 30-day Brier rather than a weekly one. The first change is the difference between a lawful free-entry contest and a purchased-odds sweepstakes, and it costs you nothing because the people who pay $3.99 for forecasting analytics are exactly the people who will pay for analytics. The second raises the resolution count per ranking decision from ~70 to ~300, which is the point at which the ladder starts measuring calibration instead of variance and the skilled cohort stops correctly concluding it is rigged. Then run the pitch's own MVP — free, no prizes, human-resolved, on-chain commit from day one — and treat 20% D7 as the go/no-go, because if a free forecasting league does not hold that, prizes will buy you farmers rather than forecasters.

name: Mono
pitch: You can make exactly one thing. Everything else you need, you buy from the other people playing.
coreLoop: Open the app. Your factory ran while you were gone — collect (idle accrual, 8-hour cap, so you check in 2-3 times a day). Spend 20 seconds tapping upgrades. Then the 40 seconds that are actually the game: your next upgrade needs 200 Copper and 40 Rubber, and you make Glass. You open the market. Copper is at 0.011 and sliding because the Copper producers are dumping into a glut; Rubber is at 0.04 and climbing because a new tier-3 recipe dropped this morning and everyone needs it. You buy Copper now, wait on Rubber, and post 60 Glass at 0.031 into a real order book against real strangers. Fill notification arrives twenty minutes later while you are doing something else. Come back in four hours and the prices have moved because 40,000 other people made the same kinds of decisions. The idle game is the excuse; the price discovery is the drug.
whyOnChain: This is the one of the three where crypto is doing real structural work. The entire game is a supply-and-demand economy between strangers, and the only property that makes such an economy interesting is that supply is CREDIBLY fixed. In every Web2 game with a market, players correctly assume the operator prints when it is convenient — because operators always do — and that assumption is what killed Diablo 3's auction house. On-chain issuance is a credible commitment device: nobody, including us, can mint Copper to relieve a shortage, and every player can verify that in ten seconds. The 2026 research is explicit that 'the issuer cannot secretly print more' is one of the very few genuine crypto adds, and this design is built entirely on it. Second: cash-out. A player who quits can sell their stockpile to players who want it, which every Web2 game forbids by TOS and which is the single most-requested thing players actually want. Now the honest caveat, because the brief demands it: an idle factory game with a fake internal market is a mediocre idle game. The market being real is doing a great deal of the work here, and Mono is closer to the yield-product line than the other two concepts. The defense is that no value enters from new-player deposits — value enters from IAP and leaves through consumption sinks — so it is a market game, not a ponzi. But that is a defense, not an exemption, and I would want the tier-3 sink instrumented from week one.
solanaPrimitives: SPL Token-2022 with Metadata Pointer — the 48 goods as real fungible tokens, metadata on-mint with no extra account (crate 11.0.0, @solana-program/token-2022 0.15.0)

Token-2022 Transfer Fees — a 1% automatic burn on every trade, which is the structural sink that keeps the economy from inflating. EXPLICITLY NOT Transfer Hook and EXPLICITLY NOT Permanent Delegate: the research flags both as the engine behind 2026's largest automated rug-pull family, and using either gets your mints flagged by scam detectors and rejected by wallets

ZK Compression (Light Protocol) — per-player inventory and factory state; compressed token accounts at ~100x cheaper and compressed ATAs at 0.0000053 SOL vs ~0.002 make 48 goods x 40,000 players economically storable
MagicBlock Cranks — time-based on-chain automation for the hourly production tick, the per-season spoilage pass, and season rollover; no keeper infrastructure to babysit

Solana L1 for the order book, no rollup — a market you touch three times a day does not need 10ms slots, and 350ms (SIMD-0525, epoch 1020) is more than enough. Critically, the book is sharded as one PDA set per good per price band, because a single hot writable account caps at 12M CU per block regardless of the 100M block limit, and one global book would be the throughput ceiling
Kora fee relayer — order placement is gasless and fees are paid in USDC, so a player never touches SOL
Privy embedded wallet — created silently at 0:30 of the first session
Metaplex Core — cosmetic factory skins, the only tradeable non-fungible in the game

Pyth Core price feeds — used ONLY at the USDC cash-out boundary, never inside gameplay; the research warns directly against pegging a game economy to an oracle and importing its latency and manipulation surface
Solana Mobile dApp Store — the distribution channel for the build that includes cash-out, at 0% platform fee and no crypto restrictions
moneyFlow: IN: $9.99 one-time Second Factory (a second good, once ever, per account); seasonal pass $6.99; cosmetic factory skins $1-$6 as Metaplex Core assets; a 1% studio fee on every market fill. OUT: players withdraw USDC by selling goods to OTHER PLAYERS. The studio never pays anyone and never buys anything back — there is no treasury obligation, no buyback, no yield, and no native token, which is what keeps this out of the Axie failure mode. NAMED SINKS, because this is precisely where P2E economies die: (1) 1% Token-2022 transfer fee burned on every trade; (2) tier-3 recipes PERMANENTLY CONSUME their inputs and produce a non-transferable season score rather than a tradeable good — this is the terminal sink and it must absorb more units per week than production emits, which is the single number the economy designer watches; (3) factory upgrades consume goods, with costs scaling ~1.55x per tier against ~1.4x output gains, so the marginal upgrade always gets more expensive in real terms; (4) 15% spoilage on any inventory carried across a 12-week season boundary, forcing liquidation and preventing multi-season hoarding. FAUCET: hourly production only, hard-capped per account, sublinear in upgrade level. E <= S + X - C holds because E is capped per account and per hour rather than being a function of playtime, which is the exact structural error Axie made with SLP.
firstSession: 0:00 Open. Twelve illustrated little factories on a wheel — Copper, Glass, Rubber, Yeast. You pick Glass because it looks nice. No sign-in. 0:30 Factory is running, first collection ticks in 60 seconds, and a Privy wallet quietly exists. 1:00 First upgrade needs 40 Rubber and you make Glass. The game does not explain this, it just shows a BUY button. You tap; 40 Rubber arrives, paid from a $1 starter balance the game gave you. 1:40 'You have 60 Glass. Sell some?' A price ladder appears with real live orders from real people. You post 60 at 0.031. 2:20 Fill notification. Your balance moves. That is the moment the game lands — you sold something to a stranger. 3:00 One line, once: 'Your stockpile is worth $0.83. It's yours, and you can take it out any time.' That is the only crypto sentence in the session and it is phrased entirely as ownership. 4:00 Push scheduled for 4 hours out: 'Rubber is up 22%.' The word wallet, token, gas, chain, and earn appear nowhere.
viralMechanic: Forced interdependence makes referral structurally profitable rather than a bonus code. Because you can only produce one good, every friend you recruit who makes a DIFFERENT good directly cheapens your own supply chain — you are recruiting a supplier, not a headcount. That is the same reason real trading communities recruit. On top of it, producers of the same good naturally organize into 48 cartels that coordinate price, share recipe intelligence, and poach each other's buyers, and cartels recruit aggressively because market share is literally their income. Third and quieter: when a producer quits, the whole market feels the supply hole within a day, which writes its own re-engagement notification ('Yeast supply dropped 30% this week') without any fake urgency.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks: 12 goods, 2 tiers only, idle accrual with an 8-hour cap, a fixed-tick order book on L1 with a genuinely good mobile UI (this is where the whole budget goes — a bad ladder kills the game), ZK-compressed inventories, and a keeper bot instead of MagicBlock Cranks. CRUCIALLY: NO CASH-OUT AND NO REAL USDC IN V1. Goods are internal-only, which means zero money-transmission exposure while you answer the only question that matters — do people actually trade, or do they treat it as a single-player idle game and ignore the market. CUTS: real USDC and withdrawals, tier 3 and the terminal sink, seasons and spoilage, guilds, Token-2022 transfer fees, cosmetics, native mobile builds, Pyth, and the dApp Store listing. If trade volume per DAU is under about 2 orders a day in the closed economy, opening it to real money will not fix that, it will just add regulators.
biggestRisk: Money transmission, and it is the one that quietly kills small teams far more often than securities law does. The moment real USDC flows out to arbitrary third parties, you are arguably an MSB requiring FinCEN registration and state MTLs across 40+ jurisdictions at roughly $50k-$150k per state in bonds and fees. There are architectures that mitigate it (fully non-custodial, studio never holds player funds, transfers are peer-to-peer program-mediated), but 'arguably' is not a defense you want to be testing with a seed round. Second risk, purely as design: one well-capitalized player can corner a tier-1 good in the first week and hold the entire playerbase hostage. EVE Online has a full-time economics team to manage this and you will have one designer with a spreadsheet. Third, and it is the honest one: this is the concept where the fun-without-the-token test is closest to failing. Strip out the real market and you have a mediocre idle game, so a meaningful share of the appeal is the money itself — which means the retention you measure in a live test may be measuring speculators, exactly the mistake that made 1M Nyan Heroes playtesters convert to zero.

critique.name: Mono
technicalBlockers: Verified blocker: ZK Compression does not support the Token-2022 transfer-fee extension. Light Protocol's compressed token accounts support only MetadataPointer, TokenMetadata, InterestBearingConfig, GroupPointer, GroupMemberPointer, TokenGroup and TokenGroupMember; all other mint extensions are explicitly unsupported. The design's two load-bearing primitives — ~100x-cheaper compressed inventories and the 1% transfer-fee burn as the primary sink — cannot coexist as specified. Uncompressed is expensive: at 8 goods held per player x 40k players = 320,000 Token-2022 accounts x ~0.00204 SOL = 653 SOL ≈ $52,240 in locked rent (worst case 48 goods x 40k = 1.92M accounts = 3,917 SOL ≈ $313,000), all of it funded by the studio because players hold no SOL by design. The workable fix is to burn 1% inside your own matching program and drop the extension — but then the sink is enforced by your program rather than the token, so any peer-to-peer transfer outside your book bypasses both the burn AND your 1% revenue fee. With 2% round-trip friction on goods whose spreads are already wide, trading will migrate to Discord OTC and take your sink and your revenue with it.

Throughput is genuinely not the problem and I will say so rather than manufacture one. A match instruction at ~40k CU against the 12M CU per-writable-account per-block cap gives ~300 matches per block per book account; at 350ms slots that is ~857 matches/sec per shard. 40k DAU at 3 orders/day is 1.4 orders/sec. You have three orders of magnitude of headroom, and the per-good/per-price-band sharding is correct engineering that you do not actually need yet.

Liquidity is the problem, and the comparable is brutal. Star Atlas's Galactic Marketplace — a AAA MMO with eight years of development and a token behind it — does roughly 20,000 USDC/week. Mono at 40k DAU with a realistic 15% trading participation and 2 trades each at $0.15 is 12,000 trades/day ≈ $12,600/week spread across 48 markets, i.e. ~$262/week per market. A central limit order book at that volume shows three resting orders and a 20-50% spread. The first-session hook at 2:20 — 'fill notification arrives, you sold something to a stranger' — requires a market maker on the other side, and the pitch explicitly forbids a treasury, so there is nobody to be that counterparty. The primitive that actually works at this volume is a bonding curve or AMM, which requires seeded liquidity, which requires the treasury the design correctly refuses.

Gasless order placement plus refundable rent is a free denial-of-service. If resting orders occupy accounts at ~0.002 SOL rent-exempt each and Kora sponsors placement, an attacker posts 100,000 resting orders and locks ~$16,000 of studio SOL at zero personal cost, or simply stuffs and cancels against a hot band account until real fills stop landing. You must either charge for order placement (breaking the no-SOL UX) or rate-limit per attested identity (breaking the no-sign-in UX).
economicHoles: The sink arithmetic is off by roughly four orders of magnitude and this is the finding that matters most. Faucet: 40k players x a 10 unit/hour cap = 400k units/hour = 67.2M units emitted per week. Sink 1, the 1% trade burn: ~12,600 trades/week x ~60 units average = 756k units traded, of which 1% = 7,560 units burned — that is 0.011% of weekly emission. Sink 3, upgrades, is finite per player and asymptotes as players finish their tiers. Sink 4, 15% spoilage, fires once per 12-week season on standing stock only. So roughly 99% of the entire sink load falls on the tier-3 terminal sink, and the tier-3 sink is the one mechanic in the design with no reason for a player to engage with it.

The terminal sink is not a sink, it is an unanswered question, and there is no third option. Tier-3 recipes permanently consume tradeable goods and output a non-transferable season score. If that score is worthless, no rational player burns sellable inventory for it and the sink has zero throughput, production accumulates, and prices go to zero. If the score is worth something — prizes, next-season advantage, status with cash value — it is a second currency and you have rebuilt the dual-token treadmill the pitch spends a paragraph claiming to have avoided. E <= S + X - C does not hold; it is asserted.

'48 cartels that coordinate price' is presented as a viral feature and is actually the reason the game cannot onboard. Because you produce exactly one good and must buy 47, a cartel in any tier-1 input is a monopoly with a fully captive customer base. A player joining on day 90 faces cartel pricing on every input while selling one good into a market the incumbent cartel controls. New-player NPV is negative from the moment cartels form, which is week two. EVE survives this on scale, a 20-year head start, and a full-time economics team; the pitch concedes Mono will have one designer with a spreadsheet.

Cornering is cheap. With ~$262/week of volume per market, the float actually resting on the book at any moment is perhaps 2% of weekly production. Sweeping a tier-1 input that a popular tier-3 recipe requires costs low four figures and holds the entire playerbase's progression hostage for as long as you care to fund it. In a 12-good MVP that is one motivated whale away from an unplayable economy in week one.

The pitch's own honest caveat is the correct one and it is worse than stated: strip the real market and this is a mediocre idle game, which means a large share of measured retention in any live test is speculators, not players. That is the precise error that made Nyan Heroes' 1M playtesters convert to zero paying users.
legalFlags: Securities. The 'no native token' framing is backwards — you have issued 48 of them. Howey is met on all four prongs and the fourth is stated as a feature: (1) investment of money via the $9.99 Second Factory, the $6.99 season pass, and USDC purchases of goods; (2) common enterprise, horizontally among all holders of a given good and vertically with a studio taking 1% of every fill; (3) expectation of profit, established by the pitch's own first-session script at 3:00 — 'Your stockpile is worth $0.83. It's yours, and you can take it out any time'; (4) from the efforts of others, since the studio sets emission caps, recipe costs, spoilage rates, sink parameters and season rollovers, and the pitch describes that balancing as the core ongoing work. The consumptive-commodity defence is the right argument and is fact-dependent, but it survives only if goods are genuinely consumed and marketing never gestures at value — and the marketing copy in the design document violates that on the first screen.

Money transmission, as the pitch identifies, but with a sharper edge than it allows: FinCEN's 2019 CVC guidance turns on control, and the studio operates the matching engine, takes 1% of every fill, and can halt or reparameterise the market. Non-custodial-by-architecture is a genuine defence but those three facts are exactly what regulators point at to find control. FinCEN MSB registration is free but carries an AML program, SAR/CTR obligations and a named compliance officer; state MTLs across 40+ jurisdictions at $50k-$150k each in bonds and fees is the number the pitch already cites and it is correct.
Sanctions/OFAC and travel-rule exposure once USDC leaves to arbitrary third-party addresses, with no KYC in a flow whose entire UX premise is that the word 'wallet' never appears.

Token-2022 transfer fees on player-tradeable assets will be read by some wallets and scam detectors as a tax token; the design correctly avoids Transfer Hook and Permanent Delegate, but transfer fees alone still generate marketplace and wallet friction on 48 separate mints.
critique.priorArt: Extensively precedented and the results are unambiguous. Entropia Universe is the strongest positive case and the most instructive: the only long-running genuine real-cash game economy (PED pegged at 10:1 to USD, ATM card withdrawals, ~$420M of annual economic activity), and MindArk obtained an actual Swedish banking licence in 2009, complete with government deposit insurance up to ~$60k per customer, in order to run it. That is the compliance altitude of 'players can cash out', and it is the answer to the question the pitch defers. On the negative side: Diablo 3's real-money auction house was removed in 2014 precisely because a real market cannibalised the game loop; Alien Worlds ran 30-45% bots against ~170k daily miners with no working sinks; Prospectors (EOS) built almost exactly this player-driven resource economy and never escaped a few thousand players; Star Atlas's marketplace is at ~20k USDC/week today; and Serum/OpenBook demonstrated that on-chain CLOBs die from liquidity fragmentation long before they die from throughput. EVE Online is the only version that works and it employs staff economists.
critique.suggestedFix: Make production require ongoing consumption of other players' goods as recurring fuel or maintenance, not just one-time upgrades, and delete the tier-3 leaderboard score entirely. Right now the faucet is a per-hour function of player count while the sinks are one-time (upgrades), decorative (a 1% burn on 0.011% of emission) or unmotivated (a score nobody wants), which is why the arithmetic misses by four orders of magnitude. If every factory burns a basket of other goods every hour to keep producing, then C scales 1:1 with E by construction, demand exists for structural reasons rather than because a designer hopes players want a leaderboard, every player is a permanent buyer proportional to their own output, and cartels lose their grip because a cartel that starves its customers starves its own input supply. Then rewrite the 3:00 first-session line — it is the single most expensive sentence in this document — and ship the closed-economy MVP exactly as scoped, with the weekly E-versus-C ratio instrumented from day one as the only metric that decides whether real money ever gets switched on.

name: Dead Drop
pitch: Everyone can see every account and every transfer, forever — so hide 5 dollars in plain sight for 24 hours while 200 strangers try to trace it back to you.
coreLoop: You buy in for 5 USDC. The program takes 5% and puts 4.75 into vaults you control. A vault must hold at least 0.20 USDC, so you can spread across at most 23 of them. Hiding phase (hours 0-6): you submit hop transactions moving value between your vaults. Hops do not execute individually — they queue into 5-minute BATCHES, and at batch close every input in that batch is pooled and every output paid, with the input-to-output mapping stored as a hash commitment, not published. The batch's live participant count is public on screen: 'batch closes in 1:47 — 37 players queued.' Moving alone in a quiet batch means your route is trivially readable; moving inside a crowd of 37 buys you an anonymity set of 37. So the 30-second loop is: watch the traffic gauge, decide whether the crowd is thick enough, commit, and watch your own balances scatter into a graph you can no longer fully explain to yourself. Seeking phase (hours 6-22): claim(vault, asserted_origin_seat) costs 0.25 USDC. Right, you take 60% of that vault and the owner keeps 40%. Wrong, your 0.25 goes to the vault's real owner as a counter-surveillance bounty. Balances are quantized to a 0.20/0.40/0.80/1.60 ladder so amounts carry no fingerprint. Settlement (hours 22-24): every commitment is revealed, every mapping published permanently, every vault closed and its rent refunded. The finished round becomes a fully solved public puzzle that next week's players study — the corpus of old rounds is the game's tutorial and its metagame at the same time.
whyOnChain: This is not portable. The board is a real public ledger where account creation costs a published, non-negotiable amount, balances are readable by anyone including non-players, history is permanent, and pseudonymous identity is cheap but not free. The tension is that surveillance is TOTAL and obfuscation is priced in real money at rates you did not set. A Web2 version means the server tells you what you can see, which means the server is lying to you for balance reasons, which destroys the only thing that makes it interesting: that nobody is protecting you and nobody is hiding anything on your behalf. The cost model is also inherited, not invented — the reason you can only hold 23 vaults is rent exemption plus a minimum balance, not a designer's cap.
solanaPrimitives: L1 PDAs per vault — rent-exemption deposit ~6,960 lamports/byte, ~0.002 SOL per small account, fully refunded on close; the refundable deposit IS the game's capital constraint
Per-writable-account local fee markets — vaults are sharded per player so a 256-player round never touches a hot global account or the 12M CU/writable-account/block ceiling
5,000 lamports/signature base fee — hops cost ~$0.0004, so the binding constraint is deliberately capital, not gas
Kora fee relayer (Solana Foundation, shipped Apr 2026) — players pay all fees in USDC and never hold SOL
MagicBlock Cranks — phase transitions (hide → seek → reveal → settle) and the 5-minute batch close fire on-chain with no operator in the loop
Helius/Triton Yellowstone gRPC + DAS API — powers the in-client transaction-graph view; also the exact tooling a player's own solver bot would use, which is the point
Metaplex Core (mpl-core 1.10.0, ~0.0029 SOL/asset) — a 'Case File' asset minted at settlement recording who traced whom
Solana Attestation Service — one buy-in per attested identity, since multi-accounting is the obvious exploit
Anchor 1.1.2 (@anchor-lang/core) with Surfpool + LiteSVM tests and Mollusk CU benchmarking in CI
moneyFlow: Value enters only as a 5 USDC buy-in. 5% (0.25) is the house rake and the only studio revenue — no token, no emissions, no treasury. The remaining 4.75 is redistributed strictly between players: seekers take 60% of vaults they correctly trace, and wrong claims pay 0.25 to the traced player. Sinks: the 5% rake, ~0.000005 SOL per hop burned/paid to validators (50% of base fee burned), and temporary rent lockup that is returned at settlement. Value exits only at settlement, and only back to the wallet that bought in or to the wallet that won it. Critically, the program NEVER transfers a player's value to a third-party address of their choosing — vaults are program-owned PDAs, movement is program-mediated, and settlement destinations are fixed at buy-in. That is a deliberate compliance boundary: the mechanic is shaped like a mixer, so the money must be structurally incapable of mixing between persons. At 3,000 players/day at 5 USDC that is 750 USDC/day gross — this is an indie business, and should be budgeted as one.
firstSession: 0:00 Land on the site. 'Sign in with Google' creates a Privy embedded wallet; no seed phrase, no extension, no SOL. 0:30 Deposit 5 USDC, or claim a studio-funded 1 USDC trial stake for your first round (~$1 CAC, capped per attested identity). 1:00 Tutorial is a FINISHED round from last week, rendered as an animated graph with the answers hidden. You get 3 free practice claims against real historical data. 2:20 Your first correct trace: the route lights up hop by hop across six vaults and two batches, and the game shows you the tell you actually used — a hop made alone in a batch of 2. 3:00 You are dropped into the live round. Your 4.75 USDC is sitting in one fat, obvious vault; a countdown reads 'next batch closes in 1:47 — 22 players queued'; a gauge shows traffic rising. You split into 6 vaults and commit into the crowd. Total elapsed 3 minutes, one signature prompt (the buy-in), zero SOL touched.
viralMechanic: Two structural hooks, both mechanical rather than promotional. First, PASS-THROUGH: you may route a hop through another player's vault, but only if they accept with one transaction. A hop that terminates in someone else's account is the single strongest ambiguity you can buy, and it is impossible to buy alone. A lone player's hops are isolable; a player with six accomplices is not. So your defense literally scales with how many people you drag in, and crews form because crews are load-bearing, not because of a referral bonus. Second, the settlement reveal is a public accusation. Every round publishes a permanent Case File naming who traced whom, with the graph attached. Being cracked by a named rival, publicly, with a shareable diagram of exactly how you were sloppy, is the thing people post — and the thing that makes them come back to the next round with a grudge.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks, one Anchor 1.1.2 program (~700 lines): vault PDA create/hop/close, batch commit-reveal, claim resolution, settlement. Tests in LiteSVM, CU benchmarks in Mollusk, local runs on Surfpool. Web client on @solana/kit 7.1.1 with a graph view fed by a thin indexer over Helius RPC. Scope: ONE 24-hour round, 64 players, 5 USDC, mainnet, quantized balance ladder, Kora for gasless USDC fees. IN: batching, anonymity-set gauge, claims, settlement reveal, the solved-round replay viewer (it is the tutorial, it is not optional). CUT: pass-through routing, Private ERs, Core Case File assets, Solana Attestation Service, mobile, seasons, ranked ladder, any leaderboard beyond a single results table. If 64 people do not spend the full 6 hours arguing about batch timing, the pass-through and season layers will not save it.
biggestRisk: Two, and they are different kinds of fatal. The design killer: this is a public, deterministic, fully-logged puzzle, so someone will publish an open-source solver within two rounds. Amount quantization kills the obvious fingerprint, but timing correlation, batch co-membership across rounds, and funding-source clustering may still be enough to make hiding unwinnable — at which point the game is a bot fee farm and dies in a week. This is testable before writing the client: simulate 10,000 rounds and try to break your own scheme. If a solver hits above ~40% attribution, there is no game. The existence killer: the product is shaped exactly like a mixer, and it takes real money from consumers with both skill and chance present. Structurally the funds cannot move between persons except as game outcomes, which is a real and defensible distinction — but it is a distinction a regulator has to accept, in a 2026 environment where Louisiana and Oklahoma statutes reach suppliers, geolocation vendors and promoters personally, and 50 AGs have asked DOJ to prioritize offshore gambling enforcement. Geofence hard, get a gaming/money-transmission opinion before the first mainnet round, and expect to be misread as a laundering tool regardless of how the accounts are actually wired.

critique.name: Dead Drop
technicalBlockers: THE QUANTIZATION LADDER IS ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE. Every rung (0.20/0.40/0.80/1.60) is a multiple of 0.20. Any sum of them is a multiple of 0.20. The player's balance is 4.75 USDC. 4.75/0.20 = 23.75 — not an integer. A player's holdings can NEVER sum to 4.75 on the ladder. The design's own '23 vaults' number is 4.75/0.20 floored, leaving a 0.15 remainder that is off-ladder by construction. Either conservation breaks or every player carries an identical off-ladder dust vault, and the count of off-ladder vaults is exactly the live player count — a free headcount oracle for every solver. This is not a rounding nit; the core state invariant does not close.

THE ADVERTISED ANONYMITY SET EXCEEDS SOLANA'S TRANSACTION LIMITS. A batch of 37 players averaging 4 hops = ~148 transfers = ~296 writable account locks. Solana's hard cap is 64 account locks per transaction (ALT-resolved), and the tx is 1,232 bytes. CU is not the binding constraint (148 SPL transfers ≈ 666k CU, under the 1.4M/tx ceiling) — account locks are. A 37-player batch close therefore requires 6–15 NON-ATOMIC transactions. The partition of the batch across those txs, and their landing order, is public and permanently recorded. The effective anonymity set is not 37; it is the ~8–16 hops that share a settlement transaction. The gauge on screen — the single UI element the entire 30-second loop is built around — displays a number the protocol cannot deliver.

RENT IS ~40x LARGER THAN THE DESIGN ACCOUNTS FOR, AND KORA DOES NOT COVER IT. If vaults hold real USDC they must be SPL token accounts: 165 bytes → 0.00204 SOL → $0.163 at SOL=$80. 23 vaults = $3.75 against a $5.00 buy-in — 75% of the stake locked as rent. Even with 16-byte ledger PDAs ((16+128)×6,960 = 0.001 SOL = $0.08 each), 24 accounts = $1.92, or 38% of the buy-in. Kora sponsors transaction FEES; rent-exemption is a capital deposit, not a fee. Someone must front it. At the stated 3,000 players/day on a 24-hour round, steady-state locked float is 3,000 × 24 × 0.00204 = 147 SOL ≈ $11,750 — 15.7 days of gross revenue, denominated in SOL, stranded if a settlement crank fails.

THE STATED DERIVATION OF THE 23-VAULT CAP IS FALSE. The pitch claims the cap comes from 'rent exemption plus a minimum balance' and that 'the cost model is inherited, not invented.' 23 = floor(4.75/0.20) — it is derived entirely from a designer-chosen 0.20 minimum and contains no rent term whatsoever. The one claim that makes this concept crypto-native rather than a skin is arithmetically not true.

A SINGLE-LEDGER ARCHITECTURE FIXES THE TX LIMIT BUT DESTROYS THE PREMISE. Batching 1,472 vault entries into one 35KB program account settles atomically in one tx and stays far under the 12M CU/writable-account/block cap at one batch per 5 minutes. But then vaults are not accounts, rent is not the constraint, balances are not readable by non-players as token balances, and 'the board is a real public ledger where account creation costs a published, non-negotiable amount' is no longer true. The only architecture that works is the one that invalidates the design thesis.
economicHoles: THE CLAIM PRICE EXCEEDS THE MAXIMUM PAYOUT ON HALF THE LADDER, WHICH DELETES THE GAME. A claim costs 0.25 USDC and pays 60% of the vault. A 0.20 vault pays 0.12. A 0.40 vault pays 0.24. Both are below the 0.25 cost AT 100% ACCURACY. Break-even accuracy (crediting the 0.25 back on a correct claim): 0.20 vault → p>67.6%; 0.40 → p>51%; 0.80 → p>34.2%; 1.60 → p>20.7%. Without the credit: 0.20 → p>208%, 0.40 → p>104%. Therefore the dominant strategy is: split into 23 × 0.20 vaults on turn one and never hop again. You are then mathematically unclaimable at a profit regardless of whether every seeker knows exactly which vaults are yours. Anonymity is irrelevant when the bounty is capped below the ticket price. The Nash equilibrium of Dead Drop is to not play Dead Drop — one transaction, then six hours of nothing.

THE PASSIVE STRATEGY IS ALSO THE MAX-EV STRATEGY, MAKING THE GAME STRICTLY NEGATIVE-SUM WITH NO REASON TO ENGAGE. Total value is fixed at 4.75/player after rake. Claims are the only redistribution. A passive minimum-splitter loses exactly the 5% rake (-0.25) and nothing else. Every active player loses the rake PLUS negative-EV claim spend. So the risk-minimizing line is also the highest-EV line, and it involves zero interaction with the batch gauge, the crowd, the hop timing, or the metagame. The designer's stated failure threshold — 'if a solver hits above ~40% attribution, there is no game' — is the wrong test: the game is already dead at 0% attribution.

THE ANONYMITY SET IS MANUFACTURABLE AND THE MANUFACTURER GETS A PRIVATE EDGE. The 'batch closes in 1:47 — 37 players queued' gauge is the game's only real information signal, and it is an unauthenticated count. One operator running 20 sybil buy-ins ($100) inflates every gauge they touch. Real players see 37 and believe they bought an anonymity set of 37; the sybil operator knows 20 of those are theirs and is solving a 17-way problem, not a 37-way one. Solana Attestation Service is the stated mitigation and is (a) explicitly cut from the MVP and (b) described in your own landscape research as producing 'low-quality attestations [that] are manipulable.'

WRONG-CLAIM PAYOUT DIRECTION IS UNDEFINED AND SELF-DEALABLE. 'Right, you take 60% and the owner keeps 40%' does not say where the 0.25 goes on a CORRECT claim. If it is refunded, two accounts you control can shuttle value between themselves at zero cost via correct self-claims, which is a free, program-blessed, non-attributable transfer channel between two addresses — precisely the capability the compliance section swears cannot exist. If it is burned or raked, the rule is fine but it is not written down. Undefined settlement rules on a money game are exploit surface, not TBD.

UNIT ECONOMICS ARE INVERTED AT THE STATED CAC. Gross margin per player-round is 0.25 USDC. The stated acquisition offer is a $1 studio-funded trial stake. A player must complete FOUR full rounds just to repay their own trial stake, before Helius ($499–999/mo plus LaserStream $500–6,000/mo for the graph view that IS the client), before the SOL float, before the mandatory gaming/MTL opinion. At 3,000 players/day — an aggressive assumption for a category where 93% of titles are dead — gross is $273k/year. The compliance opinion alone is a meaningful fraction of that.
legalFlags: 18 U.S.C. §1960 / UNLICENSED MONEY TRANSMITTING. This is the flag that ends it. Roman Storm was convicted 6 Aug 2025 on conspiracy to operate an unlicensed money transmitting business for shipping Tornado Cash; DOJ requested an October 2026 retrial on the deadlocked counts and he remains under a five-year statutory maximum. Samourai's founders pled guilty. FinCEN's 2019 guidance treats anonymizing service providers as money transmitters. The stated defense — 'the program NEVER transfers a player's value to a third-party address of their choosing' — is contradicted by the design's own rules three times over: a correct claim moves 60% of a stranger's balance to the seeker, a wrong claim moves 0.25 to a stranger, and PASS-THROUGH ROUTING is explicitly value moving through another person's account with their consent. That last mechanic is a two-party CoinJoin with a game skin. Value demonstrably moves between persons through an obfuscation layer at user direction.

WILLFULNESS IS PRE-WRITTEN INTO THE MARKETING. 'Hide $5 in plain sight,' 'counter-surveillance bounty,' 'a graph you can no longer fully explain to yourself,' 'the mechanic is shaped like a mixer.' The concept document itself states the product is shaped like a mixer and then argues it should not be treated as one. In a §1960 prosecution, that paragraph is the government's exhibit, not the defense's.

ILLEGAL GAMBLING BUSINESS, 18 U.S.C. §1955 + STATE LAW. Consideration (5 USDC), prize (other players' money), and chance (batch composition, opponent behavior, opponent solver quality) are all present, with the operator taking a 5% rake on peer-to-peer stakes. §1955 attaches at five or more persons, 30 days of operation, or $2,000 in a single day — all trivially met at 64 players. Roughly ten states apply an 'any chance' rather than 'predominant purpose' test. Your own landscape research flags that Louisiana and Oklahoma statutes now reach suppliers, geolocation vendors and promoters personally, and that 50 AGs asked DOJ to prioritize offshore enforcement.

BSA/AML AND OFAC AS A PRACTICAL MATTER. Accepting USDC from pseudonymous wallets, obfuscating the linkage, and paying out to different wallets is the fact pattern that triggers SAR/KYC obligations if you are found to be a money transmitter — and Circle can and does freeze USDC in program-owned accounts, which would strand an entire live round mid-hide-phase with no recovery path in your state machine.

GDPR / EDPB. The permanent settlement reveal publishes a transaction graph linking pseudonymous identities. EDPB Guidelines 02/2025 (v2.0 adopted 7 July 2026) hold that technical impossibility does not excuse non-compliance with erasure, and recommend not registering cleartext, encrypted, or hashed personal data on-chain.
critique.priorArt: The mechanic exists — as infrastructure, and it was prosecuted. Tornado Cash (Storm convicted Aug 2025 under §1960, retrial sought Oct 2026), Samourai Wallet (guilty pleas), Wasabi/CoinJoin. The de-anonymization side is a mature academic field, not an open question: Maurer et al.'s 2017 knapsack-mixing work, cluster-intersection attacks that link mixed coins back to originating address clusters because outputs mixed in different transactions are later spent together (exactly the pattern your settlement phase creates), and BlockSci-class tooling. Subset-sum on a naive large CoinJoin is exponential — but your instance is not large: 64 players, 4 denominations, a hard 4.75 per-player sum constraint, and Kora as a single common fee payer across every vault creation. That is a heavily-constrained matching problem, not a hard one. On the GAME side I found no prior art at all, which is itself the signal: dozens of teams have looked at gamifying chain forensics and the compliance surface is visible from orbit. The closest shipped things are puzzle-hunts with on-chain prizes (Satoshi's Treasure, Cipher Hunt) — which take no consideration and redistribute nothing between players, which is precisely why they were legal.
critique.suggestedFix: Remove the money. Not reduce it, not geofence it — remove it. Run Dead Drop as free-to-play with a non-cashable point currency and cosmetic monetization, and the §1960 exposure, the §1955 exposure, the BSA obligations, and the OFAC freeze risk all evaporate simultaneously, because there is no value to transmit. This also lets you fix the fatal claim-EV inversion, since claim cost and payout no longer have to be denominated in something a player deposited: pay correct traces from a fixed round prize pool proportional to accuracy rather than from the traced vault, so tracing a 0.20 vault is worth the same as tracing a 1.60 one and 'split into minimums and go idle' stops being the dominant line. Fix the ladder so player totals are exactly representable (make the buy-in 4.80 = 24 × 0.20 rather than 4.75) and settle batches through a single ledger account so a 37-player batch is genuinely atomic. Then run the designer's own solver simulation — 10,000 rounds, adversarial — BEFORE building anything, because a free-to-play version still dies if attribution is easy. Test in this order: solver first (three days, kills it cheapest), equilibrium second, client last.

name: Frontrun
pitch: A 6-minute arena where you must announce your next move to everyone before you make it — and then bid against them for the right to go first.
coreLoop: 6 players, 7x7 grid, 600ms game blocks, 600 blocks per match. Every block you may submit exactly one Intent: MOVE to an adjacent tile, GRAB, or BLOCK a tile. The instant your Intent is received it is PUBLIC to all six players, and it does not execute until the end of the NEXT block. So every action in the game carries a full 600ms window in which your opponents can see precisely what you are about to do and act on it. Each Intent carries a bid, an integer from 0 to your Credit balance. Within a block, Intents resolve in descending bid order. If two Intents contest the same tile, only the higher bid resolves; the loser's Intent fails, their bid is refunded, and they collect 50% of the winner's bid as a REBATE — the other 50% is burned. You start with 300 Credits. Three Relics spawn every 20 blocks by VRF; a successful GRAB is +40 Credits. Final Credit balance is your score. The 30-second loop: read the queue, see that the player to your left has posted 'GRAB relic at (4,3), bid 12', decide in under 600ms whether to outbid at 13, drop a BLOCK on (4,3) instead for cheaper, or let them have it and bank the tempo. And because being outbid PAYS, the deepest move in the game is the bait: post a real Intent you are happy to lose, watch someone burn 40 Credits to beat you, and collect 20 for free. Cancelling a pending Intent costs 50% of the posted bid, burned — so bluffs are not free, and a bluff you get called on is a real hole in your balance. It is Liar's Poker fused with a fighting game's startup frames, and the whole thing is a playable model of a block-builder auction.
whyOnChain: Honest answer: the mechanic itself is buildable in Web2. A server could absolutely show everyone's pending inputs and auction the ordering. What is NOT buildable in Web2 is a version anyone should trust. The entire premise of this game is 'ordering is for sale,' which makes the operator the single most suspicious entity in the room; 'we ran the auction honestly, trust us' is unfalsifiable and every close loss reads as a rigged one. On-chain, every Intent is a signed message from the player, and the hash of each block's ordered Intent log is committed to L1, so any player can prove after the fact that the sequencer reordered them. Caveat, stated plainly: MagicBlock's ER is a trusted low-latency sequencer today — fraud proofs and DA guarantees are not documented publicly — so this gives you DETECTABLE cheating, not PREVENTED cheating. That is still categorically better than the Web2 version, and the ER is also the only thing that makes 600ms verifiable blocks cost approximately nothing (0 SOL base fee per ER transaction).
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock Ephemeral Rollups — ~10ms slots and 64KB transactions; the 600ms game block is a batch of ER slots, and 64KB lets a full ordered Intent log commit inline with no ALT gymnastics

Per-match PDA delegated to the ER, undelegated at match end — shards state per match so 500 concurrent matches never contend on one writable account (0.0003 SOL/session + 0.0001 SOL/commit, so a match settles for well under a cent)
MagicBlock Session Keys (@magicblock-labs/gum-react-sdk) — one signature buys a whole match; 600 blocks of play with zero wallet popups
MagicBlock VRF inside the ER — free, sub-50ms, used for Relic spawn positions so spawn timing cannot be predicted or grinder-farmed
MagicBlock Magic Router — routes gameplay transactions to the ER and settlement to L1 automatically based on delegation state
MagicBlock Cranks — the 600ms block tick fires on-chain, so no off-chain scheduler is trusted with pacing
Pinocchio 0.11.2 for the tick/resolve instruction — hot path runs 600 times a match across every live table; CU is a direct line item, benchmarked with Mollusk 0.15.0 in CI
Kora fee relayer — tournament entries in USDC, no SOL held by players
@solana/kit 7.1.1 with the new React hooks (usePlanTransaction, useSendTransaction)
moneyFlow: Credits are match-internal points. They are not a token, never leave the match, and cannot be bought — 300 in, burned down by contested bids, scored at the end. There is NO game token, deliberately. Value enters two ways only: cosmetic purchases in USDC (board skins, Intent-queue themes, replay badges as Metaplex Core assets), and 2 USDC entries to ranked tournament tables where 6 players make a 12 USDC pot paid 55/25/10 to the top three with 10% to the house. Sinks inside a match: the 50% burn on every contested bid and the 50% burn on every cancel — without them credits inflate, the bait strategy dominates, and late-game bids become meaningless. Sinks outside: the 10% tournament rake and cosmetic spend. The free ladder is the product and the majority of sessions; paid tables are an optional geofenced mode, not the business plan. If the free ladder is not fun, there is no paid table worth playing.
firstSession: 0:00 Web page, click Play. No wallet, no email, no download. A session keypair is generated in-browser and a bot match starts on MagicBlock devnet. 0:20 The tutorial is a single block: one AI Intent sits in the queue reading 'GRAB Relic (4,3) — bid 5', a countdown bar drains over 600ms, and there is one button: 'Outbid — 6'. You click. You get the relic. That is the entire game taught in six seconds. 0:45 Block two teaches the rebate: the AI outbids YOU, and +6 Credits lands in your balance with the label 'you were frontrun — rebate paid'. The 'wait, I get paid when I lose?' moment is the hook, and it happens inside the first minute. 1:10 First full 6-minute match, three humans and three bots, seamlessly mixed. ~3:00 Around block 200 you post your first deliberate bait and someone burns 40 Credits to beat you to a tile you did not want. 7:30 Match ends, results screen offers a replay link. NO wallet is requested until after your third match, and only if you want a ranked ladder rating or a paid table — at which point Privy embedded wallet plus Kora means you still never touch SOL.
viralMechanic: Every match emits a complete, deterministic, publicly replayable Intent tape: 600 blocks of every bid, bluff, cancel and rebate, reconstructible by anyone from the committed logs. The shareable unit is not the match, it is a block — 'block 412' is a three-second clip of a triple outbid ending in someone cancelling for 60 Credits, and it is legible to a spectator in one viewing, which is rare for a strategy game. More structurally, and more uncomfortably: because outbidding pays the loser, a predictable opponent is a revenue stream. Bringing a friend into your table is straightforwardly +EV for you. That is the poker referral engine — extremely effective, and worth naming honestly rather than dressing up. The clean version of it is bot-vs-bot spectating: the intent tape is machine-readable, so bot authors publish their agents, and watching two published agents bid-war over 600 blocks is a genuinely watchable format.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks: 5x5 grid, 4 players, 4-minute (400-block) matches, bots filling every empty seat. One Pinocchio program for the hot path (submit intent, resolve block, resolve conflict, pay rebate, burn) plus a thin Anchor wrapper for match lifecycle and delegation. Per-match PDA delegated to a MagicBlock devnet ER, session keys, in-ER VRF for spawns, cranks driving the tick. Web client on @solana/kit, no wallet required, no money anywhere. IN: the public intent queue, bidding, conflict resolution, rebates, cancel penalty, the 60-second tutorial. CUT: 6 players, relic variety, cosmetics, tournaments, USDC, ranked ladder, replays and the intent-tape viewer (add week 4 — it is the growth feature, not the validation feature), mobile, mainnet. The single question the MVP answers: does a 600ms decision window with a visible opponent queue feel like tension or like noise? If ten playtesters cannot tell you what they were thinking during block 200, stop.
biggestRisk: An automated agent reads the intent queue and counter-bids in 20ms; a human needs 250ms. In ranked play, bots win, and they win in a way that is undetectable and unpatchable — the queue is public by design, so 'reading the queue faster' is not cheating, it is the stated rule. There are only two honest resolutions and they are a real fork in the product. One: lean in, declare it a bot-permitted arena, ship an agent SDK, and accept that the audience is a few thousand engineers rather than a mass game. Two: make the per-block decision strategic rather than reflexive — one intent per player per block, meaningful bid-economy management, information asymmetry about bankrolls — so that reaction speed saturates quickly and reading opponents dominates, the way an RTS decision cycle stays human-scale. I would build for (2) and instrument reaction-time-vs-winrate from the first playtest; if winrate keeps climbing past 150ms reaction time, (2) has failed and the honest move is to pivot to (1) rather than fight it. Secondary risk: the ER is a trusted sequencer with an undocumented failure and fraud-proof story, and this game's entire pitch is ordering integrity — that question needs a direct answer from MagicBlock before a single dollar of entry fee flows through it.

critique.name: Frontrun
technicalBlockers: THE 600ms WINDOW IS BELOW HUMAN CHOICE-REACTION TIME BEFORE NETWORK LATENCY. Simple visual reaction is ~200–250ms. A three-option choice reaction (outbid / block / pass), per Hick's law, is ~350–450ms. Add client render, input, session-key sign, and submit: ~30–50ms. Add RTT to a MagicBlock validator: ~30–60ms intra-region, 150–250ms cross-region. A US player on a US ER node: ~450–500ms of a 600ms window consumed, leaving ~100ms of margin — exactly the regime where reaction-time delta, not strategy, decides outcomes. A São Paulo or Mumbai player against a US-East node: 250ms RTT + 400ms decision = 650ms, which is LONGER THAN THE BLOCK. They cannot legally act at all. The design's own abort condition — 'if winrate keeps climbing past 150ms reaction time, (2) has failed' — is guaranteed to trigger at 600ms by arithmetic, before a single playtest.

THE LAST-MOVER ADVANTAGE IS PURE COLOCATION AND IS UNPATCHABLE UNDER THE STATED RULES. Because bids resolve by VALUE, not arrival order, the only thing timing buys is information. A bot posts at t+595ms having read every intent in the queue. A human must commit by ~t+200ms to be safe. This is not 'reading the queue faster' as a skill — it is a strictly-dominant information asymmetry that scales with proximity to one datacenter. Jito BAM, 92%+ of Solana stake on Jito-Solana, ~70% of non-vote txs as bundles, and 200+ bots competing in the first half-second of a launch are the empirical answer to what happens to a latency-sensitive public auction on this network. You are shipping the retail side of that trade as a consumer product.

THE ORDERING-INTEGRITY PITCH SOLVES A PROBLEM THE GAME DOESN'T HAVE AND FAILS TO SOLVE THE ONE IT DOES. Committing a hash of the ordered intent log proves nothing about reordering, because the ER sequencer both receives the intents AND produces the log it is hashing. To detect reordering you need sequencer-signed receipts issued at submission time with monotonic sequence numbers — a primitive MagicBlock does not document and you did not budget. Worse: intents resolve by bid value, so intra-block ORDER is irrelevant under your own rules. The sequencer's only real levers are CENSORSHIP (dropping a late intent) and BLOCK-BOUNDARY PLACEMENT (pushing an intent into the next block), and neither of those is detectable from a hash of the log the sequencer wrote. The whyOnChain section is load-bearing for the entire concept and it does not hold weight.

PER-BLOCK VERIFIABILITY COSTS 4x THE MAXIMUM RAKE. At 0.0001 SOL per commit and SOL=$80: per-block commits = 600 × 0.0001 = 0.06 SOL = $4.80/match. A 6-player 2 USDC table produces a 12 USDC pot with a 10% rake = $1.20. You are paying $4.80 to earn $1.20. At a 10-block cadence: $0.48/match, or 40% of gross rake, before RPC, staff, or the 0.0003 SOL session fee. At one commit per match: $0.032/match — affordable, and the ordering proof is gone, which was the whole argument for being on-chain. There is no cadence at which both the pitch and the P&L survive.

FREE-LADDER COGS IS NOT ZERO. The design says 'the free ladder is the product and the majority of sessions.' At 0.0003 SOL/session + one commit, a match floors at ~0.0004 SOL = $0.032. 10,000 free matches/day = $320/day = $117k/year of pure cost against $0 revenue. And 500 concurrent matches at 7 txs per 600ms = ~5,800 TPS on a single non-voting ER validator — MagicBlock's own flagship reference, Supersize, is one arena at one tx per ~30ms per player. There is no public evidence of 500 concurrent delegated sessions on one public node, which means a dedicated node at undisclosed enterprise pricing, which means the '0 SOL base fee' economics you costed against do not apply at the scale you need.
economicHoles: LOSING A CONTEST IS ~20x MORE PROFITABLE THAN WINNING IT. THIS IS FATAL TO THE CORE LOOP AND IT IS PURE ARITHMETIC. Per the stated rules: the loser's bid is REFUNDED and they collect 50% of the winner's bid. So a losing contest has zero cost and non-negative payoff. A relic is worth +40 Credits. If A bids 39 and B bids 1: A nets 40 − 39 = +1. B nets 0 + 19.5 = +19.5. Contesting with the minimum legal bid is a RISKLESS FREE OPTION on every tile any opponent wants, available to every player, every block. Every rational player therefore bids 1 on every contested tile and no one ever bids high, so rebates collapse to 0.5 Credits, so the auction layer becomes inert, so the game reduces to 'who is standing nearer the relic.' The bait play the pitch calls 'the deepest move in the game' is in fact the trivially dominant move, costs nothing, and is available to a player who understands nothing. The entire bidding mechanic self-destructs in the first serious playtest.

THE CANCEL PENALTY DOESN'T PRICE ANYTHING AT EQUILIBRIUM. Cancelling costs 50% of the posted bid, burned. Once bids collapse to 1 (see above), a cancel costs 0.5, which rounds to 0 on an integer currency. Bluffs are free to post and free to withdraw. The one mechanism holding the bluff economy together only functions at bid levels the equilibrium eliminates.

THE SCOREBOARD IGNORES THE AUCTION ENTIRELY. Credit supply: 6 × 300 = 1,800 starting, plus 3 relics per 20 blocks × 30 spawns × 40 = 3,600 injected, versus burns that only occur on contests. With contests collapsed to minimum bids, burns are ~0 and final Credit balance ≈ 300 + 40 × (relics grabbed). 'Final Credit balance is your score' therefore means 'relic count is your score.' The auction contributes nothing to the ranking it is supposed to determine.

COLLUSION IS CORRECTLY DISINCENTIVIZED — CREDIT WHERE DUE. Two colluding players moving value via a deliberate loss burn 50% of the transfer, so pair-wise collusion is -50% EV. This one piece of the economy is well-designed and should survive whatever redesign follows.

THE VIRAL MECHANIC IS HONESTLY LABELED AND STILL A PROBLEM. 'A predictable opponent is a revenue stream... bringing a friend into your table is straightforwardly +EV for you' is the poker affiliate model, and the pitch says so. On a free ladder it is harmless. The moment 2 USDC tables exist, you have built a recruitment incentive for experienced players to seat inexperienced friends against them for money, which is the exact fact pattern gaming regulators use to distinguish a game from a proposition. Keep them structurally separate or don't ship the paid tables.

TRADEABLE COSMETICS REINTRODUCE THE PRIZE ELEMENT. Metaplex Core 'replay badges' earned through play and resellable on a secondary market convert an achievement into a cash-out path. That is the mechanism by which several 2025–26 'no-gambling, cosmetics-only' products were reclassified. If badges are earned, make them soulbound (Bubblegum V2 supports it); if they are tradeable, make them purchased-only.
legalFlags: The free ladder plus purchased cosmetics is genuinely clean and this is the least legally exposed of the three concepts. The 2 USDC entry / 12 USDC pot / 10% rake tables are a real-money peer contest with a house cut, which needs geofencing (the standard skill-gaming exclusions), and in the ~10 'any chance' states the VRF relic spawns are a chance element materially affecting outcomes — that is a weaker skill argument than poker's, not a stronger one.
NY and FL prize-promotion registration/bonding attaches above $5,000 in aggregate prizes; a ladder with tournaments will cross that faster than expected.
Earned-and-tradeable cosmetic assets create a cash-out path from gameplay and can convert 'cosmetics-only' into 'prize.' Soulbind anything earned.
No securities exposure — the deliberate decision to ship no token is correct and is the single best judgment call across all three concepts.
critique.priorArt: Directly tried, and the outcome is documented. 0xMonaco (Paradigm CTF, 2022) is the same idea: an on-chain PvP game where actions are bought through a gradual Dutch auction with prices floating exponentially on short-term demand. It ran 24 hours, competitors were smart contracts written by teams, and the finish was OpenSea, JustLurking and one other trading the lead in the final races. It was excellent — as a developer competition. It was never a consumer game and was never revived as one, which is the finding. Dark Forest is the second data point: v0.4 was won by two players who 'built out a powerful suite of mods, automations, and mining tools to dominate the universe' — the canonical outcome for any on-chain game with fully public state. The third and most damning is that the real version already exists and is a professional market: Jito BAM lets searchers bid for specific block positions, 92%+ of Solana stake runs Jito-Solana, bundles are ~70% of non-vote transactions, and 200+ bots contest the first half-second of any launch. You are not building a playable model of a block-builder auction; you are building an amateur bracket next to a professional one, and the professionals can enter it.
critique.suggestedFix: Change the auction to ALL-PAY and lengthen the block to 2,000ms. All-pay (every bidder forfeits their bid, only the top bid wins the tile) is a one-line change that fixes the fatal hole outright: losing a contest becomes costly rather than a free-roll, bluffing is priced without needing a cancel penalty, credits deflate on their own, and the read-your-opponent depth the pitch wants actually emerges because a failed bluff burns real resource. Then move the block from 600ms to ~2,000ms. At 2,000ms a human has ~1,500ms of thinking time after network latency, geography stops determining winrate, reaction speed saturates almost immediately, and the last-mover bot edge shrinks from decisive to marginal — which is the difference between the author's Option 2 being a hope and being a consequence. A 2s block also lets you commit every block for 0.0001 SOL × 180 blocks per 6-min match = $1.44, still too much, so pair it with committing only signed player intents (not the sequencer's log) and drop the ordering-proof claim from the pitch entirely — the honest on-chain argument here is verifiable non-custodial escrow of entry fees and portable replay data, not sequencer integrity you cannot actually prove. Ship the MVP exactly as scoped otherwise: devnet, bots, no wallet, no money. It is the cheapest and best-designed validation plan on this page.

name: Rap Sheet
pitch: A bluffing game where the cards in your hand are true, verifiable facts about your actual wallet's past — and every lie you get caught in tells the table a little more about who you really are.
coreLoop: 5 players, ~12 minutes, ~9 hands. At the start of a 6-week season you register a SEAT: a fresh pseudonymous identity bound to a real wallet of yours with at least 180 days of history. Opponents see the Seat. They never see the wallet. The binding lives inside a TEE-backed Private ER; the program can evaluate predicates about your wallet, nobody at the table can read which wallet it is. Your Rap Sheet is 7 Claims drawn from ~120 predicate types evaluated against your bound wallet, each worth points set by measured rarity across all indexed wallets and repriced weekly: 'held through a >60% drawdown' (2), 'interacted with a program that has since been closed' (4), 'minted something in 2021' (6), 'transacted in the same block as a wallet that later did >$1M volume' (9), 'has never once sold at a loss' (11), 'was funded by an exchange that no longer exists' (14). A hand: on your turn you place one Claim face-down on the shared Docket and ANNOUNCE its point value. The value is binding; which Claim it is, is not — you can place a 2 and call it a 14. Any opponent may CHALLENGE the last placement for 0.5 Warrants. The challenged player has 30 seconds to submit a Merkle proof against the season snapshot root on L1. Valid proof: the challenger pays 1 Warrant to the challenged. No valid proof: the liar forfeits the placement and 2 Warrants, AND the predicate they falsely claimed is publicly and permanently attached to their Seat for the rest of the season. That last clause is the whole game. Predicates are fingerprints. After roughly six reveals, a diligent opponent can cross-reference the public chain and work out which wallet your Seat is — and a de-anonymized Seat can be scouted for free before the hand even starts, at which point your bluffs stop working for the remaining 30 games of the season. So the resource you are actually managing is not Warrants or points. It is anonymity, spent one revelation at a time, across six weeks.
whyOnChain: This one genuinely cannot be built anywhere else. It needs a behavioral dataset that is (a) shared by every player, (b) permanent and retroactively unforgeable, (c) readable by every player adversarially, and (d) attached to an identity the player can choose to hide or reveal. There is exactly one such dataset in the world and it is a public blockchain. Web2's nearest analogues — credit reports, Steam libraries, Strava history — are siloed, private, editable, and controlled by the party you would have to trust. More importantly, the anti-inflation mechanism is a property of the chain, not a design choice: you cannot retroactively acquire a 2021 mint, and time is the only input that cannot be farmed. Predicates that CAN be farmed get repriced toward zero automatically as they become common, so farming a predicate destroys the value of the thing farmed. That is a self-balancing supply curve you get for free from a timestamped public ledger, and there is no off-chain equivalent.
solanaPrimitives: MagicBlock Private ERs (TEE-backed) — hold the Seat-to-wallet binding and the face-down Docket; the point of the whole game is that hidden information is genuinely hidden rather than server-promised

Concurrent Merkle tree for the season predicate snapshot with the root on L1 (Bubblegum V2 / ZK Compression economics: ~$500 per 1M leaves vs $15-30k for individual accounts) — at 50k seats x 120 predicates that is 6M leaves for low four figures per season

Merkle-proof-of-claim on challenge — non-holders literally cannot produce a proof, so the burden of proof sits with the accused and verification costs one cheap instruction rather than an oracle round trip
Bubblegum V2 SOULBOUND compressed NFTs — permanent 'Perjury' marks and season titles that cannot be sold or laundered off your Seat; soulbound is a V2 feature and this is exactly what it is for
DAS API + Yellowstone gRPC (Helius/Triton) — the predicate indexer that computes 120 predicates per bound wallet and rebuilds the season tree
Solana Attestation Service — one Seat per attested human; multi-seating to launder a burnt identity is the obvious exploit
Metaplex Core (mpl-core 1.10.0) — tradeable table cosmetics, the actual monetization
Kora fee relayer + Mobile Wallet Adapter 2.3.0 — Seat registration and challenges are gasless, and on Android the sign-in is a Seed Vault fingerprint tap
MagicBlock Cranks for season rollover and weekly rarity repricing
moneyFlow: NO token, and by default no cash-out at all. Warrants are a non-cashable soft currency: 30 free per day, refilled by daily play, additionally granted with cosmetic purchases. Value enters only as USDC or card payments for Seat cosmetics, table skins, and a season pass; that is 100% of studio revenue and there is nothing for a player to withdraw. Sinks: Warrants are consumed by challenges (0.5 to challenge, 2 forfeited when caught lying) and by season reset. This is deliberate. Of the three concepts here this is the one that is structurally a poker table, and every 2026 signal says do not take real-money rake on a bluffing game against consumers — eight-plus US states now criminalize dual-currency casino-style products, Louisiana and Oklahoma extend liability to suppliers and promoters, and the PrizePicks precedent is that regulators look at what the product functionally IS. Free-to-play with cosmetic monetization removes the prize element entirely and removes the gambling analysis with it. A 2 USDC cash table is a later, geofenced, counsel-gated option, not a launch feature and not the plan.
firstSession: 0:00 Open the site or the Solana dApp Store build. 'Connect the wallet you actually use' — signature only, no transaction, no SOL, nothing on-chain yet. On Android this is one Seed Vault fingerprint tap via Mobile Wallet Adapter. 0:20 The hook, before any gameplay: the app shows your Rap Sheet — seven true, sourced, mildly invasive things the chain knows about you, each with a link to the transaction that proves it. 'You have never sold at a loss. You have also never sold.' 'You were in the same block as a wallet that went on to do $4.1M in volume, eleven months before it did.' This is shareable and self-contained and it arrives 20 seconds in. 1:30 First table: you plus four bots. Hand one, you place a 6 you genuinely hold, a bot challenges, your proof resolves in under a second, you take a Warrant. Hand two, you place a 2 and announce 14; nobody calls; you take the hand and feel like a criminal. That is the complete rule set learned in three minutes with zero on-chain writes. 4:00 Seat registration is offered — one gasless transaction paid by Kora, and the season clock starts.
viralMechanic: The Rap Sheet reveal is a personality quiz whose answers happen to be true, verifiable, and occasionally humiliating, and it exists BEFORE the player has played a hand — so the share happens at the top of the funnel rather than at the end. Every card links to the transaction that proves it, which makes it un-fakeable and therefore worth posting. Structurally, the deeper loop is de-anonymization: cross-referencing revealed predicates against the public chain is much easier when you have a prior on who the person is, so importing addresses you already know gives you a genuine competitive edge, and the most satisfying win in the game is unmasking a rival Seat as someone you actually know. Players recruit friends because friends are easier to unmask and funnier to unmask. Perjury marks are permanent, public, and mockable, which gives the community a shared vocabulary of ongoing grudges across a six-week season.
mvpScope: 2-4 weeks: an indexer computing 20 predicate types over Helius DAS and RPC history, a season snapshot published as a single on-chain Merkle root, one Anchor 1.1.2 program for table lifecycle, placement, challenge, and proof verification, five-player tables filled with bots, free Warrants only, web only. Hidden state in v1 is server-held with on-chain hash commitments — an honest, stated tradeoff, not a Private ER. IN: the Rap Sheet reveal screen (it is the marketing and the retention hook, it ships first), place/announce/challenge/prove, the permanent reveal of caught lies. CUT: Private ERs, ZK-compressed trees, soulbound Perjury cNFTs, seasons, Solana Attestation Service, cosmetics, mobile, cash tables, all 120 predicates. And before writing ANY game code, spend three days generating Rap Sheets for 10,000 random real mainnet wallets and read them. If they are boring, everything downstream is boring, and you have spent three days instead of four weeks finding out.
biggestRisk: Most wallets are boring. The median mainnet address is three swaps, a failed mint, and a dust airdrop. If 70% of players draw a hand of 2-pointers, there is no texture to bluff with, the rarity curve collapses, and the game is a shrug. This is the risk that kills it and it is also the cheapest one on this page to test — generate ten thousand real rap sheets before building anything and see whether they are funny. Related and nearly as dangerous: new wallets structurally hold worse hands than old ones, which is a pay-to-have-been-early dynamic that will read as unfair no matter how the brackets are drawn; the mitigation is bluff-driven scoring where a weak hand can still take a table, plus separate Fresh Wallet brackets, and neither is guaranteed to be enough. Third: a meaningful fraction of players will find having their financial history read back to them by a game invasive rather than delightful, and that reaction is not fixable with copy — it needs explicit opt-in per predicate category, and accepting that some people will bounce at the reveal screen on principle. Fourth, quieter: the entire hidden-information layer depends on TEE-backed Private ERs whose trust model is not publicly documented, and this game leaks a real person's identity if that seal breaks.

critique.name: Rap Sheet
technicalBlockers: THE PREDICATE INDEXER IS A DATA-WAREHOUSE PROJECT, NOT A SERVICE CALL. 'Transacted in the same block as a wallet that later did >$1M volume' is a full block-level self-join across all Solana history, evaluated for 50,000 bound wallets, rebuilt weekly. Solana passed 87M daily transactions in Q1 2026 — that is ~30B transactions/year, multi-petabyte at the archival level. Helius and Triton sell DAS and streaming, not arbitrary historical joins; LaserStream is $500–$6,000/mo per your own landscape research and only covers the live tail. Realistically this is a $5k–$30k/month warehouse line item with a dedicated data engineer, running against a free-to-play cosmetics game with no token and nothing for a player to withdraw. The fixed cost is heavy and the revenue is the thinnest in consumer software.

THE MERKLE TREE SPEC IS DECORATIVE. Bubblegum V2 / ZK Compression at '~$500 per 1M leaves' is cNFT minting economics. A season snapshot only needs a 32-byte root in one L1 account — cost is effectively zero, and proof verification is 23 sha256 syscalls at ~2,500–6,000 CU for a 6M-leaf tree. You have budgeted low four figures per season for something free. Minor, but it indicates the primitive list was assembled for plausibility rather than from the requirement.

THE PROOF BARELY FITS AN L1 TRANSACTION. A depth-23 Merkle path is 23 × 32 = 736 bytes, plus leaf, accounts, and instruction overhead ≈ 850–900 bytes against the 1,232-byte limit. It fits with nothing to spare and no batching headroom. Fine inside the ER (64KB) but it means challenge resolution is structurally ER-only, which hard-couples the game's fairness to the ER's undocumented liveness.

THE PRIVATE ER IS LOAD-BEARING FOR A REAL PERSON'S SAFETY AND ITS TRUST MODEL IS UNDOCUMENTED. Your own landscape research lists the ER trust model — fraud proofs, data availability, validator-failure recovery — as UNVERIFIED and flags it as a blocking question before shipping player funds. This concept ships something worse than funds through it: the Seat-to-real-wallet binding for 50,000 people. And the enclave does not actually protect that mapping from the party that matters, because the predicate indexer necessarily sits OUTSIDE the TEE and must know which wallet belongs to which Seat in order to compute its 120 predicates.
economicHoles: THE 'UNFARMABLE' PREDICATES COST UNDER $100. Two of the six examples the pitch uses to sell the rarity curve are cheap to manufacture. (1) 'Transacted in the same block as a wallet that later did >$1M volume' — 9 points. At 400ms slots there are 216,000 slots/day; one 1-signature transaction per slot costs 216,000 × 5,000 lamports = 1.08 SOL = $86/day. Run it a week for ~$600 and you co-occur with essentially every wallet active that week, guaranteeing the predicate against every future whale born in that window. (2) 'Interacted with a program that has since been closed' — 4 points. Deploy a trivial program, touch it, close it and recover the rent: net cost under $0.10, repeatable across unlimited wallets from a single program. A 9-point card for $86 and a 4-point card for a dime is not a rarity curve, it is a price list.

'TIME IS THE ONLY INPUT THAT CANNOT BE FARMED' IS FALSE BECAUSE AGED WALLETS ARE A COMMODITY. The 2021–2024 airdrop-farming industry manufactured millions of aged, historied, behaviorally-rich wallets and they trade OTC. The 180-day binding requirement filters out casual multi-accounting and filters in exactly the professional sybil operator who already holds inventory. Weekly rarity repricing lags farming by a week, and a farmer only needs the predicate to be valuable during the season they are playing.
